code: Model <- function(parm, Data)     {     ### Parameters     log_Ne <- parm[seq_len(Data$M)]     Ne <- exp(log_Ne)     tau <- interval(parm[Data$M + 1], 0.01, 10)     parm[Data$M + 1] <- tau     ### Log-Prior: random walk on log-Ne     first.prior <- dnorm(log_Ne[1], 0, 5, log = TRUE)     rw.prior <- 0     for (m in 2:Data$M) {         rw.prior <- rw.prior +             dnorm(log_Ne[m], log_Ne[m - 1], tau, log = TRUE)     }     tau.prior <- dhalfcauchy(tau, 1, log = TRUE)     ### Log-Likelihood     LL <- coal_loglik(Ne, Data$intervals, Data$lineages, Data$groups)     ### Log-Posterior     LP <- LL + first.prior + rw.prior + tau.prior     Modelout <- list(LP=LP, Dev=-2*LL, Monitor=LP,         yhat=rep(LL / Data$N, Data$N), parm=parm)     return(Modelout)     }

code: Model <- function(parm, Data)     {     ### Parameters     beta <- parm[Data$pos.beta]     ### Log-Prior     beta.prior <- sum(dnormv(beta, 0, 1000, log=TRUE))     ### Log-Likelihood Approximation     mu <- as.vector(tcrossprod(Data$X, t(beta)))     epsilon <- Data$y - mu     sigma <- sd(epsilon)     LL <- -sum(abs(epsilon))     ### Log-Posterior Approximation     LP <- LL + beta.prior     Modelout <- list(LP=LP, Dev=-2*LL, Monitor=c(LP,sigma),         yhat=rnorm(length(mu), mu, sigma), parm=parm)     return(Modelout)     }

code: set.seed(42206) N <- 50 J <- 4  #### True parameter values true.beta  <- c(3.0, 1.0, -0.5, 0.8) true.sigma <- 1.0  #### Design matrix with intercept X <- cbind(1, matrix(rnorm(N * (J - 1)), N, J - 1)) for (j in 2:J) X[,j] <- CenterScale(X[,j])  #### Generate response with two outliers mu.true <- as.vector(tcrossprod(X, t(true.beta))) y <- rnorm(N, mu.true, true.sigma) y[6]  <- y[6] + 8   # possible outlier y[8]  <- y[8] + 15  # extreme value  #### Assemble Data list mon.names <- c("LP", as.parm.names(list(InvL=rep(0,N)))) parm.names <- as.parm.names(list(beta=rep(0,J), sigma=0)) pos.beta <- grep("beta", parm.names) pos.sigma <- grep("sigma", parm.names) PGF <- function(Data) {     beta <- rnorm(Data$J)     sigma <- runif(1)     return(c(beta, sigma))     } Data <- list(J=J, N=N, PGF=PGF, X=X, mon.names=mon.names,     parm.names=parm.names, pos.beta=pos.beta, pos.sigma=pos.sigma, y=y)

code: Model <- function(parm, Data)     {     ### Parameters     beta <- parm[Data$pos.beta]     sigma <- interval(parm[Data$pos.sigma], 1e-100, Inf)     parm[Data$pos.sigma] <- sigma     ### Log-Prior     beta.prior <- sum(dnormv(beta, 0, 1000, log=TRUE))     sigma.prior <- dhalfcauchy(sigma, 25, log=TRUE)     ### Log-Likelihood     mu <- tcrossprod(Data$X, t(beta))     LL <- dnorm(Data$y, mu, sigma, log=TRUE)     InvL <- 1 / exp(LL)     LL <- sum(LL)     ### Log-Posterior     LP <- LL + beta.prior + sigma.prior     Modelout <- list(LP=LP, Dev=-2*LL, Monitor=c(LP,InvL),         yhat=rnorm(length(mu), mu, sigma), parm=parm)     return(Modelout)     }

title: Approximate Bayesian Computation in lucifer
text: Standard Bayesian inference requires evaluating likelihood function \(p(y \mid \theta)\) every proposed parameter value. many complex models, particularly population genetics, ecology, epidemiology, agent-based modeling, likelihood either analytically intractable computationally prohibitive evaluate, even though simulating data model straightforward. Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC) circumvents barrier replacing likelihood evaluation simulation: parameters proposed, synthetic data generated model, proposal accepted simulated data “close enough” observed data according distance metric summary statistics [1]. trade-explicit: ABC produces samples approximate posterior \(p_\varepsilon(\theta \mid y) \propto p(\theta) \, \Pr(\rho(S(y_\text{sim}), S(y_\text{obs})) \leq \varepsilon)\) rather exact posterior, \(\rho\) distance function, \(S\) computes summary statistics, \(\varepsilon\) tolerance. \(\varepsilon \0\) summary statistics become sufficient, approximate posterior converges exact posterior; practice, quality approximation depends critically choice summary statistics tolerance threshold. ABC() function lucifer implements four ABC algorithms: rejection sampling, MCMC-ABC [2], SMC-ABC [3], [4], Simulated Annealing ABC (SA-ABC) [9]. Unlike inference functions package, ABC() uses different model specification model function returns simulated data rather log-posterior.

what: Inferring the mean and variance of a normal distribution
title: Approximate Bayesian Computation in lucifer
text: example demonstrates three ABC methods simple problem posterior analytically available. model simulates normal data, summary statistics sample mean standard deviation.
code: library(lucifer)  # Simulator: returns a vector of simulated data # sigma <= 0 produces extreme data, so proposals with invalid sigma # are automatically rejected by the distance criterion Simulator <- function(parm, Data) {   mu <- parm[1]   sigma <- parm[2]   if (sigma <= 0) return(rep(1e10, Data$n))   rnorm(Data$n, mu, sigma) }  # Prior: mu ~ N(0, 10), sigma ~ Half-Cauchy(0, 5) Prior <- function() {   c(rnorm(1, 0, 10), abs(rcauchy(1, 0, 5))) }  # Summary statistics: mean and SD Summary.Stats <- function(data) {   c(mean(data), sd(data)) }  # Observed data set.seed(42) obs_data <- rnorm(100, mean = 3, sd = 1.5) Observed.Stats <- Summary.Stats(obs_data)  Data <- list(n = 100, parm.names = c("mu", "sigma"))

code: # MA(2) simulator MA2_sim <- function(parm, Data) {   theta1 <- parm[1]   theta2 <- parm[2]   n <- Data$n   e <- rnorm(n + 2)   y <- numeric(n)   for (t in 1:n) {     y[t] <- e[t + 2] + theta1 * e[t + 1] + theta2 * e[t]   }   y }  # Prior: uniform on the invertibility triangle MA2_prior <- function() {   repeat {     theta <- runif(2, -2, 2)     # Invertibility constraints: theta2 + theta1 > -1,     # theta2 - theta1 > -1, |theta2| < 1     if (theta[2] + theta[1] > -1 &&         theta[2] - theta[1] > -1 &&         abs(theta[2]) < 1) return(theta)   } }  # Summary: autocovariances at lags 1, 2 MA2_stats <- function(y) {   n <- length(y)   ybar <- mean(y)   g1 <- sum((y[-1] - ybar) * (y[-n] - ybar)) / n   g2 <- sum((y[-(1:2)] - ybar) * (y[-((n-1):n)] - ybar)) / n   c(g1, g2) }  # True parameters: theta1 = 0.6, theta2 = 0.2 set.seed(42) obs_y <- MA2_sim(c(0.6, 0.2),                  list(n = 500)) obs_stats <- MA2_stats(obs_y) MA2_Data <- list(n = 500,                  parm.names = c("theta1", "theta2")) ma2_true <- c(theta1 = 0.6, theta2 = 0.2) set.seed(123) fit_ma2_rej <- ABC(MA2_sim, MA2_Data, MA2_prior, MA2_stats, obs_stats,                    Method = "rejection", N = 2000, Status = 10000) set.seed(123) fit_ma2_mcmc <- ABC(MA2_sim, MA2_Data, MA2_prior, MA2_stats, obs_stats,                     Method = "MCMC", MCMC.iterations = 10000,                     Covar = diag(c(0.1, 0.1)), Status = 5000) set.seed(123) fit_ma2_smc <- ABC(MA2_sim, MA2_Data, MA2_prior, MA2_stats, obs_stats,                    Method = "SMC", N = 2000, Status = 100) set.seed(123) fit_ma2_sa <- ABC(MA2_sim, MA2_Data, MA2_prior, MA2_stats, obs_stats,                   Method = "SA", SA.iterations = 5000, Status = 1000) plot(fit_ma2_rej, type = "posterior", true_values = ma2_true) plot(fit_ma2_mcmc, type = "posterior", true_values = ma2_true) plot(fit_ma2_smc, type = "posterior", true_values = ma2_true) plot(fit_ma2_sa, type = "posterior", true_values = ma2_true) # Apply burn-in for MCMC (discard first 20%) ma2_mcmc_burn <- floor(0.2 * nrow(fit_ma2_mcmc$Posterior)) ma2_mcmc_post <- fit_ma2_mcmc$Posterior[(ma2_mcmc_burn + 1):nrow(fit_ma2_mcmc$Posterior), ,                                          drop = FALSE]  # SA: Posterior already contains Phase 2 (sampling phase) only ma2_sa_post <- fit_ma2_sa$Posterior  ma2_comparison <- data.frame(   Method = c("True", "Rejection", "MCMC", "SMC", "SA"),   theta1.mean = c(0.6,                   mean(fit_ma2_rej$Posterior[, "theta1"]),                   mean(ma2_mcmc_post[, "theta1"]),                   mean(fit_ma2_smc$Posterior[, "theta1"]),                   mean(ma2_sa_post[, "theta1"])),   theta1.sd = c(NA,                 sd(fit_ma2_rej$Posterior[, "theta1"]),                 sd(ma2_mcmc_post[, "theta1"]),                 sd(fit_ma2_smc$Posterior[, "theta1"]),                 sd(ma2_sa_post[, "theta1"])),   theta2.mean = c(0.2,                   mean(fit_ma2_rej$Posterior[, "theta2"]),                   mean(ma2_mcmc_post[, "theta2"]),                   mean(fit_ma2_smc$Posterior[, "theta2"]),                   mean(ma2_sa_post[, "theta2"])),   theta2.sd = c(NA,                 sd(fit_ma2_rej$Posterior[, "theta2"]),                 sd(ma2_mcmc_post[, "theta2"]),                 sd(fit_ma2_smc$Posterior[, "theta2"]),                 sd(ma2_sa_post[, "theta2"])),   Accept.rate = c(NA,                   fit_ma2_rej$Acceptance.rate,                   fit_ma2_mcmc$Acceptance.rate,                   fit_ma2_smc$Acceptance.rate,                   fit_ma2_sa$Acceptance.rate),   row.names = NULL ) knitr::kable(ma2_comparison, digits = 3,   caption = "MA(2) posterior estimates across ABC methods.")

what: Why modes matter more than means
title: Bayesian mode inference with lucifer
text: Bayesian inference typically summarizes posterior distributions mean median, practice can dangerously misleading posteriors multimodal. Consider bimodal distribution peaks 0 10: posterior mean 5 falls region near-zero density, representing value data never actually support. decision-theoretic terms, mode (maximum posteriori, MAP) minimizes 0-1 loss, mean minimizes squared-error loss, median minimizes absolute-error loss. goal identify single probable value, mode appropriate point estimate. Multimodal posteriors arise frequently practitioners expect. Mixture models, hierarchical specifications weak identifiability, models discrete latent structures routinely produce posterior surfaces multiple peaks. Detecting characterizing modes essential understanding model behavior, yet software reports means credible intervals, silently averaging qualitatively different posterior regions. problem extends beyond Bayesian inference. empirical distribution, whether posterior sample, dataset economic observations, vector biological measurements, may contain multiple modes reveal distinct subpopulations regimes. Classical tests multimodality (Silverman’s bandwidth test, Hartigan’s dip test) frequentist provide binary reject/fail--reject decisions. Bayesian mode inference, contrast, produces full posterior distribution number location modes, enabling nuanced probabilistic statements.
code: x <- c(rnorm(500, 0, 1), rnorm(500, 10, 1)) m <- Modes(x) dat <- data.frame(x = x) mode_df <- data.frame(xint = m$modes, label = "Mode") mean_df <- data.frame(xint = mean(x), label = "Mean") ggplot2::ggplot(dat, ggplot2::aes(x = x)) +   ggplot2::geom_density(fill = "#4e79a7", alpha = 0.3, color = "#4e79a7",                         linewidth = 0.8) +   ggplot2::geom_vline(data = mean_df, ggplot2::aes(xintercept = xint),                       color = "#e15759", linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +   ggplot2::geom_vline(data = mode_df, ggplot2::aes(xintercept = xint),                       color = "#59a14f", linewidth = 1) +   ggplot2::annotate("text", x = mean(x), y = Inf, label = "Mean",                     vjust = 2, color = "#e15759", fontface = "bold", size = 3.5) +   ggplot2::annotate("text", x = m$modes, y = Inf,                     label = paste0("Mode ", seq_along(m$modes)),                     vjust = 3.5, color = "#59a14f", fontface = "bold", size = 3.5) +   theme_relab() +   ggplot2::labs(x = "Value", y = "Density",                 title = "Bimodal posterior: mean vs. modes",                 subtitle = "The mean (dashed red) falls in a low-density region")

title: Bayesian mode inference with lucifer
text: lucifer provides two primary mode estimation functions. Mode(x) returns single prominent mode using kernel density estimation continuous data frequency counting discrete data. Modes(x) returns detected modes ordered density, relative size (proportion density captures). functions support four estimation methods: kernel density estimation ("kde", default), half-sample mode ("hsm"; [4]), Venter’s mode ("venter"), shortest half-range ("shorth"). half-sample mode particularly robust outliers since recursively selects densest half sample without requiring bandwidth selection. Venter’s mode finds shortest interval containing 50% data returns midpoint, providing different notion centrality. modality testing functions .unimodal(), .bimodal(), .trimodal(), .multimodal() provide quick Boolean assessments:
code: set.seed(42) x <- c(rnorm(400, -2, 0.8), rnorm(300, 3, 1.2), rnorm(300, 8, 0.6)) ms <- Modes(x) print(ms) summary(ms, compare = TRUE) plot(ms, type = "density") is.unimodal(rnorm(1000)) is.trimodal(x)

text: Classical mode detection treats distribution fixed known (bandwidth parameter). Bayesian approach, developed Cross, Hoogerheide, Ulker van Dijk [1], instead fits mixture model data extracts modes fitted mixture MCMC iteration, producing posterior distribution modes . yields three quantities classical methods provide: posterior probability distribution multimodal, posterior distribution number modes, credible intervals mode location.

previous_headings: The Bayesian approach: Sparse Finite Mixtures
title: Bayesian mode inference with lucifer
text: method uses Sparse Finite Mixtures (SFM; [2]) simultaneously fit mixture estimate number components. key idea deliberately overspecify number components \(K\) let sparsity-inducing prior Dirichlet concentration parameter \(\alpha\) shrink unnecessary components zero weight. mixture model data \(y_1, \ldots, y_n\) \[p(y_i \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}, K) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \pi_k \, f(y_i \mid \theta_k)\] \(\pi_k\) mixture weights \(f(\cdot \mid \theta_k)\) component density parameters \(\theta_k\). weights follow symmetric Dirichlet prior \((\pi_1, \ldots, \pi_K) \sim \text{Dirichlet}(\alpha, \ldots, \alpha)\), concentration parameter Gamma hyperprior \(\alpha \sim \text{Gamma}(a_\alpha, b_\alpha)\) \(E(\alpha) = a_\alpha / b_\alpha\) set small value (default \(1/200\)) strongly favors parsimony.

text: Normal mixture \(f(y \mid \mu_k, \sigma_k) = \mathcal{N}(y; \mu_k, \sigma_k^2)\): Weights: \(\boldsymbol{\pi} \mid \mathbf{z} \sim \text{Dirichlet}(\alpha + n_1, \ldots, \alpha + n_K)\) Mean: \(\mu_k \mid \sigma_k, \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\frac{b_0 / B_0 + \bar{y}_k n_k / \sigma_k^2}{1/B_0 + n_k / \sigma_k^2}, \; \frac{1}{1/B_0 + n_k/\sigma_k^2}\right)\) Variance: \(\sigma_k^{-2} \mid \mu_k, \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{z} \sim \text{Gamma}\left(c_0 + \frac{n_k}{2}, \; C_0 + \frac{1}{2}\sum_{: z_i = k}(y_i - \mu_k)^2\right)\)

title: Bayesian quadrature in lucifer
text: Bayesian quadrature (BQ) treats numerical integration statistical inference problem. Rather returning point estimate integral, BQ models integrand Gaussian process surrogate computes posterior distribution integral value . paradigm, introduced O’Hagan (1991) [1] developed substantially Rasmussen Ghahramani (2003) [2], provides three advantages classical quadrature: uncertainty-calibrated marginal likelihood estimates model comparison, superior sample efficiency model evaluations expensive, principled active learning selecting evaluate model next. BayesianQuadrature() function lucifer implements four modern BQ methods share standard Model(parm, Data) interface lucifer(), IterativeQuadrature(), VariationalBayes(). four methods model unnormalized posterior density \(f(\theta) = \exp(\mathrm{LP}(\theta))\) Gaussian process equipped squared exponential kernel, exploit closed-form kernel mean embeddings Gaussian reference measure compute integral posterior analytically.

previous_headings: Mathematical foundations
title: Bayesian quadrature in lucifer
text: central computational task Bayesian inference evaluating marginal likelihood (normalizing constant): \[Z = \int \exp\bigl(\mathrm{LP}(\theta)\bigr) \, d\theta = \int L(\theta) \pi(\theta) \, d\theta\] \(L(\theta)\) likelihood \(\pi(\theta)\) prior. Classical quadrature rules like Gauss-Hermite (implemented IterativeQuadrature()) compute \(Z\) deterministic weighted sums \(\hat{Z} = \sum_i w_i f(\theta_i)\) uncertainty quantification estimate. MCMC avoids computing \(Z\) altogether, many tasks, notably Bayes factor computation model selection, require .

previous_headings: Mathematical foundations
title: Bayesian quadrature in lucifer
text: BQ places Gaussian process prior integrand \(f\): \[f \sim \mathcal{GP}\bigl(0, k(\theta, \theta')\bigr)\] squared exponential (SE) kernel featuring automatic relevance determination (ARD): \[k(\theta, \theta') = \sigma_f^2 \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} \sum_{d=1}^D \frac{(\theta_d - \theta'_d)^2}{\ell_d^2}\right)\] observing \(f\) points \(\Theta = \{\theta_1, \dots, \theta_n\}\) values \(\mathbf{y} = (f(\theta_1), \dots, f(\theta_n))^\top\), GP posterior : \[f \mid \mathbf{y} \sim \mathcal{GP}\bigl(\mu_n(\cdot), k_n(\cdot, \cdot)\bigr)\] \(\mu_n(\theta) = \mathbf{k}(\theta)^\top K^{-1} \mathbf{y}\) \(k_n(\theta, \theta') = k(\theta, \theta') - \mathbf{k}(\theta)^\top K^{-1} \mathbf{k}(\theta')\), \(K_{ij} = k(\theta_i, \theta_j)\) \(\mathbf{k}(\theta)_i = k(\theta_i, \theta)\).

previous_headings: Mathematical foundations
title: Bayesian quadrature in lucifer
text: integral \(Z = \int f(\theta) \pi(\theta) d\theta\) linear functional \(f\), GP model inherits Gaussian posterior: \[Z \mid \mathbf{y} \sim \mathcal{N}\bigl(\hat{Z}, \hat{V}\bigr)\] \(\hat{Z} = \boldsymbol{\mu}_k^\top K^{-1} \mathbf{y}\) \(\hat{V} = z_0 - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k^\top K^{-1} \boldsymbol{\mu}_k\). kernel mean embedding vector \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\) prior integral \(z_0\) admit closed-form expressions \(\pi(\theta) = \mathcal{N}(\mu_0, \Sigma_0)\) kernel SE: \[[\boldsymbol{\mu}_k]_i = \sigma_f^2 |\Lambda^{-1}\Sigma_0 + |^{-1/2} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\theta_i - \mu_0)^\top (\Lambda + \Sigma_0)^{-1} (\theta_i - \mu_0)\right)\] \[z_0 = \sigma_f^2 |\Lambda^{-1} (2\Sigma_0) + |^{-1/2}\] \(\Lambda = \mathrm{diag}(\ell_1^2, \dots, \ell_D^2)\). computed C++ OpenMP parallelization.

title: Bayesian quadrature in lucifer
text: baseline method Rasmussen Ghahramani (2003) [2]. iteration, BQ generates candidate evaluation points reference measure, selects candidate maximally reduces integral posterior variance \(\hat{V}\), evaluates model , updates GP. Hyperparameters \((\sigma_f, \boldsymbol{\ell})\) re-optimized periodically via marginal likelihood maximization multi-start L-BFGS-B.
code: library(lucifer)  # Normal-normal conjugate model Model <- function(parm, Data) {   mu <- parm[1]   LL <- sum(dnorm(Data$y, mu, 1, log = TRUE))   LP <- LL + dnorm(mu, 0, 1000, log = TRUE)   list(LP = LP, Dev = -2 * LL,        Monitor = LP, yhat = rep(mu, length(Data$y)),        parm = parm) }  set.seed(42) y <- rnorm(50, mean = 3) Data <- list(y = y, mon.names = "LP", parm.names = "mu")  fit_bq <- BayesianQuadrature(Model, parm = 3, Data = Data,   Covar = matrix(0.1), Iterations = 50, Algorithm = "BQ")  print(fit_bq) summary(fit_bq)

title: Bayesian quadrature in lucifer
text: Gunter et al. (2014) [3] observed likelihood integrand \(f(\theta) = \exp(\mathrm{LP}(\theta))\) strictly non-negative, standard GP models can predict negative values. WSABI-L applies square-root warping \(g(\theta) = \sqrt{2(f(\theta) - \alpha)}\) \(\alpha < \min f\), fits GP \(g\), linearizes inverse warping \(f = \alpha + g^2/2\) closed-form integral moment propagation. enforces non-negativity recommended marginal likelihood estimation.

title: Bayesian quadrature in lucifer
text: example demonstrates BQ two-parameter logistic regression model analytical solutions unavailable.
code: # Logistic regression model LogisticModel <- function(parm, Data) {   beta0 <- parm[1]   beta1 <- parm[2]   eta <- beta0 + beta1 * Data$x   p <- 1 / (1 + exp(-eta))   p <- pmax(pmin(p, 1 - 1e-10), 1e-10)  # numerical safety   LL <- sum(Data$y * log(p) + (1 - Data$y) * log(1 - p))   LP <- LL + dnorm(beta0, 0, 10, log = TRUE) + dnorm(beta1, 0, 10, log = TRUE)   list(LP = LP, Dev = -2 * LL,        Monitor = c(LP, beta0, beta1),        yhat = p, parm = parm) }  set.seed(42) n <- 100 x <- rnorm(n) p_true <- 1 / (1 + exp(-(1 + 2 * x))) y_log <- rbinom(n, 1, p_true)  Data_log <- list(y = y_log, x = x,   mon.names = c("LP", "beta0", "beta1"),   parm.names = c("beta0", "beta1"))  # Fit with BQ (start near MLE for efficiency) mle <- coef(glm(y_log ~ x, family = binomial)) fit_log <- BayesianQuadrature(LogisticModel, parm = as.numeric(mle),   Data = Data_log, Iterations = 60, Algorithm = "BQ",   sir = TRUE, Samples = 1000)  print(fit_log) summary(fit_log) plot(fit_log, Data = Data_log)

title: Bayesian quadrature in lucifer
text: three-dimensional multivariate normal model known covariance, providing analytical benchmark BQ integral estimate.
code: MVNModel <- function(parm, Data) {   mu <- parm   diff <- sweep(Data$Y, 2, mu)   LL <- -0.5 * sum(diff %*% Data$Sigma_inv * diff) -     (nrow(Data$Y) / 2) * determinant(Data$Sigma, logarithm = TRUE)$modulus   LP <- as.numeric(LL)   list(LP = LP, Dev = -2 * LL,        Monitor = LP, yhat = rep(0, nrow(Data$Y)),        parm = parm) }  set.seed(42) k <- 3 n <- 100 Sigma_true <- diag(k) * 0.5 + 0.5 Y <- MASS::mvrnorm(n, mu = c(1, 2, 3), Sigma = Sigma_true)  Data_mvn <- list(Y = Y, Sigma = Sigma_true,   Sigma_inv = solve(Sigma_true),   mon.names = "LP",   parm.names = paste0("mu", 1:k))  # BQ with initial values near posterior mode fit_mvn <- BayesianQuadrature(MVNModel, parm = colMeans(Y),   Data = Data_mvn, Covar = Sigma_true / n * 4,   Iterations = 80, Algorithm = "BQ", sir = TRUE)  summary(fit_mvn)

text: Every MCMC iteration lucifer requires evaluating log-posterior , gradient-based samplers like NUTS, gradient. model R function, evaluation crosses R/C++ boundary: C++ sampler marshals parameters R objects, calls R function, unmarshals result. NUTS \(n\) parameters, finite-difference gradients require \(2n + 1\) round-trips per gradient evaluation, single iteration \(L\) leapfrog steps demands \(L \times (2n + 1)\) R function calls. 10 parameters \(L = 30\), 600 R calls per iteration. compiled model backend eliminates bottleneck. model specified via model_spec(), system can generate self-contained C++ source file evaluates log-posterior analytical gradient without R callbacks. generated code compiled runtime via Rcpp::sourceCpp(), cached reuse, integrated transparently lucifer’s sampler infrastructure. result: gradient computation becomes single C++ function call instead hundreds R round-trips, yielding speedups 100–500x gradient evaluation 5–15x end--end NUTS sampling. vignette demonstrates complete workflow, validates correctness R models, benchmarks performance across model types sizes, documents full API.

title: Working with compiled C++ models
text: simplest path model specification compiled C++ sampling requires three steps: specify model model_spec(), compile compile(), pass compiled object lucifer(). compiled object can passed directly lucifer(), automatically extracts analytical gradient registers native function pointers sampler loop. Since compiled model operates unconstrained space (log-transformed positive parameters), posterior samples need back-transformation interpretation.
code: # 1. Specify model spec <- model_spec("     y ~ Normal(mu, sigma)     mu = X %*% beta     beta[j] ~ Normal(0, 10), j = 1,...,J     sigma ~ HalfCauchy(2.5) ", backend = "cpp")  # 2. Generate data set.seed(42) N <- 100; J <- 3 X <- cbind(1, matrix(rnorm(N * (J - 1)), N, J - 1)) true_beta <- c(2, -1, 0.5) true_sigma <- 1.5 y <- as.numeric(X %*% true_beta + rnorm(N, 0, true_sigma))  # 3. Compile to C++ Data <- spec$data_template(y = y, X = X, J = J) compiled <- compile(spec, Data, verbose = FALSE) print(compiled) iv <- compiled$initial_values(Data) fit <- lucifer(compiled, Data, iv,                Iterations = 2000, Status = 2000,                Thinning = 1, Chains = 1,                Algorithm = "NUTS",                Specs = list(A = 1000, delta = 0.65,                             epsilon = 0.1, Lmax = 10)) post <- fit$Posterior2 post[, J + 1] <- exp(post[, J + 1])  # sigma = exp(log_sigma) colnames(post) <- c(paste0("beta[", 1:J, "]"), "sigma")  knitr::kable(     data.frame(         parameter = colnames(post),         true = c(true_beta, true_sigma),         mean = round(colMeans(post), 3),         sd = round(apply(post, 2, sd), 3),         q025 = round(apply(post, 2, quantile, 0.025), 3),         q975 = round(apply(post, 2, quantile, 0.975), 3)     ),     caption = "Posterior summary from compiled NUTS (2000 iterations)",     row.names = FALSE ) par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1)) for (j in 1:ncol(post)) {     plot(post[, j], type = "l", col = "#2E5090",          ylab = colnames(post)[j], xlab = "Iteration",          main = colnames(post)[j])     abline(h = c(true_beta, true_sigma)[j], col = "#E07020", lwd = 2, lty = 2) }

title: Working with compiled C++ models
text: compilation pipeline transforms model specification four stages, producing well-defined intermediate product. Stage 1: parsing IR construction. model_spec() function parses probabilistic notation topologically sorted directed acyclic graph (DAG). node classified data, parameter, hyperparameter, deterministic quantity. Constraint types (positive, unit, bounded) inferred distribution support. stage identical R C++ backends. Stage 2: C++ code generation. compile() function walks DAG emits self-contained C++ source file containing three functions: init_data_HASH() populates static data struct R Data list; eval_model_HASH() computes log-posterior Jacobian-adjusted parameter transforms; grad_model_HASH() computes analytical gradient via distribution-specific formulas chain rule deterministic compositions. Stage 3: runtime compilation. generated source compiled via Rcpp::sourceCpp() cached tools::R_user_dir("lucifer", "cache"). Subsequent calls model specification skip compilation entirely. Stage 4: native dispatch. lucifer() receives compiled model, registers C-style function pointers sampler infrastructure. call_model() compute_gradient() functions C++ sampler loop detect pointers dispatch directly, bypassing R function call mechanism, marshaling, RNG synchronization overhead.

title: Working with compiled C++ models
text: critical design decision: compiled model operates entirely unconstrained space. Parameters positivity constraints log-transformed; unit-interval parameters use logit transform; bounded parameters use scaled logit. log-Jacobian determinant transformation added log-posterior HMC/NUTS samples correct target density. differs R model_spec() backend, uses interval() (clamping) enforce constraints. Clamping zero gradient boundaries introduces discontinuities break gradient-based samplers. differentiable bijections used C++ backend essential correct HMC dynamics. transforms Jacobians, implemented inst/include/lucifer/transforms.h, : \[ \begin{aligned} \text{Positive: } & x = e^y, \quad \log|J| = y \\ \text{Unit: } & x = \text{logit}^{-1}(y), \quad \log|J| = \log x + \log(1-x) \\ \text{Bounded } [,b]\text{: } & x = + (b-)\,\text{logit}^{-1}(y), \quad \log|J| = \log(b-) + \log x' + \log(1-x') \end{aligned} \] \(x' = (x-)/(b-)\). initial_values() function compiled model automatically converts constrained starting values unconstrained space using inverse transforms.

text: Poisson GLM uses lambda = exp(X %*% beta), requires gradient chain-rule exponential function. compiled backend handles automatically: derivative exp(z) evaluated z = X %*% beta exp(z) = \lambda , gradient contribution likelihood \(X^\top \cdot (y - \lambda)\) per observation.
code: spec_pois <- model_spec("     y ~ Poisson(lambda)     lambda = exp(X %*% beta)     beta[j] ~ Normal(0, 5), j = 1,...,J ")  set.seed(10) N_p <- 80; J_p <- 3 X_p <- cbind(1, matrix(rnorm(N_p * (J_p - 1)), N_p, J_p - 1)) true_beta_p <- c(0.5, 0.3, -0.2) y_p <- rpois(N_p, exp(X_p %*% true_beta_p))  Data_p <- spec_pois$data_template(y = y_p, X = X_p, J = J_p) compiled_p <- compile(spec_pois, Data_p, verbose = FALSE) iv_p <- compiled_p$initial_values(Data_p)  # Gradient check grad_p <- compiled_p$Grad(iv_p, Data_p) fd_p <- numeric(length(iv_p)) for (i in seq_along(iv_p)) {     p <- m <- iv_p; p[i] <- iv_p[i] + eps; m[i] <- iv_p[i] - eps     fd_p[i] <- (compiled_p$Model(p, Data_p)$LP -                 compiled_p$Model(m, Data_p)$LP) / (2 * eps) }  knitr::kable(     data.frame(         parameter = paste0("beta[", seq_along(iv_p), "]"),         analytic = grad_p,         finite_diff = fd_p,         abs_error = abs(grad_p - fd_p)     ),     digits = 6, row.names = FALSE,     caption = "Poisson GLM gradient validation (chain rule through exp)" ) fit_p <- lucifer(compiled_p, Data_p, iv_p,                  Iterations = 2000, Status = 2000,                  Thinning = 1, Chains = 1,                  Algorithm = "NUTS",                  Specs = list(A = 1000, delta = 0.65,                               epsilon = 0.05, Lmax = 10)) post_p <- fit_p$Posterior2  knitr::kable(     data.frame(         parameter = paste0("beta[", 1:J_p, "]"),         true = true_beta_p,         posterior_mean = round(colMeans(post_p), 3),         posterior_sd = round(apply(post_p, 2, sd), 3)     ),     row.names = FALSE,     caption = paste0("Poisson GLM posterior (acceptance: ",                      round(fit_p$Acceptance.Rate, 3), ")") )

code: spec_logit <- model_spec("     y ~ Bernoulli(p)     p = invlogit(X %*% beta)     beta[j] ~ Normal(0, 5), j = 1,...,J ")  set.seed(20) N_l <- 120; J_l <- 3 X_l <- cbind(1, matrix(rnorm(N_l * (J_l - 1)), N_l, J_l - 1)) true_beta_l <- c(-0.5, 1.0, -0.3) p_true <- plogis(X_l %*% true_beta_l) y_l <- rbinom(N_l, 1, p_true)  Data_l <- spec_logit$data_template(y = y_l, X = X_l, J = J_l) compiled_l <- compile(spec_logit, Data_l, verbose = FALSE) iv_l <- compiled_l$initial_values(Data_l)  # Gradient check grad_l <- compiled_l$Grad(iv_l, Data_l) fd_l <- numeric(length(iv_l)) for (i in seq_along(iv_l)) {     p <- m <- iv_l; p[i] <- iv_l[i] + eps; m[i] <- iv_l[i] - eps     fd_l[i] <- (compiled_l$Model(p, Data_l)$LP -                 compiled_l$Model(m, Data_l)$LP) / (2 * eps) }  knitr::kable(     data.frame(         parameter = paste0("beta[", seq_along(iv_l), "]"),         analytic = grad_l, finite_diff = fd_l,         abs_error = abs(grad_l - fd_l)     ),     digits = 6, row.names = FALSE,     caption = "Logistic regression gradient validation (chain rule through invlogit)" ) fit_l <- lucifer(compiled_l, Data_l, iv_l,                  Iterations = 2000, Status = 2000,                  Thinning = 1, Chains = 1,                  Algorithm = "NUTS",                  Specs = list(A = 1000, delta = 0.65,                               epsilon = 0.05, Lmax = 10)) post_l <- fit_l$Posterior2  knitr::kable(     data.frame(         parameter = paste0("beta[", 1:J_l, "]"),         true = true_beta_l,         posterior_mean = round(colMeans(post_l), 3),         posterior_sd = round(apply(post_l, 2, sd), 3)     ),     row.names = FALSE,     caption = paste0("Logistic regression posterior (acceptance: ",                      round(fit_l$Acceptance.Rate, 3), ")") )

title: Working with compiled C++ models
text: compare wall-clock time repeated model evaluations across increasing data sizes, holding number parameters fixed \(J + 1 = 6\). configuration measured median 3 timing runs, 5000 evaluations, reduce noise OS scheduling garbage collection. C++ compiled model consistently faster, advantage growing \(N\) increases compiled code eliminates R boundary crossing overhead interpretive overhead R-level distribution calls.
code: spec_bench <- model_spec("     y ~ Normal(mu, sigma)     mu = X %*% beta     beta[j] ~ Normal(0, 10), j = 1,...,J     sigma ~ HalfCauchy(2.5) ")  J_bench <- 5 N_values <- c(50, 100, 200, 500, 1000)  # Helper: median of k timing runs for stability. # fn must be a zero-argument function (closure). bench_median <- function(fn, n_reps, k = 3) {     times <- numeric(k)     for (j in seq_len(k))         times[j] <- system.time(for (i in seq_len(n_reps)) fn())[3]     median(times) / n_reps }  set.seed(666) eval_results <- do.call(rbind, lapply(N_values, function(N) {     X <- cbind(1, matrix(rnorm(N * (J_bench - 1)), N, J_bench - 1))     yy <- as.numeric(X %*% rnorm(J_bench) + rnorm(N))     D <- spec_bench$data_template(y = yy, X = X, J = J_bench)     cc <- compile(spec_bench, D, verbose = FALSE)     iv_r <- spec_bench$initial_values(D)     iv_c <- cc$initial_values(D)      # Warmup     for (w in 1:50) { spec_bench$Model(iv_r, D); cc$Model(iv_c, D) }      t_r <- bench_median(function() spec_bench$Model(iv_r, D), n_reps = 5000)     t_c <- bench_median(function() cc$Model(iv_c, D), n_reps = 5000)     data.frame(N = N, R_ms = t_r * 1000,                Cpp_ms = t_c * 1000,                speedup = t_r / max(t_c, 1e-9)) }))  knitr::kable(eval_results, digits = c(0, 4, 4, 1), row.names = FALSE,              col.names = c("N", "R (ms/call)", "C++ (ms/call)", "Speedup"),              caption = "Model evaluation: median of 3 runs, 5000 calls each (J = 5)") eval_long <- rbind(     data.frame(N = eval_results$N, backend = "R model", ms = eval_results$R_ms),     data.frame(N = eval_results$N, backend = "C++ compiled", ms = eval_results$Cpp_ms) ) ggplot(eval_long, aes(x = N, y = ms, color = backend)) +     geom_line(linewidth = 1) +     geom_point(size = 3) +     scale_color_manual(values = c("R model" = "#2E5090",                                    "C++ compiled" = "#E07020")) +     labs(x = "Number of observations (N)", y = "Time per evaluation (ms)",          color = "Backend",          title = "Model evaluation cost",          subtitle = paste0("J = ", J_bench, " parameters, median of 3 runs")) +     theme_relab() +     theme(legend.position = "bottom")

R model requires \(2n + 1\) model evaluations central finite differences; compiled model computes exact analytical gradient single C++ call. fix \(N = 200\) increase number parameters \(J\) show linear scaling. theoretical speedup \(2n + 1\) (\(n\) number parameters), since finite differences require exactly many model evaluations analytical gradient requires one. Finite-difference cost grows linearly number parameters (parameter requires two model evaluations), analytical gradient cost remains nearly constant. theoretical speedup therefore scales approximately \(2n + 1\). ratio theoretical practice ~7x theoretical formula counts model evaluations, practice R model evaluation overhead C++ gradient call (R interpreter, marshaling, PutRNGstate, etc.).:
code: N_grad <- 200 J_values <- c(3, 5, 8, 12, 20)  set.seed(666) grad_results <- do.call(rbind, lapply(J_values, function(J) {     X <- cbind(1, matrix(rnorm(N_grad * (J - 1)), N_grad, J - 1))     yy <- as.numeric(X %*% rnorm(J) + rnorm(N_grad))     D <- spec_bench$data_template(y = yy, X = X, J = J)     cc <- compile(spec_bench, D, verbose = FALSE)     iv_r <- spec_bench$initial_values(D)     iv_c <- cc$initial_values(D)     n_parm <- J + 1      # Warmup     for (w in 1:20) { spec_bench$Model(iv_r, D); cc$Grad(iv_c, D) }      # Finite-difference gradient (R)     n_fd <- max(100, 500 %/% n_parm)     fd_fn <- function() {         g <- numeric(length(iv_r))         for (k in seq_along(iv_r)) {             p <- m <- iv_r             p[k] <- iv_r[k] + 1e-6; m[k] <- iv_r[k] - 1e-6             g[k] <- (spec_bench$Model(p, D)$LP -                      spec_bench$Model(m, D)$LP) / 2e-6         }     }     t_fd <- bench_median(fd_fn, n_reps = n_fd) * 1000      # Analytical gradient (C++): many reps since each call is ~5us     t_cpp <- bench_median(function() cc$Grad(iv_c, D), n_reps = 20000) * 1000      data.frame(J = J, n_parm = n_parm,                FD_ms = t_fd, Cpp_ms = t_cpp,                speedup = t_fd / max(t_cpp, 1e-6)) }))  knitr::kable(grad_results, digits = c(0, 0, 3, 4, 0), row.names = FALSE,              col.names = c("J", "n_parm", "FD (ms/call)", "C++ (ms/call)", "Speedup"),              caption = "Gradient computation per call (N = 200, median of 3 runs)") grad_long <- rbind(     data.frame(n_parm = grad_results$n_parm,                method = "R finite differences", ms = grad_results$FD_ms),     data.frame(n_parm = grad_results$n_parm,                method = "C++ analytical", ms = grad_results$Cpp_ms) ) ggplot(grad_long, aes(x = n_parm, y = ms, color = method)) +     geom_line(linewidth = 1) +     geom_point(size = 3) +     scale_y_log10() +     scale_color_manual(values = c("R finite differences" = "#2E5090",                                    "C++ analytical" = "#E07020")) +     labs(x = "Number of parameters",          y = "Time per gradient call (ms, log scale)",          color = "Method",          title = "Gradient computation cost",          subtitle = "N = 200 observations, median of 3 timing runs") +     theme_relab() +     theme(legend.position = "bottom") # Add theoretical speedup line grad_results$theoretical <- 2 * grad_results$n_parm + 1  speedup_long <- rbind(     data.frame(n_parm = grad_results$n_parm,                type = "Measured", speedup = grad_results$speedup),     data.frame(n_parm = grad_results$n_parm,                type = "Theoretical (2n+1)", speedup = grad_results$theoretical) )  ggplot(speedup_long, aes(x = n_parm, y = speedup, color = type,                           linetype = type)) +     geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +     geom_point(data = speedup_long[speedup_long$type == "Measured", ],                size = 3.5) +     geom_text(data = speedup_long[speedup_long$type == "Measured", ],               aes(label = paste0(round(speedup), "x")),               vjust = -1.2, size = 3.5, fontface = "bold", show.legend = FALSE) +     scale_color_manual(values = c("Measured" = "#C04040",                                    "Theoretical (2n+1)" = "grey50")) +     scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Measured" = "solid",                                       "Theoretical (2n+1)" = "dashed")) +     labs(x = "Number of parameters",          y = "Speedup (FD time / analytical time)",          color = NULL, linetype = NULL,          title = "Gradient speedup: analytical C++ vs finite differences",          subtitle = "Dashed line: theoretical 2n+1 scaling") +     theme_relab() +     expand_limits(y = max(grad_results$speedup) * 1.1)

code: library(lucifer)  # Simulate data set.seed(42) N <- 50 y <- rnorm(N, mean = 3, sd = 1.5)  Data <- list(   N = N, y = y,   mon.names = "LP",   parm.names = c("mu", "log.sigma") )  Model <- function(parm, Data) {   mu    <- parm[1]   sigma <- exp(parm[2])   LL <- sum(dnorm(Data$y, mu, sigma, log = TRUE))   LP <- LL + dnorm(mu, 0, 100, log = TRUE) +     dcauchy(sigma, 0, 25, log = TRUE)   yhat    <- rep(mu, Data$N)   Monitor <- LP   list(LP = LP, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = Monitor,        yhat = yhat, parm = parm) }

title: Cross-validation for Bayesian models
text: gold standard evaluating predictive accuracy expected log pointwise predictive density [1], defined \[\text{elpd} = \sum_{=1}^{N} \int \log p(\tilde{y}_i \mid y) \, f(\tilde{y}_i) \, d\tilde{y}_i\] \(f(\tilde{y}_i)\) true data-generating distribution new observation \[p(\tilde{y}_i \mid y) = \int p(\tilde{y}_i \mid \theta) \, p(\theta \mid y) \, d\theta\] posterior predictive density. Since \(f\) unknown, must estimate elpd observed data. Cross-validation provides nearly unbiased estimate using portions data surrogate “future” observations.

title: Cross-validation for Bayesian models
text: LOO-CV estimate elpd \[\widehat{\text{elpd}}_{\text{loo}} = \sum_{=1}^{N} \log p(y_i \mid y_{-})\] \(p(y_i \mid y_{-}) = \int p(y_i \mid \theta) \, p(\theta \mid y_{-}) \, d\theta\) leave-one-predictive density obtained fitting model data except observation \(\). Direct computation requires \(N\) model refits, PSIS provides efficient single-fit approximation [2] [3]. key insight LOO predictive density can rewritten importance sampling estimate: \[p(y_i \mid y_{-}) = \frac{\int p(y_i \mid \theta) \, p(\theta \mid y_{-}) \, d\theta}{1} = E_{p(\theta \mid y)} \left[ \frac{1}{p(y_i \mid \theta)} \right]^{-1}\] importance ratios \(r_i(\theta) = 1 / p(y_i \mid \theta)\) potentially infinite variance, PSIS stabilizes upper tail fitting generalized Pareto distribution (GPD) largest ratios, following Zhang Stephens [4], replacing extreme values smoothed quantiles. shape parameter \(\hat{k}\) fitted GPD diagnoses reliability: \(\hat{k} < 0.5\): estimate reliable; central limit theorem importance ratios holds convergence rate close \(1/\sqrt{S}\). \(0.5 \leq \hat{k} < 0.7\): estimate acceptable Monte Carlo error may non-negligible; convergence rate slower parametric rate. \(0.7 \leq \hat{k} < 1.0\): estimate problematic; importance weights highly variable finite-sample bias may substantial. \(\hat{k} \geq 1.0\): estimate unreliable; moment importance ratios required estimate consistent exist, meaning importance sampling approximation converge rate.

text: Widely Applicable Information Criterion (WAIC) Watanabe [5] provides alternative estimate elpd asymptotically equivalent LOO-CV. computed \[\widehat{\text{elpd}}_{\text{waic}} = \text{lppd} - p_{\text{waic}}\] log pointwise predictive density \(\text{lppd} = \sum_{=1}^{N} \log \left( \frac{1}{S} \sum_{s=1}^{S} p(y_i \mid \theta^s) \right)\) effective number parameters \(p_{\text{waic}} = \sum_{=1}^{N} \text{Var}_s \left[ \log p(y_i \mid \theta^s) \right]\), variance computed across \(S\) posterior samples. latter formula (\(p_{\text{waic2}}\)) preferred Gelman et al. [1] alternative \(p_{\text{waic1}} = 2 \sum_i \left[ \log \left( \frac{1}{S} \sum_s p(y_i \mid \theta^s) \right) - \frac{1}{S} \sum_s \log p(y_i \mid \theta^s) \right]\) closely matches LOO-CV practice. Unlike LOO-PSIS, WAIC provides per-observation diagnostic. posterior dominated observations (high leverage), WAIC can silently produce unreliable estimates. reason, Vehtari et al. [2] recommend LOO-PSIS Pareto \(\hat{k}\) diagnostics default method, resorting WAIC computational constraints prevent PSIS computation.

previous_headings: Leave-future-out cross-validation for time series
title: Cross-validation for Bayesian models
text: Leave-future-cross-validation (LFO-CV) evaluates predictive performance expanding training window forward time, making predictions future observations used inference [6]. LFO-CV estimate elpd \(M\)-step-ahead prediction \[\widehat{\text{elpd}}_{\text{lfo}} = \sum_{=L}^{N-M} \log p(y_{+1:+M} \mid y_{1:})\] \(L\) minimum training window \(p(y_{+1:+M} \mid y_{1:}) = \int p(y_{+1:+M} \mid y_{1:}, \theta) \, p(\theta \mid y_{1:}) \, d\theta\) posterior predictive density future block given data time \(\). Exact LFO-CV requires refitting model time step, prohibitively expensive. approximate algorithm Burkner et al. [6] reduces number refits using PSIS approximate successive posteriors single fit, refitting importance sampling approximation becomes unreliable.

previous_headings: Leave-future-out cross-validation for time series
title: Cross-validation for Bayesian models
text: algorithm proceeds follows. Starting model fitted \(y_{1:L}\), accumulate importance weights training window expands: Fit model \(y_{1:L}\) obtain posterior samples \(\theta^{(1)}, \ldots, \theta^{(S)} \sim p(\theta \mid y_{1:L})\). Compute cumulative log-importance-ratios since last refit \(^*\): \[\log r_i(\theta^{(s)}) = \sum_{j=^*+1}^{} \log p(y_j \mid y_{1:j-1}, \theta^{(s)})\] Apply PSIS importance ratios obtain normalized weights \(w_i^{(s)}\) Pareto \(\hat{k}\) diagnostic. \(\hat{k} > k_{\text{threshold}}\) (default 0.7): refit model \(y_{1:}\), reset importance ratios, set \(^* = \). Compute weighted predictive log-density: \[\log p(y_{+1:+M} \mid y_{1:}) \approx \log \sum_{s=1}^{S} w_i^{(s)} \, p(y_{+1:+M} \mid y_{1:}, \theta^{(s)})\] number refits depends quickly posterior evolves new data arrives. well-specified models stable parameters, posterior changes slowly refits needed (typically < 5% total time steps). misspecified models models time-varying parameters, frequent refits indicate importance sampling approximation degrades quickly, informative model adequacy.

text: following example fits AR(1) model evaluates one-step-ahead predictive performance using LFO-CV initial training window 10 observations. two-panel plot shows cumulative elpd time (top panel) refit points marked vertical dashed lines, Pareto \(\hat{k}\) diagnostics (bottom panel) colored reliability category. Refit locations cluster data informative parameter changes, providing diagnostic view model stability time. prediction horizon M controls multi-step-ahead evaluation. Setting M = 1 gives one-step-ahead predictions (default common choice); M = 4 evaluates four-step-ahead predictive performance, stringent directly relevant forecasting applications. Note \(M > 1\), predictive block \(y_{+1:+M}\) evaluated jointly, total number evaluated predictions \(N - L - M + 1\). L parameter sets minimum training window. defaults \(\max(10, 2d)\) \(d\) number parameters, ensuring initial posterior seen enough data relative model complexity. small value \(L\) yields unreliable initial fits; large value wastes data used evaluation. reasonable heuristic set \(L\) smallest sample size model can produce stable posterior estimates.
code: # AR(1) model specification Model <- function(parm, Data) {     phi <- parm[1]     sigma <- exp(parm[2])     mu <- phi * Data$y[-Data$n]     LL <- sum(dnorm(Data$y[-1], mu, sigma, log = TRUE))     LP <- LL + dnorm(phi, 0, 1, log = TRUE) +         dgamma(sigma, 1, 1, log = TRUE)     yhat <- c(Data$y[1], mu)     list(LP = LP, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = LP, yhat = yhat, parm = parm) }  set.seed(123) y <- arima.sim(list(ar = 0.7), n = 30) Data <- list(y = as.numeric(y), n = 30,              parm.names = c("phi", "log.sigma"),              mon.names = "LP")  # Fit the model fit <- lucifer(Model, Data, c(0, 0), Iterations = 2000,                Status = .Machine$integer.max,                Algorithm = "HARM", Specs = NULL, Chains = 1)  # One-step-ahead LFO-CV with initial window of 10 observations lfo_result <- LFO(fit, Model, Data, L = 10, M = 1, verbose = FALSE) print(lfo_result) summary(lfo_result) plot(lfo_result)

previous_headings: K-fold cross-validation
title: Cross-validation for Bayesian models
text: K-fold cross-validation partitions \(N\) observations \(K\) non-overlapping folds \(F_1, \ldots, F_K\), refits model \(K\) times (time leaving one fold test set), evaluates predictive log density held-observation. K-fold estimate elpd \[\widehat{\text{elpd}}_{\text{kfold}} = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \sum_{\F_k} \log p(y_i \mid y_{-F_k})\] \(p(y_i \mid y_{-F_k}) = \int p(y_i \mid \theta) \, p(\theta \mid y_{-F_k}) \, d\theta\) predictive density observation \(\) posterior obtained data except fold \(k\). Unlike LOO-PSIS, K-fold CV exact sense rely importance sampling approximations. works even Pareto \(\hat{k}\) diagnostics indicate PSIS-LOO unreliable. tradeoff computational cost: K model refits required, making K-fold CV \(K\) times expensive single fit (\(N/K\) times cheaper exact LOO via refitting). choice \(K\) balances bias variance. Larger \(K\) reduces bias (training set closer full data) increases variance (\(K\) training sets overlap , making fold-level estimates correlated). \(K = 10\) common default provides reasonable tradeoff; \(K = N\) gives exact LOO via refitting; \(K = 2\) gives split-half validation maximum diversity folds [8].

code: # Normal model Model <- function(parm, Data) {     mu <- parm[1]     sigma <- exp(parm[2])     LL <- sum(dnorm(Data$y, mu, sigma, log = TRUE))     LP <- LL + dnorm(mu, 0, 100, log = TRUE) +         dgamma(sigma, 1, 1, log = TRUE)     yhat <- rep(mu, Data$n)     list(LP = LP, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = LP, yhat = yhat, parm = parm) }  set.seed(456) Data <- list(y = rnorm(30, 5, 2), n = 30,              parm.names = c("mu", "log.sigma"),              mon.names = "LP")  fit <- lucifer(Model, Data, c(0, 0), Iterations = 2000,                Status = .Machine$integer.max,                Algorithm = "HARM", Specs = NULL, Chains = 1)  # 5-fold CV kfold_result <- Kfold(Model, Data, fit = fit, K = 5, verbose = FALSE) print(kfold_result) summary(kfold_result) plot(kfold_result) plot(kfold_result, type = "folds") # Blocked folds for time series (contiguous blocks) N <- 100; K <- 5 folds <- rep(seq_len(K), each = N / K)  # Group-level folds (leave-one-group-out) group_membership <- Data$group  # integer vector of group IDs folds <- as.integer(as.factor(group_membership))

title: Cross-validation for Bayesian models
text: Model selection picks single model discards rest, wasting information predictive value non-selected models. Model averaging addresses combining predictions multiple models data-determined weights. classical Bayesian model averaging (BMA) approach weights models marginal likelihoods, problematic candidate models misspecified (always practice), marginal likelihoods favor models closest data-generating process particular KL sense may align predictive performance [9]. Bayesian stacking [9] directly optimizes predictive performance finding weights \(w = (w_1, \ldots, w_K)\) maximize leave-one-predictive log density combined model: \[\hat{w} = \arg\max_{w} \sum_{=1}^{N} \log \left( \sum_{k=1}^{K} w_k \exp\left(\widehat{\text{elpd}}_{k,}\right) \right) \quad \text{subject } \quad w_k \geq 0, \quad \sum_k w_k = 1\] convex optimization problem simplex. stacking_weights() function solves via unconstrained optimization softmax parameterization \(w_k = \exp(\alpha_k) / \sum_j \exp(\alpha_j)\), automatically satisfies simplex constraints. Stacking accounts model complementarity: model lower overall elpd may still receive positive weight captures aspects data models miss. makes stacking fundamentally different model selection, ignores possibility different models may best predicting different subsets data.

code: # Normal-normal model Model <- function(parm, Data) {     mu <- parm[1]     sigma <- exp(parm[2])     LL <- sum(dnorm(Data$y, mu, sigma, log = TRUE))     LP <- LL + dnorm(mu, 0, 100, log = TRUE) +         dhalfcauchy(sigma, 25, log = TRUE)     yhat <- rep(mu, Data$N)     return(list(LP = LP, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = LP,                 yhat = yhat, parm = parm)) }  set.seed(42) Data <- list(N = 50, y = rnorm(50, 5, 2),              mon.names = "LP",              parm.names = c("mu", "log.sigma")) IV <- c(5, log(2))  # Run Crucible with 3 methods, 2 refinement rounds cr <- Crucible(Model, Data, IV,                n_methods = 3,                max_rounds = 2,                Chains = 2, CPUs = 1,                families = c("MCMC"))  # Compact dashboard print(cr) Crucible: automated Bayesian inference ────────────────────────────────────────── Model: 2 parameters | 50 observations | Profiled in 0.0s    Method  Category  Rounds Appeased  ESS.min  Minutes Rank   ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────   AMWG    MCMC         1/2      ✔      2132     0.01    1   DEMC    MCMC         2/2      ✘         2     0.29    2   AIES    MCMC         2/2      ✘         2     0.79    3  ✔ Best overall: AMWG (MCMC) Total time: 68.5 seconds summary(cr)

code: # Neal's funnel: d-dimensional version d_funnel <- 3 FunnelModel <- function(parm, Data) {     v <- parm[1]     theta <- parm[2:Data$d]      # Log-likelihood of hierarchical structure     LL_v <- dnorm(v, 0, 3, log = TRUE)     LL_theta <- sum(dnorm(theta, 0, exp(v / 2), log = TRUE))     LL <- LL_v + LL_theta      # Flat prior (the model IS the posterior)     LP <- LL     yhat <- rep(0, Data$N)     return(list(LP = LP, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = LP,                 yhat = yhat, parm = parm)) }  FunnelData <- list(     N = 1,     d = d_funnel,     y = 0,     mon.names = "LP",     parm.names = c("v", paste0("theta.", 1:(d_funnel - 1))) ) FunnelIV <- rep(0, d_funnel)  # Run Crucible: compare gradient-based vs componentwise vs slice. cr_funnel <- Crucible(FunnelModel, FunnelData, FunnelIV,                       methods = c("NUTS", "AMWG", "Slice"),                       max_rounds = 2,                       Chains = 2, CPUs = 1)  print(cr_funnel) summary(cr_funnel) # Inspect the best method's diagnostics plot(cr_funnel, type = "diagnostics")  # Compare ESS trajectories across methods plot(cr_funnel, type = "convergence") plot(cr_funnel, type = "refinement") # Scorecard for the best method's consort diagnostics plot(cr_funnel$Best$consort, type = "scorecard")

previous_headings: Theoretical foundations
title: Data cloning: maximum likelihood estimation via Bayesian MCMC
text: Consider observed data \(y = (y_1, \ldots, y_n)\) parametric model likelihood \(L(\theta \mid y) = \prod_{=1}^n f(y_i \mid \theta)\) prior \(\pi(\theta)\). standard Bayesian posterior \[\pi(\theta \mid y) \propto L(\theta \mid y) \, \pi(\theta).\] data cloning idea construct artificial dataset \(y^{(K)}\) replicating \(y\) exactly \(K\) times. likelihood cloned data \(L(\theta \mid y^{(K)}) = [L(\theta \mid y)]^K\), corresponding posterior \[\pi_K(\theta \mid y) \propto [L(\theta \mid y)]^K \, \pi(\theta).\] \(K\) increases, factor \([L(\theta \mid y)]^K\) concentrates exponentially around maximum likelihood estimate \(\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}\), overwhelming prior contribution \(\pi(\theta)\). limit, posterior becomes point mass MLE regardless prior, provided MLE exists unique.

Asymptotic normality. cloned posterior converges distribution multivariate normal: \[\theta \mid y^{(K)} \xrightarrow{d} N\!\left(\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}},\; K^{-1} (\hat{\theta})^{-1}\right).\] result mirrors classical Bernstein–von Mises theorem increasing sample sizes, except data cloning achieves concentration repeating observations rather collecting new ones.

title: Data cloning: maximum likelihood estimation via Bayesian MCMC
text: Consider simplest possible case: normal model unknown mean \(\mu\) known variance \(\sigma^2 = 1\), observed \(n = 100\) independent observations. MLE sample mean \(\hat{\mu} = \bar{y}\) asymptotic standard error \(\mathrm{SE} = 1/\sqrt{n} = 0.1\). prior intentionally diffuse (\(\mu \sim N(0, 100^2)\)) demonstrate data cloning overcomes prior influence. Running DataCloning() five clone sizes:
code: library(lucifer)  set.seed(42) n <- 100 true_mu <- 3.0 y <- rnorm(n, mean = true_mu, sd = 1)  Data <- list(     mon.names = "LP",     parm.names = "mu",     y = y, n = n )  Model <- function(parm, Data) {     mu <- parm[1]     LL <- sum(dnorm(Data$y, mu, 1, log = TRUE))     LP <- LL + dnorm(mu, 0, 100, log = TRUE)     list(LP = LP, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = LP,          yhat = rep(mu, Data$n), parm = parm) } dc <- DataCloning(     Model = Model,     Data = Data,     Initial.Values = 0,     n_clones = c(1, 2, 4, 8, 16),     Iterations = 10000,     Thinning = 10,     Algorithm = "NUTS",     Chains = 3L,     CPUs = 3L,     update_prior = TRUE,     verbose = TRUE )

title: The frequentist bridge: maximum likelihood inference with Bayesian machinery in lucifer
text: Binary outcomes logit link provide first non-trivial test. log-likelihood \(\ell(\beta) = \sum_i \left[y_i \log p_i + (1 - y_i) \log(1 - p_i)\right]\) \(p_i = \text{logit}^{-1}(X_i^T \beta)\). estimates standard errors match glm() uses iteratively reweighted least squares (Fisher scoring), converges mode lucifer’s SPG optimizer finds, invert Hessian.
code: set.seed(123) n <- 300 x1 <- rnorm(n) x2 <- rnorm(n) true_beta_logistic <- c(0.5, 1.2, -0.8) p <- plogis(true_beta_logistic[1] + true_beta_logistic[2] * x1 +             true_beta_logistic[3] * x2) y_bin <- rbinom(n, 1, p) glm_fit <- glm(y_bin ~ x1 + x2, family = binomial) knitr::kable(coef(summary(glm_fit)), digits = 4,              caption = "Reference: glm() logistic regression") X_logistic <- cbind(1, x1, x2) Data_logistic <- list(     parm.names = c("beta0", "beta1", "beta2"),     mon.names  = "LL",     X = X_logistic, y = y_bin, n = n, N = n ) Model_logistic <- function(parm, Data) {     eta <- Data$X %*% parm     p   <- plogis(eta)     p   <- pmin(pmax(p, 1e-10), 1 - 1e-10)     LL  <- sum(dbinom(Data$y, 1, p, log = TRUE))     list(LP = LL, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = LL,          yhat = rbinom(Data$n, 1, p), parm = parm) } fit_logistic <- LaplaceApproximation(Model_logistic, c(0, 0, 0),                                      Data_logistic, Iterations = 200,                                      Method = "SPG", sir = FALSE) fs_logistic <- freq_summary(fit_logistic) print(fs_logistic) plot(fit_logistic, Data = Data_logistic) comp_logistic <- data.frame(     glm.Estimate     = coef(summary(glm_fit))[, 1],     glm.SE           = coef(summary(glm_fit))[, 2],     Laplace.Estimate = fs_logistic$coefficients[, "Estimate"],     Laplace.SE       = fs_logistic$coefficients[, "Std.Error"] ) knitr::kable(comp_logistic, digits = 4,              caption = "Logistic regression: glm() vs Laplace")

code: set.seed(456) n <- 250 x1 <- rnorm(n) true_beta_pois <- c(0.3, 0.5, -0.4) lambda <- exp(true_beta_pois[1] + true_beta_pois[2] * x1) y_count <- rpois(n, lambda) glm_pois <- glm(y_count ~ x1, family = poisson) knitr::kable(coef(summary(glm_pois)), digits = 4,              caption = "Reference: glm() Poisson regression") X_pois <- cbind(1, x1) Data_pois <- list(     parm.names = c("beta0", "beta1"),     mon.names  = "LL",     X = X_pois, y = y_count, n = n, N = n ) Model_pois <- function(parm, Data) {     eta    <- Data$X %*% parm     lambda <- exp(eta)     LL     <- sum(dpois(Data$y, lambda, log = TRUE))     list(LP = LL, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = LL,          yhat = rpois(Data$n, lambda), parm = parm) } fit_pois <- LaplaceApproximation(Model_pois, c(0, 0), Data_pois,                                  Iterations = 200, Method = "SPG",                                  sir = FALSE) fs_pois <- freq_summary(fit_pois) print(fs_pois) comp_pois <- data.frame(     glm.Estimate     = coef(summary(glm_pois))[, 1],     glm.SE           = coef(summary(glm_pois))[, 2],     Laplace.Estimate = fs_pois$coefficients[, "Estimate"],     Laplace.SE       = fs_pois$coefficients[, "Std.Error"] ) knitr::kable(comp_pois, digits = 4,              caption = "Poisson regression: glm() vs Laplace") ic_pois_lucifer <- freq_ic(fit_pois, n = n) ic_pois_glm <- c(AIC = AIC(glm_pois), BIC = BIC(glm_pois)) knitr::kable(data.frame(lucifer = ic_pois_lucifer[c("AIC", "BIC")],                          glm = ic_pois_glm),              digits = 2, caption = "Information criteria: lucifer vs glm()")

text: Nonlinear regression Bayesian machinery begins add genuine value classical optimizers. use Michaelis-Menten kinetics running example: \[y_i = \frac{V_{\max} \cdot x_i}{K_m + x_i} + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\] model three parameters (\(V_{\max}\), \(K_m\), \(\sigma\)), nonlinear mean function, potentially asymmetric confidence regions parameterization intrinsically curved [1]. MCMC handles naturally; nls() can struggle starting values convergence. Vmax estimate lucifer match nls() output closely. Km sigma parameters log scale lucifer, direct comparison requires back-transformation; point estimates can compared via exp() lucifer output. nonlinear models, profile likelihood curves provide accurate confidence intervals Wald approximation. profile_likelihood() function works directly lucifer fit object, computing profiles fixing parameter re-optimizing nuisance parameters: asymmetry ratios log.Km log.sigma typically 1.0 linear regression case, indicating Wald approximation less adequate. profile intervals (solid vertical lines) may differ visibly Wald intervals (dashed teal lines), particularly rate constant \(K_m\). Residual diagnostics nonlinear fit: Data cloning provides alternative route profile likelihood curves via plot(fit_dc, type = "profile"):
code: set.seed(789) x_mm <- seq(0.1, 10, length.out = 50) true_Vmax <- 5.0 true_Km   <- 2.0 true_sigma_mm <- 0.3 y_mm <- true_Vmax * x_mm / (true_Km + x_mm) + rnorm(50, 0, true_sigma_mm) nls_fit <- nls(y_mm ~ Vmax * x_mm / (Km + x_mm),                start = list(Vmax = 4, Km = 1)) knitr::kable(coef(summary(nls_fit)), digits = 4,              caption = "Reference: nls() Michaelis-Menten fit") Data_mm <- list(     parm.names = c("Vmax", "log.Km", "log.sigma"),     mon.names  = "LL",     x = x_mm, y = y_mm, n = 50, N = 50 ) Model_mm <- function(parm, Data) {     Vmax  <- parm[1]     Km    <- exp(parm[2])     sigma <- exp(parm[3])     mu    <- Vmax * Data$x / (Km + Data$x)     LL    <- sum(dnorm(Data$y, mu, sigma, log = TRUE))     list(LP = LL, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = LL,          yhat = rnorm(Data$n, mu, sigma), parm = parm) } fit_mm <- LaplaceApproximation(Model_mm, c(4, log(1), log(0.5)),                                Data_mm, Iterations = 300,                                Method = "SPG", sir = FALSE) fs_mm <- freq_summary(fit_mm) print(fs_mm) nls_coef <- coef(nls_fit) comp_nls <- data.frame(     nls      = c(nls_coef["Vmax"], nls_coef["Km"]),     Laplace  = c(fs_mm$coefficients["Vmax", "Estimate"],                  exp(fs_mm$coefficients["log.Km", "Estimate"])) ) rownames(comp_nls) <- c("Vmax", "Km") knitr::kable(comp_nls, digits = 4,              caption = "Michaelis-Menten: nls() vs Laplace (Km back-transformed)") prof_mm <- profile_likelihood(fit_mm, Model_mm, Data_mm) summary(prof_mm) plot(prof_mm) rd_mm <- freq_residuals(fit_mm, Model_mm, Data_mm) plot(rd_mm) fit_dc_mm <- DataCloning(Model_mm, Data_mm,                          Initial.Values = c(4, log(1), log(0.5)),                          n_clones = c(1, 2, 4, 8, 16),                          Algorithm = "NUTS", Iterations = 5000) plot(fit_dc_mm, type = "profile", Model = Model_mm, Data = Data_mm)

title: The frequentist bridge: maximum likelihood inference with Bayesian machinery in lucifer
text: Hierarchical models present strongest case frequentist bridge. random-intercept model \[y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{ij} + u_j + \varepsilon_{ij}, \qquad u_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_u^2), \quad \varepsilon_{ij} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\] can fitted either integrating random effects (marginal likelihood) treating parameters. lucifer can . compare nlme::lme() method = "ML" (REML, since flat priors target marginal ML, restricted ML). lucifer, write marginal likelihood integrating \(u_j\) analytically. random-intercept model, marginal distribution \(\mathbf{y}_j = (y_{j1}, \ldots, y_{jn_j})^T\) multivariate normal: \[\mathbf{y}_j \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\beta_0 \mathbf{1} + \beta_1 \mathbf{x}_j,\; \sigma_u^2 \mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^T + \sigma^2 \right)\] Two points deserve attention. First, lme() method = "REML" estimates variance components differently method = "ML". flat-prior lucifer model targets ML log-posterior equals full marginal log-likelihood, restricted log-likelihood. variance component comparison, always use method = "ML" lme() side. Second, \(\sigma_u^2\) near zero, MLE can lie boundary parameter space (exactly zero), log-scale parameterization lucifer maps \(-\infty\). Data cloning’s identifiability diagnostic can detect boundary issue.
code: set.seed(321) n_groups  <- 20 n_per     <- 10 n_total   <- n_groups * n_per group     <- rep(1:n_groups, each = n_per) x_mixed   <- rnorm(n_total) true_b0   <- 2.0 true_b1   <- 1.5 true_su   <- 0.8 true_se   <- 0.5 u         <- rnorm(n_groups, 0, true_su) y_mixed   <- true_b0 + true_b1 * x_mixed + u[group] + rnorm(n_total, 0, true_se) df_mixed <- data.frame(y = y_mixed, x = x_mixed, group = factor(group)) lme_fit <- nlme::lme(y ~ x, random = ~ 1 | group, data = df_mixed,                      method = "ML") knitr::kable(summary(lme_fit)$tTable, digits = 4,              caption = "Fixed effects (nlme::lme, method = ML)") vc <- data.frame(     Component = c("sigma_u (random intercept)", "sigma_e (residual)"),     Estimate  = c(as.numeric(nlme::VarCorr(lme_fit)[1, "StdDev"]),                   lme_fit$sigma),     True      = c(true_su, true_se) ) knitr::kable(vc, digits = 4, row.names = FALSE,              caption = "Variance components: lme vs true values") Data_mixed <- list(     parm.names = c("beta0", "beta1", "log.sigma_u", "log.sigma_e"),     mon.names  = "LL",     y = y_mixed, x = x_mixed, group = group,     n = n_total, N = n_total,     n_groups = n_groups, n_per = n_per )  Model_mixed <- function(parm, Data) {     beta0   <- parm[1]     beta1   <- parm[2]     sigma_u <- exp(parm[3])     sigma_e <- exp(parm[4])      ## Marginal log-likelihood: sum over groups     LL <- 0     for (j in seq_len(Data$n_groups)) {         idx <- which(Data$group == j)         nj  <- length(idx)         mu_j <- beta0 + beta1 * Data$x[idx]         ## Marginal covariance: sigma_u^2 * 11' + sigma_e^2 * I         V_j <- sigma_u^2 * matrix(1, nj, nj) + sigma_e^2 * diag(nj)         diff <- Data$y[idx] - mu_j         ## Use Woodbury for efficiency (not critical for nj=10)         cholV <- chol(V_j)         log_det <- 2 * sum(log(diag(cholV)))         z <- backsolve(cholV, diff, transpose = TRUE)         LL <- LL - 0.5 * (nj * log(2 * pi) + log_det + sum(z^2))     }      yhat <- beta0 + beta1 * Data$x     list(LP = LL, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = LL,          yhat = rnorm(Data$n, yhat, sigma_e), parm = parm) }  fit_mixed <- LaplaceApproximation(Model_mixed, c(0, 0, 0, 0),                                   Data_mixed, Iterations = 300,                                   Method = "SPG", sir = FALSE) fs_mixed <- freq_summary(fit_mixed) print(fs_mixed)

text: Right-censored survival data Weibull model demonstrate bridge model class likelihood takes non-standard form. observation \(\) event time \(t_i\) censoring indicator \(\delta_i\): \[\ell(\theta) = \sum_{=1}^n \left[\delta_i \log f(t_i \mid \theta) + (1 - \delta_i) \log S(t_i \mid \theta)\right]\] \(f\) Weibull density \(S\) survival function. Weibull parameterization used survival::survreg() accelerated failure time (AFT) model: \(\log(T) = \mu + \sigma W\) \(W \sim \text{EV}(0, 1)\) standard extreme value. advantage lucifer approach extensibility: user can replace Weibull density custom hazard function, add time-varying covariates, introduce frailties, within Model interface. survreg() limited fixed set parametric families.
code: set.seed(654) n <- 200 x_surv <- rnorm(n) ## Weibull AFT: log(T) = mu + sigma * W true_mu_surv    <- 2.0 true_beta_surv  <- 0.5 true_scale_surv <- 0.8 log_t <- true_mu_surv + true_beta_surv * x_surv +          true_scale_surv * log(rexp(n)) t_event <- exp(log_t) ## Random right censoring cens_time <- rexp(n, rate = 0.05) time_obs  <- pmin(t_event, cens_time) status    <- as.integer(t_event <= cens_time) knitr::kable(data.frame(Metric = "Censoring rate",                         Value = round(1 - mean(status), 3)),              row.names = FALSE) library(survival) surv_fit <- survreg(Surv(time_obs, status) ~ x_surv, dist = "weibull") summary(surv_fit) Data_surv <- list(     parm.names = c("mu", "beta", "log.scale"),     mon.names  = "LL",     x = x_surv, time = time_obs, status = status,     n = n, N = n )  Model_surv <- function(parm, Data) {     mu    <- parm[1]     beta  <- parm[2]     scale <- exp(parm[3])  # Weibull scale = 1/shape in survreg param     eta   <- mu + beta * Data$x      ## Standardized residuals     z <- (log(Data$time) - eta) / scale      ## Log-likelihood (extreme value / Gumbel minimum distribution)     ## f(z) = exp(z - exp(z)),  S(z) = exp(-exp(z))     LL <- sum(Data$status * (z - exp(z) - log(scale) - log(Data$time)) +               (1 - Data$status) * (-exp(z)))      list(LP = LL, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = LL,          yhat = rep(0, Data$n), parm = parm) }  fit_surv <- LaplaceApproximation(Model_surv, c(2, 0.5, log(0.8)),                                  Data_surv, Iterations = 300,                                  Method = "SPG", sir = FALSE) fs_surv <- freq_summary(fit_surv) print(fs_surv)  ## Compare lucifer vs survreg vs true values mle_surv <- fs_surv$coefficients[, "Estimate"] survreg_coef <- coef(surv_fit) surv_compare <- data.frame(     Parameter = c("mu (Intercept)", "beta (x)", "log(scale)"),     True      = c(true_mu_surv, true_beta_surv, log(true_scale_surv)),     lucifer   = as.numeric(mle_surv),     survreg   = c(as.numeric(survreg_coef), log(surv_fit$scale)) ) knitr::kable(surv_compare, digits = 4, row.names = FALSE,              caption = "Survival model: lucifer vs survreg vs true values")

text: simple linear regression simulated data known parameters demonstrates basic usage auto-FC. true values fall within 95% credible intervals. acceptance rate exactly 1.
code: library(lucifer) library(ggplot2) set.seed(42)  ## Simulate data n <- 200 true_beta <- c(2.0, -1.5, 0.8) true_sigma <- 1.5 X <- cbind(1, matrix(rnorm(n * 2), n, 2)) y <- rnorm(n, X %*% true_beta, true_sigma)  ## Data list Data <- list(     y = y, X = X, n = n,     parm.names = c("beta0", "beta1", "beta2", "sigma"),     mon.names = "LP",     pos.beta = 1:3,     pos.sigma = 4 )  ## Model Model <- function(parm, Data) {     beta  <- parm[Data$pos.beta]     sigma <- interval(parm[Data$pos.sigma], 1e-100, Inf)     parm[Data$pos.sigma] <- sigma     mu <- Data$X %*% beta     LL <- sum(dnorm(Data$y, mu, sigma, log = TRUE))     LP <- LL + sum(dnorm(beta, 0, 10, log = TRUE)) +         dhalfcauchy(sigma, 25, log = TRUE)     list(LP = LP, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = LP,          yhat = rnorm(Data$n, mu, sigma), parm = parm) }  ## Fit with auto-FC Gibbs (no Specs) fit <- lucifer(Model, Data,     Initial.Values = c(rep(0, 3), 1),     Iterations = 50000, Status = 10000,     Thinning = 50, Algorithm = "Gibbs",     Chains = 3)  ## Compare posteriors to truth post <- fit$Posterior1 true_vals <- c(true_beta, true_sigma) pnames <- Data$parm.names results <- data.frame(     Parameter = pnames,     True = true_vals,     Mean = sapply(seq_along(pnames), function(i) mean(post[, i])),     Lower = sapply(seq_along(pnames), function(i) quantile(post[, i], 0.025)),     Upper = sapply(seq_along(pnames), function(i) quantile(post[, i], 0.975)),     row.names = NULL ) results$Coverage <- ifelse(true_vals >= results$Lower & true_vals <= results$Upper,                            "Yes", "No") knitr::kable(results, digits = 3, align = "lrrrrr",              col.names = c("Parameter", "True", "Mean", "2.5%", "97.5%", "Covered"),              caption = "Posterior summaries vs. true values (linear regression)") ## Posterior density vs. true values via lucifer's native ground-truth grid gt_lin <- setNames(true_vals, pnames) plot(fit, ground_truth = gt_lin)

code: set.seed(42)  ## Same data as Example 1, but introduce missing values n <- 200 true_beta <- c(2.0, -1.5, 0.8) true_sigma <- 1.5 X <- cbind(1, matrix(rnorm(n * 2), n, 2)) y_complete <- rnorm(n, X %*% true_beta, true_sigma)  ## Randomly mask 20% of observations missing_idx <- sort(sample(n, 40)) y_obs <- y_complete y_obs[missing_idx] <- NA n_miss <- length(missing_idx)  ## Augment parameter vector: original params + imputed y values parm.names <- c("beta0", "beta1", "beta2", "sigma",                 paste0("y_imp_", missing_idx)) n_parm <- length(parm.names) pos.beta  <- 1:3 pos.sigma <- 4 pos.imp   <- 5:n_parm  Data <- list(     y_obs = y_obs, X = X, n = n,     missing_idx = missing_idx,     n_miss = n_miss,     parm.names = parm.names,     mon.names = "LP",     pos.beta = pos.beta,     pos.sigma = pos.sigma,     pos.imp = pos.imp )  ## Model: fill in missing y from parameters before computing likelihood Model <- function(parm, Data) {     beta  <- parm[Data$pos.beta]     sigma <- interval(parm[Data$pos.sigma], 1e-100, Inf)     parm[Data$pos.sigma] <- sigma      ## Reconstruct complete y     y <- Data$y_obs     y[Data$missing_idx] <- parm[Data$pos.imp]      mu <- Data$X %*% beta     LL <- sum(dnorm(y, mu, sigma, log = TRUE))     LP <- LL + sum(dnorm(beta, 0, 10, log = TRUE)) +         dhalfcauchy(sigma, 25, log = TRUE)     list(LP = LP, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = LP,          yhat = rnorm(Data$n, mu, sigma), parm = parm) }  ## Initial values: 0 for betas, 1 for sigma, mean(y_obs) for imputed iv <- c(rep(0, 3), 1, rep(mean(y_obs, na.rm = TRUE), n_miss))  fit_miss <- lucifer(Model, Data,     Initial.Values = iv,     Iterations = 1000, Status = 100,     Thinning = 1, Algorithm = "Gibbs",     Chains = 3)  ## Check regression parameters (should match Example 1 closely) post <- fit_miss$Posterior1 true_reg <- c(true_beta, true_sigma) reg_results <- data.frame(     Parameter = parm.names[1:4],     True = true_reg,     Mean = sapply(1:4, function(i) mean(post[, i])),     SD = sapply(1:4, function(i) sd(post[, i])),     Lower = sapply(1:4, function(i) quantile(post[, i], 0.025)),     Upper = sapply(1:4, function(i) quantile(post[, i], 0.975)),     row.names = NULL ) knitr::kable(reg_results, digits = 3, align = "lrrrrr",              col.names = c("Parameter", "True", "Mean", "SD", "2.5%", "97.5%"),              caption = "Posterior summaries with 20% missing data")  ## Check imputed values against truth imp_means <- colMeans(post[, pos.imp]) imp_rmse <- sqrt(mean((imp_means - y_complete[missing_idx])^2)) knitr::kable(data.frame(Metric = "RMSE (imputed vs. true)", Value = round(imp_rmse, 3)),              align = "lr", col.names = c("Metric", "Value"),              caption = "Imputation accuracy") plot_imputed(fit_miss, data = y_obs, ground_truth = y_complete) plot_imputed(fit_miss, data = y_obs, Style = "ribbon",              ground_truth = y_complete) plot_imputed(fit_miss, data = y_obs, Style = "draws", n_draws = 80,              ground_truth = y_complete)

code: set.seed(13) Tt <- 60; J <- 3 true_phi   <- c(0.7, -0.4, 0.85) true_sigma <- c(0.4, 0.6, 0.3)  ## Simulate three independent AR(1) processes Y_complete <- matrix(0, Tt, J) for (j in 1:J) {     Y_complete[1, j] <- rnorm(1, 0, true_sigma[j])     for (t in 2:Tt) {         Y_complete[t, j] <- true_phi[j] * Y_complete[t - 1, j] +             rnorm(1, 0, true_sigma[j])     } } colnames(Y_complete) <- c("series A", "series B", "series C")  ## Mask: 8 NAs in series A, 5 NAs in series C, series B complete Y_obs <- Y_complete Y_obs[sort(sample(2:Tt,  8)), 1] <- NA Y_obs[sort(sample(2:Tt,  5)), 3] <- NA  ## NA positions in column-major order (lucifer convention) na_flat <- which(is.na(as.vector(Y_obs))) n_imp   <- length(na_flat) n_imp parm.names <- c(paste0("phi[",   1:J, "]"),                 paste0("sigma[", 1:J, "]"),                 paste0("y_imp[", na_flat, "]"))  Data_mv <- list(     Y          = Y_obs, Tt = Tt, J = J,     na_flat    = na_flat,     parm.names = parm.names,     mon.names  = "LP",     pos.phi    = 1:J,     pos.sigma  = (J + 1):(2 * J),     pos.imp    = (2 * J + 1):(2 * J + n_imp) )  Model_mv <- function(parm, Data) {     phi   <- parm[Data$pos.phi]     sigma <- interval(parm[Data$pos.sigma], 1e-100, Inf)     parm[Data$pos.sigma] <- sigma      ## Reconstruct the complete matrix by filling NAs from the     ## augmented parameter vector     Yfull <- Data$Y     Yfull[Data$na_flat] <- parm[Data$pos.imp]      LL <- 0     for (j in 1:Data$J) {         LL <- LL + sum(dnorm(Yfull[-1, j],                              phi[j] * Yfull[-Data$Tt, j],                              sigma[j], log = TRUE))     }     LP <- LL +         sum(dnorm(phi, 0, 1, log = TRUE)) +         sum(dhalfcauchy(sigma, 5, log = TRUE))     list(LP = LP, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = LP,          yhat = as.vector(Yfull), parm = parm) }  iv_mv  <- c(rep(0, J), rep(0.5, J), rep(0, n_imp)) fit_mv <- lucifer(Model_mv, Data_mv, iv_mv,                   Iterations = 1000, Status = 1000,                   Thinning = 5, Algorithm = "Gibbs", Chains = 1) plot_imputed(fit_mv, data = Y_obs, ground_truth = Y_complete) plot_imputed(fit_mv, data = Y_obs, Style = "ribbon",              ground_truth = Y_complete)

code: Model <- function(parm, Data) {     alpha <- parm[Data$pos.alpha]     Gamma <- matrix(parm[Data$pos.Gamma], Data$J, Data$J)     Phi   <- matrix(parm[Data$pos.Phi],   Data$J, Data$J)     Phi.Sigma <- ifelse(Gamma == 1, sqrt(10), 0.1)     sigma <- interval(parm[Data$pos.sigma], 1e-100, Inf)     parm[Data$pos.sigma] <- sigma      ## Log-prior     alpha.prior <- sum(dnormv(alpha, 0, 1000, log = TRUE))     Gamma.prior <- sum(dbern(Gamma, 0.5, log = TRUE))     Phi.prior   <- sum(dnorm(Phi, 0, Phi.Sigma, log = TRUE))     sigma.prior <- sum(dhalfcauchy(sigma, 25, log = TRUE))      ## Log-likelihood     mu <- matrix(alpha, Data$TT - 1, Data$J, byrow = TRUE) +         Data$Y[1:(Data$TT - 1), ] %*% t(Gamma * Phi)     Sigma_mat <- matrix(sigma, Data$TT - 1, Data$J, byrow = TRUE)     LL <- sum(dnorm(Data$Y[2:Data$TT, ], mu, Sigma_mat, log = TRUE))      LP <- LL + alpha.prior + Gamma.prior + Phi.prior + sigma.prior     yhat <- rnorm(length(mu), mu, Sigma_mat)     list(LP = LP, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = LP,          yhat = yhat, parm = parm) }

title: Gibbs sampling in lucifer
text: Holding parameters fixed, log-posterior function \(\alpha_j\) quadratic, yielding normal full conditional. Define residuals excluding \(\alpha_j\): \[r_{t,j} = Y_{t,j} - \sum_{p=1}^{P} \sum_{=1}^{J} \Gamma_{,j,p}\, \Phi_{,j,p}\, Y_{t - L_p,\, }, \qquad t = L_P + 1, \ldots, T.\] \(r_{t,j} \sim \mathcal{N}(\alpha_j, \sigma_j^2)\) independently, prior \(\alpha_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1000)\): \[\alpha_j \mid \text{rest} \sim \mathcal{N}(m_j, v_j),\] \(v_j = (T_{\text{eff}} / \sigma_j^2 + 1/1000)^{-1}\) \(m_j = v_j \cdot \sum_t r_{t,j} / \sigma_j^2\), \(T_{\text{eff}} = T - L_P\).

code: FC_varssvs <- function(parm, Data) {     alpha <- parm[Data$pos.alpha]     Gamma <- matrix(parm[Data$pos.Gamma], Data$J, Data$J)     Phi   <- matrix(parm[Data$pos.Phi],   Data$J, Data$J)     sigma <- interval(parm[Data$pos.sigma], 1e-100, Inf)     T_eff <- Data$TT - Data$L[Data$P]     t_idx <- (Data$L[Data$P] + 1):Data$TT      ## --- alpha_j ---     for (j in 1:Data$J) {         resid_j <- Data$Y[t_idx, j]         t_lag <- (Data$L[Data$P] - Data$L[1] + 1):(Data$TT - Data$L[1])         resid_j <- resid_j -             Data$Y[t_lag, ] %*% (Gamma[, j] * Phi[, j])         prec <- T_eff / sigma[j]^2 + 1 / 1000         m_j  <- sum(resid_j) / sigma[j]^2 / prec         alpha[j] <- rnorm(1, m_j, 1 / sqrt(prec))     }      ## --- Gamma_{i,k} and Phi_{i,k} ---     for (k in 1:Data$J) {         for (i in 1:Data$J) {             t_lag <- (Data$L[Data$P] - Data$L[1] + 1):(Data$TT - Data$L[1])             x_t <- Data$Y[t_lag, i]             ## Residual for Y_{t,k} excluding this term             resid_ik <- Data$Y[t_idx, k] - alpha[k]             for (ii in 1:Data$J) {                 if (ii == i) next                 resid_ik <- resid_ik -                     Gamma[ii, k] * Phi[ii, k] * Data$Y[t_lag, ii]             }              ## Gamma_{i,k}: compare LP at 0 and 1             lp1 <- log(0.5) + dnorm(Phi[i, k], 0, sqrt(10), log = TRUE) +                 sum(dnorm(resid_ik, Phi[i, k] * x_t, sigma[k], log = TRUE))             lp0 <- log(0.5) + dnorm(Phi[i, k], 0, 0.1, log = TRUE) +                 sum(dnorm(resid_ik, 0, sigma[k], log = TRUE))             prob1 <- 1 / (1 + exp(lp0 - lp1))             Gamma[i, k] <- rbinom(1, 1, prob1)              ## Phi_{i,k} | Gamma_{i,k}             if (Gamma[i, k] == 0) {                 Phi[i, k] <- rnorm(1, 0, 0.1)             } else {                 prec_prior <- 1 / 10                 prec_lik   <- sum(x_t^2) / sigma[k]^2                 v <- 1 / (prec_prior + prec_lik)                 m <- v * sum(resid_ik * x_t) / sigma[k]^2                 Phi[i, k] <- rnorm(1, m, sqrt(v))             }         }     }      ## sigma unchanged (sampled by MWG)     c(alpha, as.vector(Gamma), as.vector(Phi), sigma) } fit_manual <- lucifer(Model, MyData,     Initial.Values = IV,     Iterations = 10000, Status = 1000,     Thinning = 10, Algorithm = "Gibbs",     Specs = list(FC = FC_varssvs, MWG = pos.sigma),     Chains = 3)
