what: Architecture: how Stan, JAGS, and lucifer differ
title: Interoperability: bridging Stan, JAGS, and the R posterior ecosystem in lucifer
text: three systems make fundamentally different design choices model representation, compilation strategy, sampler architecture. JAGS uses interpreted, graph-based approach. user writes model BUGS language, specifying stochastic deterministic nodes. JAGS builds directed acyclic graph (DAG) specification exploits conjugacy relationships select efficient samplers node. Normal-normal, gamma-Poisson, beta-binomial conjugate pairs handled Gibbs sampling exact conditional distributions; non-conjugate nodes receive Metropolis-Hastings updates slice sampling. graph-aware strategy means JAGS can remarkably efficient hierarchical models many conjugate relationships, struggles highly correlated posteriors models lack conjugacy. Stan takes opposite approach. Models compiled C++ code evaluates log-posterior density gradient via reverse-mode automatic differentiation. NUTS sampler explores posterior using Hamiltonian dynamics, adapting step size mass matrix warmup. Stan’s strength generality: model differentiable log-density can sampled efficiently, regardless conjugacy. price compilation time (30-60 seconds new model) restriction continuous parameters (discrete parameters must marginalized ). lucifer occupies middle ground. text: Stan compiles model C++ requires working C++ toolchain host. prerequisites per platform : Rtools Windows (match version R installation, available CRAN https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/); Xcode Command Line Tools macOS (install xcode-select --install, configure via rstan quickstart guide); build-essential plus libv8-dev Debian/Ubuntu (sudo apt install build-essential libv8-dev) @development-tools Fedora/RHEL. toolchain place, four R packages wrap Stan installed independently: four Stan wrappers, rstanarm one works without user-level C++ toolchain, models pre-compiled package build time. makes easiest entry point applied users want fit generalised linear mixed models without writing Stan code without setting Rtools Xcode. brms provides comparably high-level interface compiles new model runtime, inherits full toolchain requirement. rstan low-level hand-written Stan route, cmdstanr modern, lightweight alternative rstan faster compilation smaller memory footprint, cost one-time install_cmdstan() step fetches builds CmdStan binary. rstantools package occasionally comes context; developer-side scaffolding tool used create new R packages embed Stan code. code: # Low-level Stan interface; writing Stan code by hand install.packages("rstan")  # High-level formula interface; compiles to Stan code under the hood install.packages("brms")  # Pre-compiled GLM/GLMM collection; no compilation at runtime install.packages("rstanarm")  # CmdStanR: the modern, lightweight alternative to rstan install.packages("cmdstanr",                  repos = c("https://stan-dev.r-universe.dev",                            getOption("repos"))) # After installing the R package, fetch and compile the CmdStan binary # (one-time, ~5 min). This is the only step that requires the full # C++ toolchain; subsequent model fits reuse the compiled CmdStan. cmdstanr::install_cmdstan()

title: Interoperability: bridging Stan, JAGS, and the R posterior ecosystem in lucifer
text: lucifer accepts either model_spec() DSL specification raw Model function returns five-element contract list(LP, Dev, Monitor, yhat, parm). 8-schools use raw function lets us express non-centered parameterisation three lines monitor derived \(\theta_j\) alongside sampled \((\eta_j, \mu, \tau)\). interval() wrapper enforces \(\tau > 0\) transparently, samplers can propose unconstrained moves without explicit log-transform bookkeeping.
code: parm_names <- c(paste0("eta[", 1:J, "]"), "mu", "tau") mon_names  <- c("LP", "mu", "tau", paste0("theta[", 1:J, "]"))  Model_8s <- function(parm, Data) {     eta   <- parm[1:Data$J]     mu    <- parm[Data$J + 1]     tau   <- parm[Data$J + 2]     tau   <- interval(tau, 1e-10, Inf)     parm[Data$J + 2] <- tau      # Deterministic: theta_j = mu + tau * eta_j (non-centered)     theta <- mu + tau * eta      # log-priors on the unconstrained (eta, mu, tau)     lp <- sum(dnorm(eta, 0, 1, log = TRUE)) +           dnorm(mu, 0, 10, log = TRUE) +           dhalfcauchy(tau, 5, log = TRUE)      # log-likelihood on the derived theta     LL <- sum(dnorm(Data$y, theta, Data$sigma, log = TRUE))      LP <- LL + lp     list(LP      = LP,          Dev     = -2 * LL,          Monitor = c(LP = LP, mu = mu, tau = tau, theta),          yhat    = rnorm(length(Data$y), theta, Data$sigma),          parm    = parm) }  Data_luc <- list(J = J, y = y_obs, sigma = sigma_obs,                  parm.names = parm_names, mon.names = mon_names) IV <- c(rep(0, J), mean(y_obs), 5) names(IV) <- parm_names

text: extract posterior means 95% credible intervals \(\mu\), \(\tau\), \(\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_8\) every fit, harmonise parameter names across engines (brms uses b_Intercept \(\mu\) r_school[j,Intercept] centered offset; rstanarm uses b[(Intercept) school:X]; lucifer stores \(\theta_j\) Monitor matrix), plot 14 engines side side faceted engine family.
code: library(ggplot2)  extract_post <- function(name, f) {     get_luc_theta_mutau <- function(eta_mat, mu_vec, tau_vec) {         theta <- sapply(seq_len(J), function(j)             mu_vec + tau_vec * eta_mat[, j])         colnames(theta) <- paste0("theta[", 1:J, "]")         cbind(theta, mu = mu_vec, tau = tau_vec)     }     if (name %in% c("rjags", "runjags", "rstan")) {         P <- f$Posterior1         return(P[, c(paste0("theta[", 1:J, "]"), "mu", "tau"),                  drop = FALSE])     }     if (name == "brms") {         P <- f$Posterior1         mu <- P[, "b_Intercept"]         tau <- P[, "sd_school__Intercept"]         theta <- sapply(1:J, function(j)             P[, paste0("r_school[", LETTERS[j], ",Intercept]")] + mu)         colnames(theta) <- paste0("theta[", 1:J, "]")         return(cbind(theta, mu = mu, tau = tau))     }     if (name == "rstanarm") {         P <- f$Posterior1; cn <- colnames(P)         intercept_col <- cn[cn == "(Intercept)"][1]         tau_col <- grep("^Sigma\\[school:", cn, value = TRUE)[1]         b_cols <- grep("^b\\[\\(Intercept\\) school:", cn, value = TRUE)         b_cols <- grep("_NEW_", b_cols, invert = TRUE, value = TRUE)         b_cols <- b_cols[order(sub(".*school:(.).*", "\\1", b_cols))]         mu <- P[, intercept_col]         tau <- sqrt(P[, tau_col])         theta <- sapply(seq_along(b_cols),                         function(i) P[, b_cols[i]] + mu)         colnames(theta) <- paste0("theta[", 1:J, "]")         return(cbind(theta, mu = mu, tau = tau))     }     # lucifer fits (non-centered): reconstruct theta from eta, mu, tau     P <- if (!is.null(f$Posterior2) && is.matrix(f$Posterior2) &&              nrow(f$Posterior2) > 0) f$Posterior2 else          if (!is.null(f$Posterior1)) f$Posterior1 else          if (!is.null(f$Posterior) && is.matrix(f$Posterior) &&              nrow(f$Posterior) > 1) f$Posterior else NULL     if (is.null(P)) return(NULL)     eta_mat <- P[, paste0("eta[", 1:J, "]"), drop = FALSE]     return(get_luc_theta_mutau(eta_mat, P[, "mu"], P[, "tau"])) }  posts <- lapply(names(fits), function(nm) extract_post(nm, fits[[nm]])) names(posts) <- names(fits) posts <- Filter(Negate(is.null), posts)  pretty_params <- c("mu", "tau", paste0("theta[", 1:J, "]")) comp_rows <- list() for (nm in names(posts)) {     for (p in pretty_params) {         v <- posts[[nm]][, p] title: Introduction to lucifer: a complete Bayesian inference workflow
text: lucifer package modern continuation LaplacesDemon, one earliest ambitious R packages general-purpose Bayesian inference. Bayesian software constrains user fixed model grammar (BUGS, JAGS, Stan), lucifer takes fundamentally different approach: user writes plain R function evaluates log-posterior parameter vector, package provides computational machinery explore posterior. design places restrictions model structure. probability model can expressed R function, including hierarchical specifications, mixture models, state-space systems, stochastic differential equations, models custom likelihoods closed-form density, can fitted without modification interface. package grown substantially beyond origins. current release implements 130 inference algorithms spanning eight families: 82 MCMC samplers organized across 13 subcategories (gradient-based, adaptive random-walk, componentwise, slice, ensemble, quasi-Monte Carlo, geometric, piecewise-deterministic, multimodal tempering, constraint-handling, flow-enhanced, surrogate, augmentation methods), 8 variational Bayes algorithms, 18 Laplace optimizers, 3 iterative quadrature methods, population Monte Carlo, sequential Monte Carlo, 4 approximate Bayesian computation methods, 6 simulation-based inference methods. C++ backend OpenMP parallelization accelerates core computations, model specification DSL (model_spec()) allows declarative model building compiles native C++ additional speed. unifying contract across methods single Model function signature Model(parm, Data) returns list containing five elements: LP (log-posterior), Dev (deviance, equal \(-2 \times\) log-likelihood), Monitor (quantities track), yhat (fitted values posterior predictive checks), parm (parameter vector constraint enforcement). contract means every diagnostic, comparison, visualization tool package works identically regardless inference engine produced fit. package name continues historical thread. Pierre-Simon Laplace independently developed Bayes’ theorem 1774, “Essai Philosophique sur les Probabilites” (1814) envisioned vast intellect , given complete knowledge present state universe, predict future states. Later biographers called hypothetical intellect Lucifer, light-bearer. package aspires goal: bringing computational light high-dimensional posterior distributions otherwise remain opaque. vignette guided tour complete Bayesian workflow. code: Model_manual <- function(parm, Data) {     # Extract parameters     beta0 <- parm[1]     beta1 <- parm[2]      # Enforce constraints: sigma > 0, nu > 2     sigma <- interval(parm[3], 1e-100, Inf)     parm[3] <- sigma     nu <- interval(parm[4], 2, Inf)     parm[4] <- nu      # Deterministic transformation     mu <- beta0 + beta1 * Data$x      # Log-likelihood     LL <- sum(dst(Data$y, mu = mu, sigma = sigma, nu = nu, log = TRUE))      # Log-prior     LP <- LL +         dnormv(beta0, 0, 10^2, log = TRUE) +         dnormv(beta1, 0, 10^2, log = TRUE) +         dhalfcauchy(sigma, 2.5, log = TRUE) +         dexp(nu - 2, rate = 0.1, log = TRUE)      # Fitted values for posterior predictive checks     yhat <- mu      # Monitored quantities     Monitor <- LP      return(list(LP = LP, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = Monitor,                 yhat = yhat, parm = parm)) } Data_manual <- list(     x = x, y = y, N = N,     mon.names = "LP",     parm.names = c("beta0", "beta1", "sigma", "nu") ) IV_manual <- c(0, 0, 1, 5)

code: ## PG is restricted to logistic / binomial / negative-binomial regression ## with a logit link, and so cannot fit the Gaussian linear regression ## model used by every other example in this vignette. The snippet below ## defines a self-contained logistic regression and runs PG on it. set.seed(42) N_pg  <- 200L X_pg  <- cbind(1, rnorm(N_pg), rnorm(N_pg)) beta_true <- c(-0.5, 1.2, -0.8) y_pg  <- rbinom(N_pg, 1, 1 / (1 + exp(-as.vector(X_pg %*% beta_true))))  Data_pg <- list(N = N_pg, J = ncol(X_pg), X = X_pg, y = y_pg,                 mon.names = "LP", parm.names = paste0("beta", 1:3),                 PGF = function(Data) rnorm(Data$J))  Model_pg <- function(parm, Data) {     eta <- as.vector(Data$X %*% parm)     LL  <- sum(Data$y * eta - log1p(exp(eta)))     LP  <- LL + sum(dnorm(parm, 0, 10, log = TRUE))     list(LP = LP, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = LP,          yhat = plogis(eta), parm = parm) }  IV_pg <- GIV(Model_pg, Data_pg, PGF = TRUE)  fit <- lucifer(Model_pg, Data_pg, IV_pg,                Iterations = 2000, Status = 1000, Thinning = 2,                Algorithm = "PG", Specs = NULL,                Chains = 3) plot(fit) ppc <- predict(fit, Model = Model_pg, Data = Data_pg) plot(ppc, Style = "Fitted", Data = Data_pg) ppc_dens_overlay(ppc) plot(fit, ground_truth = setNames(beta_true, Data_pg$parm.names))

text: New MCMC algorithm lucifer Randomized HMC introduced [80] modification standard Hamiltonian Monte Carlo draws trajectory length exponential distribution rather fixing . standard HMC, number leapfrog steps \(L\) fixed hyperparameter; poor choices \(L\) can cause near-periodic orbits degrade mixing. Randomized HMC eliminates problem drawing \(L \sim \text{Poisson}(\bar{L})\) (equivalently, running trajectory random time \(T \sim \text{Exp}(1/\bar{L})\)). randomization breaks periodicity produces sampler , continuous-time limit, converges PDMP ergodic without velocity refreshment. randomization also provides theoretical advantage: Bou-Rabee Sanz-Serna show randomized variant achieves faster convergence equilibrium deterministic variant certain target classes. Randomized HMC two algorithm specifications: epsilon leapfrog step size, mean_L mean Poisson distribution number leapfrog steps drawn (default 10). Metropolis acceptance step uses standard HMC accept/reject criterion based Hamiltonian error.

text: Initialize parameters \(\theta_0\), step size \(\epsilon\), mean trajectory length \(\bar{L}\) Draw momentum \(p \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_d)\) Draw number leapfrog steps \(L \sim \max(1, \text{Poisson}(\bar{L}))\) Integrate \(L\) leapfrog steps: \((\theta^*, p^*) = \text{Leapfrog}(\theta_{t-1}, p, \epsilon, L)\) Compute \(\log \alpha = \log \pi(\theta^*) - \frac{1}{2}\|p^*\|^2 - \log \pi(\theta_{t-1}) + \frac{1}{2}\|p\|^2\) probability \(\min(1, \exp(\log \alpha))\), accept \(\theta^*\); otherwise retain \(\theta_{t-1}\) Return \(\{\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_T\}\)

text: Riemannian geometric MCMC methods exploit curvature target distribution’s parameter space achieve efficient sampling. Instead treating parameter space flat Euclidean space (standard HMC constant mass matrix), methods equip space position-dependent metric tensor \(G(\theta)\) derived Fisher information matrix Hessian negative log-posterior. resulting dynamics follow geodesics statistical manifold, automatically adapting step sizes directions local geometry. particularly advantageous targets strong correlations, funnel geometries, varying curvature across parameter space.

title: A bestiary of the MCMC algorithms provided by lucifer
text: New MCMC algorithm lucifer Riemannian Manifold Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (RMHMC) introduced [81] extension HMC replaces constant mass matrix \(M\) position-dependent metric tensor \(G(\theta)\), typically chosen Fisher information matrix negative Hessian log-posterior. Hamiltonian becomes \(H(\theta, p) = -\log \pi(\theta) + \frac{1}{2}\log|G(\theta)| + \frac{1}{2}p^\top G(\theta)^{-1} p\), resulting dynamics follow geodesics statistical manifold. \(G(\theta)\) varies position, standard leapfrog integrator longer sufficient; RMHMC uses generalized leapfrog (implicit midpoint) integrator requires fixed-point iterations step. SoftAbs metric [82] provides smooth, positive-definite regularization Hessian avoids singularities can occur raw Hessian, using \(G(\theta) = H \cdot \text{coth}(\alpha H)\) \(H\) Hessian \(\alpha\) controls softness absolute value. RMHMC six algorithm specifications: epsilon leapfrog step size, L number leapfrog steps, metric selects metric tensor type ("softabs", "hessian", "identity", default "softabs"), softabs_alpha SoftAbs regularization parameter (default 1.0), fixedpoint_maxiter maximum number fixed-point iterations implicit integrator (default 8), fixedpoint_tol convergence tolerance fixed-point iterations (default \(10^{-6}\)).

text: New MCMC algorithm lucifer Relativistic Monte Carlo introduced [85] modification HMC replaces standard quadratic kinetic energy \(K(p) = \frac{1}{2}p^\top M^{-1}p\) relativistic kinetic energy \(K(p) = c\sqrt{\|p\|^2 + m^2c^2} - mc^2\), inspired special relativity. crucial property velocity \(\dot{\theta} = \nabla_p K = cp / \sqrt{\|p\|^2 + m^2c^2}\) bounded speed light \(c\), regardless large momentum becomes. imposes natural speed limit sampler, preventing catastrophically large jumps can occur standard HMC gradient large step size big. momentum marginal distribution becomes multivariate hyperbolic distribution (heavier tails Gaussian), makes sampler robust targets heavy tails varying curvature. \(c \\infty\), method reduces standard HMC. Relativistic MC three algorithm specifications: epsilon leapfrog step size, L number leapfrog steps, c speed light parameter (default 10.0). Smaller values \(c\) impose tighter speed limit produce conservative exploration.

text: New MCMC algorithm lucifer Projected Langevin dynamics studied [86] method sampling log-concave distributions convex sets. idea simple: run overdamped Langevin step \(\tilde{\theta} = \theta + \frac{\epsilon}{2}\nabla \log \pi(\theta) + \sqrt{\epsilon}\,\xi\) (\(\xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_d)\)) project back onto constraint set: \(\theta^* = \text{Proj}_{\mathcal{C}}(\tilde{\theta})\). box constraints \([, b]^d\), projection componentwise clamping \(\theta_j^* = \max(a_j, \min(b_j, \tilde{\theta}_j))\). simplex \(\{\theta : \theta_j \geq 0, \sum_j \theta_j = 1\}\), projection uses algorithm Duchi, Shalev-Shwartz, Singer, Chandra (2008), sorts components finds threshold KKT conditions. Metropolis correction applied, output asymptotic bias order \(O(\epsilon)\), often acceptable constrained problems alternative use transformation distorts geometry. Projected Langevin four algorithm specifications: epsilon step size, constraint constraint type ("box" "simplex", default "box"), lower vector lower bounds box constraints (default 0), upper vector upper bounds box constraints (default \(\infty\)).

title: A bestiary of the MCMC algorithms provided by lucifer
text: New MCMC algorithm lucifer ProxMCMC developed [87] framework sampling posterior distributions non-smooth penalty terms form \(\pi(\theta) \propto \exp(-f(\theta) - \lambda \cdot g(\theta))\), \(f\) smooth log-likelihood \(g\) non-smooth penalty (L1 norm, total variation, etc.). Standard gradient-based MCMC handle \(g\) differentiable everywhere. ProxMCMC replaces gradient step proximal step: instead \(\theta + \epsilon \nabla f(\theta)\), uses \(\text{prox}_{\epsilon \lambda g}(\theta + \epsilon \nabla f(\theta))\), proximal operator \(\text{prox}_{\tau g}(x) = \arg\min_z \{g(z) + \frac{1}{2\tau}\|z - x\|^2\}\). L1 penalty, proximal operator soft-thresholding function \(\text{sign}(x) \max(|x| - \tau\lambda, 0)\); total variation, TV denoising operator. proximal step handles non-smoothness exactly, Metropolis-Hastings correction ensures correct stationary distribution using Moreau-Yosida envelope \(g\) acceptance ratio. ProxMCMC three algorithm specifications: epsilon step size, prox penalty type ("l1" "tv", default "l1"), lambda_reg regularization strength (default 0.1).

previous_headings: Constraint-handling samplers exploreon restricted domains > ProxMCMC
title: A bestiary of the MCMC algorithms provided by lucifer
text: Initialize parameters \(\theta_0\), step size \(\epsilon\), penalty strength \(\lambda\) Compute smooth gradient \(g = \nabla f(\theta_{t-1})\) Gradient step: \(\tilde{\theta} = \theta_{t-1} + \epsilon g + \sqrt{2\epsilon}\,\xi\), \(\xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_d)\) Proximal step: \(\theta^* = \text{prox}_{\epsilon \lambda \|\cdot\|}(\tilde{\theta})\) Compute acceptance ratio using Moreau-Yosida envelope Accept probability \(\min(1, \alpha)\); otherwise retain \(\theta_{t-1}\) Return \(\{\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_T\}\)

text: New MCMC algorithm lucifer Pseudo-Marginal MCMC (PMCMC) introduced [89] formalized [88], proved replacing intractable likelihood unbiased estimate thereof still targets exact posterior distribution. key insight standard Metropolis-Hastings algorithm, log-posterior current position never re-evaluated, Model function returns noisy unbiased estimate log-likelihood, resulting Markov chain correct stationary distribution. makes PMCMC applicable problems likelihood computed analytically, instance models latent variables integrated via importance sampling particle filters. PMCMC one algorithm specification: B accepts list blocks defaults single block containing parameters. proposal mechanism identical Random-Walk Metropolis (RWM), using multivariate normal proposal centered current state proposal covariance matrix. essential difference RWM PMCMC never re-evaluates Model current parameter values proposal accepted; stores noisy log-posterior estimate acceptance step reuses subsequent comparisons. property critical: re-evaluating noisy likelihood point introduce bias, acceptance ratio longer unbiased estimate true Metropolis-Hastings ratio. practice, user must ensure Model function returns unbiased estimate log-likelihood log scale. Common strategies include importance sampling auxiliary variables, sequential Monte Carlo (particle filtering) state-space models, Monte Carlo integration marginalizing latent variables. variance log-likelihood estimate affects mixing: [90] recommend targeting variance approximately 1-3 log scale likelihood estimate, higher variance degrades acceptance rates lower variance wastes computational effort unnecessary precision. advantage PMCMC enables exact Bayesian inference (sense targeting correct posterior) models intractable likelihoods, requiring user can construct unbiased likelihood estimator. disadvantage noisy likelihood estimates reduce effective acceptance rate compared RWM exact likelihood, variance estimator must carefully controlled. Since PMCMC adaptive, suitable final algorithm.

title: A bestiary of the MCMC algorithms provided by lucifer
text: Initialize parameters \(\theta_0\); evaluate store noisy log-posterior \(\hat{\ell}_0 = \log \hat{p}(\theta_0 \mid y)\) Propose \(\theta^* \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta_{t-1}, \Sigma)\) (RWM) Evaluate model \(\theta^*\): obtain noisy estimate \(\hat{\ell}^* = \log \hat{p}(\theta^* \mid y)\) Compute \(\alpha = \min\!\bigl(1,\; \exp(\hat{\ell}^* - \hat{\ell}_{t-1})\bigr)\) probability \(\alpha\), accept: \(\theta_t = \theta^*\), \(\hat{\ell}_t = \hat{\ell}^*\) Otherwise, retain: \(\theta_t = \theta_{t-1}\), \(\hat{\ell}_t = \hat{\ell}_{t-1}\) (re-evaluate \(\theta_{t-1}\)) Return \(\{\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_T\}\)

title: A bestiary of the MCMC algorithms provided by lucifer
text: Initialize parameters \(\theta_0\), autoregressive parameter \(\beta \(0,1)\) Draw \(\xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma)\) Propose \(\theta^* = \sqrt{1 - \beta^2}\; \theta_{t-1} + \beta\; \xi\) (first-order autoregressive) Compute \(\alpha = \min\!\bigl(1,\; p(\theta^* \mid y) / p(\theta_{t-1} \mid y)\bigr)\) probability \(\alpha\), accept \(\theta_t = \theta^*\); otherwise \(\theta_t = \theta_{t-1}\) Return \(\{\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_T\}\)

title: Probabilistic model specification with model_spec()
text: lucifer package requires users write Model functions manually: extract parameters parm vector using positional indices, compute log-priors, build log-likelihood, assemble log-posterior, return five-element list. workflow powerful flexible, boilerplate verbose, error-prone, repetitive across models differ probabilistic specification. model_spec() function addresses providing declarative front-end users write probabilistic notation system compiles valid Model function, without replacing manual approach models need . design two-phase compiler: text LaTeX notation parsed intermediate representation (IR), compiled R code follows exact patterns established across 108+ example models. generated function indistinguishable hand-written code runtime; interpretation overhead. Users outgrow DSL can call code(spec) extract generated source extend manually, means DSL productivity tool learning scaffold.

title: Probabilistic model specification with model_spec()
text: complete workflow model_spec() compresses usual four-step setup (Data list, parameter names, Model function, initial values) single declaration followed data binding. entire workflow. rest document explains every component detail, covers full distribution registry, demonstrates progressively complex examples, honestly delineates DSL can handle.
code: library(lucifer)  # Simulate data set.seed(42) N <- 100 x <- rnorm(N) y <- 3 + 1.5 * x + rnorm(N, sd = 0.8) X <- cbind(1, x) J <- ncol(X)  # Specify the model declaratively spec <- model_spec("   y ~ Normal(mu, sigma)   mu = X %*% beta   beta[j] ~ NormalV(0, 1000), j = 1,...,J   sigma ~ HalfCauchy(25) ")  # Inspect print(spec) code(spec)  # Bind data and generate initial values Data <- spec$data_template(y = y, X = X, J = J) Initial.Values <- spec$initial_values(Data)  # Fit with NUTS set.seed(123) fit <- lucifer(spec$Model, Data, Initial.Values,                Iterations = 1000, Algorithm = "NUTS") print(fit)

previous_headings: Examples
title: Probabilistic model specification with model_spec()
text: simplest case: estimate mean standard deviation normally distributed data. Traditional approach: model_spec approach: fits converge posterior: \(\mu \approx 5\), \(\sigma \approx 2\).
code: set.seed(42) y <- rnorm(50, mean = 5, sd = 2)  # Manual Model function Model_manual <- function(parm, Data) {     mu <- parm[Data$pos.mu]     sigma <- interval(parm[Data$pos.sigma], 1e-100, Inf)     parm[Data$pos.sigma] <- sigma     mu.prior <- dnorm(mu, 0, 100, log = TRUE)     sigma.prior <- dhalfcauchy(sigma, 25, log = TRUE)     LL <- sum(dnorm(Data$y, mu, sigma, log = TRUE))     LP <- LL + mu.prior + sigma.prior     yhat <- rnorm(length(Data$y), mu, sigma)     list(LP = LP, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = LP,          yhat = yhat, parm = parm) }  # Manual Data list parm.names <- as.parm.names(list(mu = 0, sigma = 0)) Data_manual <- list(     y = y, N = length(y),     parm.names = parm.names, mon.names = "LP",     pos.mu = 1, pos.sigma = 2 ) Initial.Values <- c(0, 1)  set.seed(123) fit_manual <- lucifer(Model_manual, Data_manual, Initial.Values,                       Iterations = 1000, Algorithm = "NUTS") spec <- model_spec("   y ~ Normal(mu, sigma)   mu ~ Normal(0, 100)   sigma ~ HalfCauchy(25) ")  Data_spec <- spec$data_template(y = y) Initial.Values <- spec$initial_values(Data_spec)  set.seed(123) fit_spec <- lucifer(spec$Model, Data_spec, Initial.Values,                     Iterations = 1000, Algorithm = "NUTS")

title: Probabilistic model specification with model_spec()
text: code() method reveals exact R code compiler produces. Understanding output useful debugging, learning lucifer’s Model function conventions, scaffold extending models beyond DSL’s scope. output follows structure: key conventions: parameters extracted parm via position indices stored Data$pos.*; constraints applied immediately written back parm; priors computed log-densities summed vectorized parameters; data variables accessed via Data$; log-posterior sum log-likelihood log-priors; posterior predictive samples (yhat) drawn likelihood distribution; return list contains LP, Dev (\(-2 \times \text{LL}\)), Monitor, yhat, parm.
code: spec <- model_spec("   y ~ Normal(mu, sigma)   mu = X %*% beta   beta[j] ~ NormalV(0, 1000), j = 1,...,J   sigma ~ HalfCauchy(25) ")  code(spec) function(parm, Data) {     # Parameter extraction     beta <- parm[Data$pos.beta]     sigma <- parm[Data$pos.sigma]      # Constraints     sigma <- interval(sigma, 1e-100, Inf)     parm[Data$pos.sigma] <- sigma      # Log-priors     beta.prior <- sum(dnormv(beta, 0, 1000, log = TRUE))     sigma.prior <- dhalfcauchy(sigma, 25, log = TRUE)      # Deterministic relationships     mu <- Data$X %*% beta      # Log-likelihood     LL <- sum(dnorm(Data$y, mu, sigma, log = TRUE))      # Log-posterior     LP <- LL + beta.prior + sigma.prior      # Posterior predictive     yhat <- rnorm(length(Data$y), mu, sigma)      list(LP = LP, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = LP,          yhat = yhat, parm = parm) }

title: Probabilistic model specification with model_spec()
text: Generalized linear models: Normal, Poisson, Bernoulli, Binomial, Beta, Gamma, Negative Binomial regression arbitrary link functions expressed deterministic statements. Hierarchical multilevel models nested priors hyperpriors. Scalar, vector, matrix parameters explicit indexing. 86 distributions lucifer ecosystem, including multivariate (MVN, MVT, Wishart), mixture (NormalMixture), copula (Clayton, Frank), spatial (CAR) distributions. Standard linear predictors: mu = X %*% beta, mu = X %*% beta + Z %*% gamma, etc. Arbitrary deterministic transformations: valid R expression.

previous_headings: Scope and limitations
title: Probabilistic model specification with model_spec()
text: patterns genuinely require programming language expressed notation language. DSL detects several issues warnings, suggesting manual Model writing. Time series recursive structure: AR, GARCH, state-space models require loops lag indexing (e.g., y[t] ~ Normal(phi * y[t-1], sigma)). DSL express temporal recursion. Mixture models discrete latent allocation: models like z[] ~ Categorical(pi) followed y[] ~ Normal(mu[z[]], sigma[z[]]) require array indexing discrete latent variable. Missing data augmentation: treating missing observations parameters sampled alongside parameters requires augmenting parm vector imputed values. Custom constraint patterns: ordinal thresholds sort(), sum--zero constraints, correlation matrices Cholesky decomposition. Non-standard likelihoods: CPO, ABC approximations, custom distance functions, likelihoods require loops observations. Complex control flow: /else statements within model, observation-level branching. DSL can syntactically parse patterns, generated code incorrect. instance, time series model compiles produces code referencing undefined index variables: correct approach models write Model function manually explicit loop.
code: # This compiles but the generated code won't work correctly spec_ts <- model_spec("   y[t] ~ Normal(phi * y[t-1], sigma)   phi ~ Normal(0, 1)   sigma ~ HalfCauchy(5) ") # The generated code shows Data$y[t-1] with undefined 't': code(spec_ts)

code: # Step 1: get the scaffold spec <- model_spec("   y ~ Normal(mu, sigma)   mu = X %*% beta   beta[j] ~ NormalV(0, 1000), j = 1,...,J   sigma ~ HalfCauchy(25) ")  # Step 2: extract the generated code code(spec)  # Step 3: copy, paste, and modify for your specific needs # For instance, add AR(1) structure: Model_custom <- function(parm, Data) {     beta <- parm[Data$pos.beta]     sigma <- interval(parm[Data$pos.sigma], 1e-100, Inf)     parm[Data$pos.sigma] <- sigma     phi <- parm[Data$pos.phi]  # Added manually      beta.prior <- sum(dnormv(beta, 0, 1000, log = TRUE))     sigma.prior <- dhalfcauchy(sigma, 25, log = TRUE)     phi.prior <- dnorm(phi, 0, 1, log = TRUE)  # Added manually      mu <- Data$X %*% beta     # AR(1) residual structure added manually     resid <- Data$y - mu     LL <- dnorm(resid[1], 0, sigma, log = TRUE)     for (t in 2:Data$N) {         LL <- LL + dnorm(resid[t], phi * resid[t - 1], sigma, log = TRUE)     }      LP <- LL + beta.prior + sigma.prior + phi.prior     yhat <- rnorm(Data$N, mu, sigma)     list(LP = LP, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = LP,          yhat = yhat, parm = parm) }

text: following comparison uses identical random seeds demonstrate approaches produce posterior.
code: library(lucifer) set.seed(42)  # Simulate data N <- 100 x <- rnorm(N) y <- 3 + 1.5 * x + rnorm(N, sd = 0.8) X <- cbind(1, x) J <- ncol(X)  # ======================================== # Traditional approach # ======================================== Model_trad <- function(parm, Data) {     beta <- parm[Data$pos.beta]     sigma <- interval(parm[Data$pos.sigma], 1e-100, Inf)     parm[Data$pos.sigma] <- sigma      beta.prior <- sum(dnormv(beta, 0, 1000, log = TRUE))     sigma.prior <- dhalfcauchy(sigma, 25, log = TRUE)      mu <- Data$X %*% beta     LL <- sum(dnorm(Data$y, mu, sigma, log = TRUE))     LP <- LL + beta.prior + sigma.prior      yhat <- rnorm(length(Data$y), mu, sigma)     list(LP = LP, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = LP,          yhat = yhat, parm = parm) }  parm.names <- as.parm.names(list(beta = rep(0, J), sigma = 0)) Data_trad <- list(     y = y, X = X, J = J, N = N,     parm.names = parm.names,     mon.names = "LP",     pos.beta = 1:J,     pos.sigma = J + 1 ) IV_trad <- c(rep(0, J), 1)  set.seed(123) fit_trad <- lucifer(Model_trad, Data_trad, IV_trad,                     Iterations = 1000, Algorithm = "NUTS")  # ======================================== # model_spec approach # ======================================== spec <- model_spec("   y ~ Normal(mu, sigma)   mu = X %*% beta   beta[j] ~ NormalV(0, 1000), j = 1,...,J   sigma ~ HalfCauchy(25) ")  Data_spec <- spec$data_template(y = y, X = X, J = J) IV_spec <- spec$initial_values(Data_spec)  # Use same initial values for fair comparison IV_spec <- IV_trad  set.seed(123) fit_spec <- lucifer(spec$Model, Data_spec, IV_spec,                     Iterations = 1000, Algorithm = "NUTS")  # Compare posteriors summary_trad <- fit_trad$Summary1 summary_spec <- fit_spec$Summary1 cat("Traditional beta[1]:", summary_trad["beta[1]", "Mean"], "\n") cat("model_spec beta[1]:", summary_spec["beta[1]", "Mean"], "\n") # These will be identical (same seed, same algorithm, same code)

title: Nested Laplace approximation: INLA-like inference in lucifer
text: Integrated nested Laplace approximation (INLA) deterministic strategy approximate Bayesian inference latent Gaussian models, introduced Rue, Martino, Chopin [1]. Rather sampling posterior via MCMC, INLA decomposes problem sequence Laplace approximations low-dimensional numerical integrations, achieving accuracy comparable long MCMC runs fraction time. R-INLA software implements strategy highly optimized sparse matrix routines specialized model specification language, making natural tool spatial, temporal, hierarchical models Gaussian Markov random field (GMRF) structure [2]. Reimplementing R-INLA inside lucifer neither feasible desirable: sparse Cholesky infrastructure, GMRF theory, structured model specification underpin R-INLA represent decade dedicated engineering. However, mathematical strategy behind INLA, namely nested Laplace decomposition, tied particular software architecture. lucifer already provides building blocks needed execute strategy manually: LaplaceApproximation() mode-finding Hessian estimation, VariationalBayes() Pathfinder ADVI fast approximate posteriors, lucifer() 55 MCMC algorithms ground-truth comparison. vignette demonstrates compose existing tools INLA-like workflow moderate-dimensional latent Gaussian models, “moderate” means problems tens low hundreds parameters rather thousands require sparse matrix exploitation.

previous_headings: The INLA decomposition
title: Nested Laplace approximation: INLA-like inference in lucifer
text: INLA targets specific class Bayesian hierarchical models called latent Gaussian models (LGMs). LGM three layers. observations \(y_i\) follow likelihood exponential family, conditional latent field \(\boldsymbol{x}\) hyperparameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\): \[ y_i \mid x_i, \boldsymbol{\theta} \sim p(y_i \mid \eta_i, \boldsymbol{\theta}), \qquad \eta_i = g^{-1}(x_i) \] \(\eta_i\) linear predictor \(g\) link function. latent field, includes fixed effects, random effects, linear predictor components, Gaussian conditional hyperparameters: \[ \boldsymbol{x} \mid \boldsymbol{\theta} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}(\boldsymbol{\theta}), \boldsymbol{Q}(\boldsymbol{\theta})^{-1}) \] \(\boldsymbol{Q}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) precision matrix. hyperparameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) (variance components, correlation parameters, smoothing parameters) prior \(p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\). key structural assumption \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) low-dimensional (typically 2–6 components), \(\boldsymbol{x}\) can high-dimensional. separation makes nested approximation efficient.

title: Nested Laplace approximation: INLA-like inference in lucifer
text: posterior marginals interest \(\pi(x_i \mid \boldsymbol{y})\) latent field component \(\pi(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \boldsymbol{y})\) hyperparameters. INLA obtains three nested approximations. Layer 1: marginal hyperparameters. marginal posterior \(\pi(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \boldsymbol{y})\) approximated via Laplace formula Tierney Kadane [3]: \[ \tilde{\pi}(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \boldsymbol{y}) \propto \left. \frac{p(\boldsymbol{y}, \boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{\theta})}{\tilde{\pi}_G(\boldsymbol{x} \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{y})} \right|_{\boldsymbol{x} = \boldsymbol{x}^*(\boldsymbol{\theta})} \] \(\tilde{\pi}_G(\boldsymbol{x} \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{y})\) Gaussian approximation \(\pi(\boldsymbol{x} \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{y})\) \(\boldsymbol{x}^*(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) mode. practice, reduces : \[ \log \tilde{\pi}(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \boldsymbol{y}) = \log p(\boldsymbol{y}, \boldsymbol{x}^*(\boldsymbol{\theta}), \boldsymbol{\theta}) + \frac{d_x}{2} \log(2\pi) + \frac{1}{2} \log |\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_x(\boldsymbol{\theta})| + \text{const} \] \(d_x = \dim(\boldsymbol{x})\) \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_x(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) covariance matrix Gaussian approximation (inverse negative Hessian \(\log p(\boldsymbol{y}, \boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{\theta})\) respect \(\boldsymbol{x}\), evaluated conditional mode). Layer 2: conditional marginals latent field. hyperparameter configuration \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_k\), conditional posterior latent field component \(x_i\) approximated Gaussian: \[ \tilde{\pi}(x_i \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}_k, \boldsymbol{y}) = \mathcal{N}\!\left(x_i;\, \mu_i(\boldsymbol{\theta}_k),\, \sigma_i^2(\boldsymbol{\theta}_k)\right) \] \(\mu_i(\boldsymbol{\theta}_k)\) \(\)-th component conditional mode \(\boldsymbol{x}^*(\boldsymbol{\theta}_k)\) \(\sigma_i^2(\boldsymbol{\theta}_k)\) \(\)-th diagonal element \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_x(\boldsymbol{\theta}_k)\). R-INLA offers refined corrections (simplified Laplace, full Laplace) improve accuracy skewed conditionals, Gaussian approximation fastest often sufficient. Layer 3: numerical integration. unconditional marginals obtained integrating \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) numerically grid \(\{\boldsymbol{\theta}_1, \ldots, \boldsymbol{\theta}_K\}\): \[ \tilde{\pi}(x_i \mid \boldsymbol{y}) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \tilde{\pi}(x_i \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}_k, \boldsymbol{y}) \times \tilde{\pi}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_k \mid \boldsymbol{y}) \times \Delta_k \] result Gaussian mixture, can represent asymmetry, heavy tails, non-Gaussian features single Gaussian approximation miss.

previous_headings: Example: Poisson GLMM with random intercepts
title: Nested Laplace approximation: INLA-like inference in lucifer
text: Consider Poisson generalized linear mixed model group-level random intercepts, standard example INLA literature. Counts \(y_{ij}\) group \(j\) follow Poisson distribution log-linear predictor: \[ y_{ij} \sim \text{Poisson}(\exp(\eta_{ij})), \qquad \eta_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \, x_{ij} + u_j \] \(u_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_u^2)\) group-level random intercepts. hyperparameter \(\theta = \log \sigma_u\), controls -group variability. latent field comprises \(\boldsymbol{x} = (\beta_0, \beta_1, u_1, \ldots, u_J)\), giving \(d_x = J + 2\) parameters optimize grid point.
code: library(lucifer) set.seed(42)  # Design J   <- 10       # groups n_j <- 20       # observations per group N   <- J * n_j  # total  # True parameter values beta0_true   <- 1.0 beta1_true   <- 0.5 sigma_u_true <- 0.8  # Simulate group <- rep(1:J, each = n_j) x_cov <- rnorm(N, 0, 1) u_true <- rnorm(J, 0, sigma_u_true) eta <- beta0_true + beta1_true * x_cov + u_true[group] y <- rpois(N, exp(eta))

title: Nested Laplace approximation: INLA-like inference in lucifer
text: joint model places weakly informative priors fixed effects half-Cauchy prior \(\sigma_u\). Since lucifer operates continuous, unconstrained parameter space, parameterize variance component \(\theta = \log \sigma_u\) include Jacobian correction \(|\mathrm{d}\sigma_u / \mathrm{d}\theta| = \sigma_u\) log-posterior.
code: parm.names <- c("beta[1]", "beta[2]", "log.sigma.u",                 paste0("u[", 1:J, "]")) mon.names  <- c("sigma.u", "LP")  Data <- list(   N = N, J = J, y = y, x = x_cov, group = group,   parm.names = parm.names, mon.names = mon.names )  Model <- function(parm, Data) {   # --- extract parameters ---   beta  <- parm[1:2]   log_sigma_u <- parm[3]   sigma_u <- exp(log_sigma_u)   u <- parm[4:(3 + Data$J)]    # --- priors ---   beta_prior    <- sum(dnorm(beta, 0, 10, log = TRUE))   sigma_u_prior <- dhalfcauchy(sigma_u, 5, log = TRUE) + log_sigma_u   u_prior       <- sum(dnorm(u, 0, sigma_u, log = TRUE))    # --- likelihood ---   eta <- beta[1] + beta[2] * Data$x + u[Data$group]   mu  <- exp(eta)   LL  <- sum(dpois(Data$y, mu, log = TRUE))    # --- assemble ---   LP  <- LL + beta_prior + sigma_u_prior + u_prior   Dev <- -2 * LL   yhat <- rpois(Data$N, mu)    return(list(LP = LP, Dev = Dev,               Monitor = c(sigma_u, LP),               yhat = yhat, parm = parm)) }  # Initial values parm0 <- c(0, 0, log(1), rep(0, J))

code: neg_LP_cond <- function(parm_x, log_sigma_u, Data) {   beta <- parm_x[1:2]   u    <- parm_x[3:(2 + Data$J)]   sigma_u <- exp(log_sigma_u)    beta_prior    <- sum(dnorm(beta, 0, 10, log = TRUE))   sigma_u_prior <- dhalfcauchy(sigma_u, 5, log = TRUE) + log_sigma_u   u_prior       <- sum(dnorm(u, 0, sigma_u, log = TRUE))    eta <- beta[1] + beta[2] * Data$x + u[Data$group]   mu  <- exp(eta)   LL  <- sum(dpois(Data$y, mu, log = TRUE))    -(LL + beta_prior + sigma_u_prior + u_prior) }

title: Nested Laplace approximation: INLA-like inference in lucifer
text: \(\theta_k\), maximize conditional log-posterior optim() (BFGS) compute Hessian mode Hessian(). interface Hessian(), wrap conditional log-posterior thin Model-compatible function returns standard list(LP, Dev, Monitor, yhat, parm). Hessian inverted obtain conditional covariance matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_x(\theta_k)\). Warm-starting previous grid point’s mode ensures fast convergence across grid.
code: d_x <- 2 + J  # dimension of latent field  # Initialize from joint mode (excluding log.sigma.u) parm_x_init <- joint_mode[c(1:2, 4:(3 + J))]  # Wrapper for Hessian(): given a fixed theta_k, returns a Model-compatible # function whose LP is the conditional log-posterior of the latent field make_cond_model <- function(log_sigma_u, Data) {   function(parm, Data) {     LP <- -neg_LP_cond(parm, log_sigma_u = log_sigma_u, Data = Data)     list(LP = LP, Dev = -2 * LP, Monitor = 1, yhat = 1, parm = parm)   } }  results <- vector("list", K)  for (k in seq_len(K)) {   theta_k <- theta_grid[k]    # Find conditional mode   opt <- optim(parm_x_init, neg_LP_cond,                log_sigma_u = theta_k, Data = Data,                method = "BFGS", control = list(maxit = 500))    # Hessian at mode via lucifer's Hessian() (Richardson, d = 0.1)   cond_model <- make_cond_model(theta_k, Data)   H <- -Hessian(cond_model, opt$par, Data)   Sigma <- solve(H)   log_det <- as.numeric(determinant(Sigma, logarithm = TRUE)$modulus)    results[[k]] <- list(     mode    = opt$par,     covar   = Sigma,     LP      = -opt$value,     log_det = log_det   )    # Warm-start next grid point   parm_x_init <- opt$par }

title: Nested Laplace approximation: INLA-like inference in lucifer
text: unnormalized log-weight grid point Laplace approximation \(\log \pi(\theta_k \mid \boldsymbol{y})\), computed conditional log-posterior mode log-determinant conditional covariance: marginal posterior latent field component \(x_i\) now Gaussian mixture: \[ \tilde{\pi}(x_i \mid \boldsymbol{y}) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} w_k \, \mathcal{N}\!\left(x_i;\, \mu_i^{(k)},\, \sigma_i^{2(k)}\right) \] \(\mu_i^{(k)}\) \(\sigma_i^{2(k)}\) conditional mode variance \(k\)-th grid point. define helper function evaluate mixture: marginal \(\theta\) (hence \(\sigma_u = e^\theta\)) given directly normalized weights grid. can obtain smooth density estimate via interpolation:
code: log_w <- sapply(results, function(r) {   r$LP + 0.5 * d_x * log(2 * pi) + 0.5 * r$log_det })  # Normalize (log-sum-exp for stability) log_w <- log_w - max(log_w) w <- exp(log_w) w <- w / sum(w) gmix_density <- function(x_vals, param_idx, results, weights) {   dens <- numeric(length(x_vals))   for (k in seq_along(results)) {     mu_k <- results[[k]]$mode[param_idx]     sd_k <- sqrt(results[[k]]$covar[param_idx, param_idx])     dens <- dens + weights[k] * dnorm(x_vals, mu_k, sd_k)   }   dens } # Marginal density of log(sigma_u) on the grid theta_dens <- w / diff(theta_grid)[1]  # rescale to density units  # Smooth interpolation theta_smooth <- splinefun(theta_grid, theta_dens)

title: Nested Laplace approximation: INLA-like inference in lucifer
text: Beyond visual comparison, can assess quality approximation numerically. Two useful diagnostics marginal mean standard deviation (match MCMC), coverage credible intervals.
code: # Nested Laplace: mixture mean and variance for parameter i gmix_moments <- function(param_idx, results, weights) {   mu <- sapply(results, function(r) r$mode[param_idx])   v  <- sapply(results, function(r) r$covar[param_idx, param_idx])   mean_mix <- sum(weights * mu)   var_mix  <- sum(weights * (v + mu^2)) - mean_mix^2   c(mean = mean_mix, sd = sqrt(var_mix)) }  # Compare moments for beta[1], beta[2], log.sigma.u, u[1] idx <- c(1, 2, 3, 4) rows <- lapply(idx, function(i) {   mcmc_m <- mean(posterior[, i])   mcmc_s <- sd(posterior[, i])   jla_m  <- joint_mode[i]   jla_s  <- joint_sd[i]   ci     <- if (i <= 2) i else if (i == 3) NA else i - 1   if (!is.na(ci)) {     nla <- gmix_moments(ci, results, w)   } else {     nla <- c(mean = sum(w * theta_grid),              sd = sqrt(sum(w * theta_grid^2) - sum(w * theta_grid)^2))   }   data.frame(     Parameter = Data$parm.names[i],     MCMC      = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", mcmc_m, mcmc_s),     Joint.LA  = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", jla_m, jla_s),     Nested.LA = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", nla[1], nla[2])   ) }) diag_df <- do.call(rbind, rows) knitr::kable(diag_df, align = "lccc",              col.names = c("Parameter", "MCMC (NUTS)", "Joint Laplace",                            "Nested Laplace"),              caption = "Posterior mean (sd) by approximation method")

title: Nested Laplace approximation: INLA-like inference in lucifer

title: Neural ODE inference via Bayesian gradient matching
text: central problem ecology dynamical systems science inferring interaction structure observed time series: given measurements multiple interacting variables time, variables drive , strongly? Parametric approaches, whether Lotka-Volterra models, state-space formulations, mechanistic ODEs, require specifying functional form interactions advance. true functional form unknown misspecified, parameter estimates absorb model error can lead qualitatively wrong conclusions interaction structure. Neural ordinary differential equations (NODEs; Chen et al. 2018 [3]) offer model-free alternative using neural networks represent unknown right-hand side ODE system. However, standard NODE fitting requires numerically integrating entire system every parameter update, making computational cost proportional number time steps multiplied number solver sub-steps. ecological datasets complex, potentially stiff dynamics, cost prohibitive. adjoint method reduces memory computation, backpropagation solver introduces additional numerical instabilities. Bayesian Neural Gradient Matching (BNGM; Bonnaffé 2023 [1]) solves problem decoupling ODE fitting two independent regression stages, avoiding numerical integration entirely. Stage 1 interpolates time series sinusoidal neural network whose temporal derivatives available analytically via chain rule. Stage 2 fits dual-pathway neural network predict per-capita growth rates interpolated state variables. stages reduce standard regression problems known gradients, method 100-600 times faster standard NODE fitting recovering interaction structure significantly higher accuracy (Bonnaffé 2023 reports ~5-10% error vs ~50% standard NODEs benchmark systems). NODE() function lucifer implements BNGM C++/Armadillo backend parallelized via OpenMP, providing speedups 10-50x reference R implementation. vignette develops mathematical foundations, demonstrates method four examples increasing complexity, provides practical guidelines parameter selection.

what: The inverse problem for dynamical systems

text: Consider system \(N\) interacting variables \(\mathbf{y}(t) = (y_1(t), \ldots, y_N(t))\) governed unknown ODE system: \[\frac{dy_i}{dt} = g_i(\mathbf{y}, t), \qquad = 1, \ldots, N\] functions \(g_i\) encode ecological interactions. inverse problem recover \(g_i\) (least qualitative structure, .e., partial derivatives \(\partial g_i / \partial y_j\) non-zero sign carry) discrete, noisy observations \(\{(t_n, Y_{n,1}, \ldots, Y_{n,N})\}_{n=1}^{T}\). Standard approaches parameterize \(g_i\) known functional form (e.g., \(g_i = r_i y_i (1 - \sum_j \alpha_{ij} y_j / K_i)\) competitive Lotka-Volterra) estimate parameters maximum likelihood Bayesian inference. what: Bayesian regularization via the marginal posterior
title: Neural ODE inference via Bayesian gradient matching
text: Fitting observation model uses Bayesian framework Foresee & Hagan (1997) [4], replaces standard log-posterior approximation log marginal posterior integrates noise variance: \[\log P(\omega \mid Y) \approx -\frac{T}{2} \log\Bigl(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{n=1}^{T} \varepsilon_n^2 + 1\Bigr) - c \cdot \frac{M}{2} \log\Bigl(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{M} \omega_j^2 + 1\Bigr)\] \(\varepsilon_n = Y_n - \hat{y}(t_n, \omega)\) residuals, \(M = 3H\) number parameters, \(c\) controls regularization strength. first term robust alternative sum--squares likelihood (grows logarithmically rather linearly residual magnitude, making less sensitive outliers). second term spherical Gaussian prior parameters, preventing overfitting. default regularization \(c = 1/H\) (inversely proportional number neurons) data-independent works well across wide range systems (Bonnaffé 2023). Stronger regularization (smaller \(c\)) produces smoother interpolations cost fitting fidelity; weaker regularization (larger \(c\)) allows network track high-frequency fluctuations may noise.

title: Neural ODE inference via Bayesian gradient matching
text: interpolation, per-capita growth rate variable computed: \[r_i(t) = \frac{1}{\hat{y}_i(t)} \cdot \frac{d\hat{y}_i}{dt}(t) = \frac{d}{dt}\bigl[\log \hat{y}_i(t)\bigr]\] transformation removes scaling effect population size isolates intrinsic dynamics. process model predicts \(r_i\) function state variables using dual-pathway single-layer perceptron (SLP): \[f_{p,}(\mathbf{x}) = \underbrace{\mathbf{v}_{\text{lin}}^\top \bigl(\mathbf{b}_{\text{lin}} + \mathbf{W}_{\text{lin}} \mathbf{x}\bigr)}_{\text{linear pathway}} + \underbrace{\mathbf{v}_{\exp}^\top \exp\bigl(\mathbf{b}_{\exp} + \mathbf{W}_{\exp} \mathbf{x}\bigr)}_{\text{exponential pathway}}\] pathway \(H_p\) neurons \(N\) inputs (one per state variable), giving \(H_p(2 + N)\) parameters per pathway \(2 H_p(2 + N)\) total parameters per target variable. linear pathway captures density-independent effects weak linear interactions, exponential pathway captures nonlinear density-dependent interactions predation saturation, competitive exclusion, Allee effects. separation improves interpretability (one can examine pathway’s contribution independently) fitting stability (linear pathway provides baseline exponential pathway refines). process model uses standard Gaussian log-posterior: \[\log P(\theta \mid \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{r}) = -\sum_{t} \frac{(r_i(t) - f_{p,}(\mathbf{x}(t)))^2}{\sigma_1^2} - \sum_j \frac{\theta_j^2}{\sigma_2^2}\] \(\sigma_1\) controls likelihood width (data fit tolerance) \(\sigma_2\) controls prior width (parameter regularization). title: Phylodynamic inference with lucifer
text: Bayesian phylogenetic phylodynamic inference combines molecular sequence data evolutionary models reconstruct history lineages time. dominant software task, BEAST [1] [2], jointly samples tree topologies continuous parameters (substitution rates, clock rates, coalescent demographic parameters) using specialized MCMC engine tree-specific proposal mechanisms subtree-pruning--regrafting (SPR) nearest-neighbor interchange (NNI) moves. lucifer tree sampler. SPR proposals, NNI moves, machinery traversing discrete tree space. flexible Bayesian inference engine 40 MCMC algorithms, sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) marginal likelihood estimation, modern convergence diagnostics (rank-normalized \(\hat{R}\), bulk tail ESS), leave-one-cross-validation via Pareto smoothed importance sampling (LOO-PSIS), Bayesian model stacking, automated algorithm selection Crucible pipeline. capabilities offer genuine complementary value phylodynamic problems tree topology fixed. Conditioning fixed tree toy exercise. practice, researchers routinely fix trees obtained maximum likelihood (e.g., RAxML, IQ-TREE) consensus methods estimate downstream parameters. Gao et al. [3] recently demonstrated tree-topology mixing precisely standard BEAST diagnostics fail: posterior tree landscapes inherently multimodal, multiple peaks separated deep valleys MCMC chains struggle cross even billions iterations. analysis 15 large phylodynamic datasets showed standard continuous-parameter diagnostics (ESS, \(\hat{R}\)) often fail detect tree-space sampling problems, turn distort estimates evolutionary rates, divergence times, demographic trajectories. context, explicitly conditioning tree hypotheses comparing parameter estimates across arguably transparent relying joint sampler whose topology mixing may inadequate. vignette demonstrates lucifer addresses core phylodynamic inference problems using existing infrastructure. cover five examples: (1) GTR+\(\Gamma\) substitution model estimation fixed tree; (2) model comparison among competing substitution models via SMC marginal likelihoods LOO-PSIS; (3) strict versus relaxed molecular clock estimation hierarchical model; (4) coalescent demographic inference including Bayesian skyline reconstruction; (5) multimodality detection diagnostics connecting findings Gao et al. [3]. examples use data ape [4] phangorn [5] R packages, requiring external downloads.

previous_headings: Background theory
title: Phylodynamic inference with lucifer
text: evolution nucleotide sequences along phylogenetic tree modeled continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) state space \(\{, C, G, T\}\). instantaneous rate matrix \(Q\) governs transition rates nucleotides; -diagonal entries \(q_{ij}\) represent instantaneous rate substitution nucleotide \(\) \(j\), diagonal entries satisfy \(q_{ii} = -\sum_{j \neq } q_{ij}\) row sums zero. Given branch length \(t\) (measured expected substitutions per site), transition probability matrix matrix exponential \(P(t) = \exp(Qt)\), entry \(P_{ij}(t)\) gives probability nucleotide \(\) ancestral end branch becomes nucleotide \(j\) descendant end. general time-reversible (GTR) model [6] parameterizes \(Q\) \(Q_{ij} = \rho_{ij} \pi_j\) \(\neq j\), \(\boldsymbol{\pi} = (\pi_A, \pi_C, \pi_G, \pi_T)\) stationary (equilibrium) base frequencies satisfying \(\sum_k \pi_k = 1\), \(\rho_{ij} = \rho_{ji}\) symmetric exchangeability parameters. six upper-triangular exchangeabilities conventionally written \((, b, c, d, e, f)\) corresponding pairs (AC, AG, , CG, CT, GT), \(f = 1\) fixed identifiability. GTR model thus 8 free parameters: 5 exchangeability rates 3 free base frequencies (fourth determined simplex constraint). Two important special cases reduce parameter count. Jukes-Cantor (JC69) model [7] sets exchangeabilities equal base frequencies 0.25, yielding zero free substitution parameters. Hasegawa-Kishino-Yano (HKY) model [8] distinguishes transitions (purine\(\leftrightarrow\)purine pyrimidine\(\leftrightarrow\)pyrimidine, governed \(\kappa\)) transversions (substitutions, rate 1), empirical base frequencies, giving one free substitution parameter. Rate heterogeneity across sites modeled discrete gamma distribution [9] shape parameter \(\alpha\) \(K\) rate categories (typically \(K = 4\)). \(\alpha\) small, rates vary substantially across sites; \(\alpha \\infty\), sites evolve rate. adds one free parameter substitution model. likelihood alignment \(D\) given tree \(T\) model parameters \(\theta\) computed Felsenstein’s pruning algorithm [10], traverses tree tips root, combining partial likelihood vectors internal node. \(N\) alignment sites \(K\) unique patterns pattern weights \(w_k\), total log-likelihood decomposes \(\log L(D \mid T, \theta) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} w_k \log L_k\), \(L_k\) likelihood pattern \(k\). per-pattern decomposition critical LOO-PSIS, requires per-observation log-likelihoods.

previous_headings: Background theory
title: Phylodynamic inference with lucifer
text: molecular clock relates substitution branch lengths (expected substitutions per site) divergence times (calendar units) evolutionary rates. strict clock [11], single global rate \(r\) applies branches, substitution branch length branch \(\) \(b_i = r \cdot t_i\), \(t_i\) duration branch \(\) time units. assumption restrictive: empirical data frequently show rate variation across lineages. uncorrelated relaxed lognormal clock [12] assigns branch rate \(r_i\) drawn independently lognormal distribution: \(r_i \sim \text{LogNormal}(\mu_r, \sigma_r)\). substitution branch length becomes \(b_i = r_i \cdot t_i\). hierarchical model: branch-specific rates partially pooled toward population mean shared hyperparameters \((\mu_r, \sigma_r)\). \(\sigma_r \0\), relaxed clock collapses strict clock; \(\sigma_r\) large, branches evolve different rates. hierarchical structure maps naturally onto lucifer’s Model() interface, branch rates parameters lognormal priors governed estimated hyperparameters.

previous_headings: Background theory
title: Phylodynamic inference with lucifer
text: coalescent [13] provides probabilistic framework relating genealogy (tree sampled lineages) demographic history population sampled. Given \(n\) sampled lineages, process works backward time: point \(k\) lineages coexist, waiting time next coalescence event exponentially distributed rate \(\binom{k}{2} / N_e(t)\), \(N_e(t)\) effective population size time \(t\). rooted ultrametric tree \(n\) tips \(n - 1\) coalescence events times \(t_1 < t_2 < \ldots < t_{n-1}\) (measured backward present), coalescent log-likelihood given demographic function \(N_e(t)\) \[\log L(T \mid N_e) = \sum_{j=1}^{n-1} \left[ \log \binom{k_j}{2} - \log N_e(t_j) - \int_{t_{j-1}}^{t_j} \frac{\binom{k_j}{2}}{N_e(s)} \, ds \right]\] \(k_j\) number lineages interval \(j\) (coalescence events \(j-1\) \(j\), \(t_0 = 0\)), integral represents cumulative hazard interval. Three demographic parameterizations commonly used. constant population size, \(N_e(t) = N_e\) \(t\), integral simplifies \(\binom{k_j}{2} \Delta t_j / N_e\) \(\Delta t_j = t_j - t_{j-1}\). exponential growth, \(N_e(t) = N_0 \exp(gt)\) \(g\) growth rate \(N_0\) present-day size; integral closed-form solution involving exponential function. Bayesian skyline [14] models \(N_e\) piecewise constant grouped coalescent intervals, \(M\) population size parameters \(N_1, \ldots, N_M\), governing contiguous block coalescent intervals. non-parametric approach can recover complex demographic trajectories without imposing functional form. three parameterizations yield analytical coalescent log-likelihoods can coded directly R, requiring external phylogenetic library.

previous_headings: Preparing the data
title: Phylodynamic inference with lucifer
text: define small helper function wraps phangorn::pml() accept lucifer-style parameter vector. function extracts base frequencies, GTR exchangeability rates, gamma shape parameter parameter vector, calls pml(), returns log-likelihood along per-site log-likelihoods LOO-PSIS. Since lucifer() runs parallel chains separate R processes via callr, helper functions defined calling environment accessible within Model() function. standard workaround pass helper Data list, serialized transmitted subprocess. Data lists vignette therefore include phylo_loglik element.
code: #' Compute phylogenetic log-likelihood via Felsenstein pruning #' @param bf Numeric vector of 4 base frequencies (must sum to 1) #' @param Q Numeric vector of 6 GTR exchangeability rates #' @param shape Gamma shape parameter for rate heterogeneity #' @param tree A phylo object (the fixed tree) #' @param pdat A phyDat object (the sequence alignment) #' @param k Number of gamma rate categories (default 4) #' @return List with logLik (scalar) and site_ll (per-site log-likelihoods) #' #' The closure includes a gc() call every 100 pml() evaluations. phangorn's #' C-level likelihood engine accumulates internal allocations that can #' corrupt the heap when called hundreds of thousands of times in a single #' R process; periodic garbage collection keeps the allocations compact. phylo_loglik <- local({     n <- 0L     function(bf, Q, shape, tree, pdat, k = 4) {         n <<- n + 1L         if (n %% 100L == 0L) gc(verbose = FALSE)         fit <- phangorn::pml(tree, pdat, bf = bf, Q = Q, k = k, shape = shape)         site_ll <- rep(fit$siteLik, attr(pdat, "weight"))         list(logLik = fit$logLik, site_ll = site_ll)     } })

title: Phylodynamic inference with lucifer
text: example estimates full GTR+\(\Gamma\) substitution model parameters fixed NJ tree. parameter vector 9 components: 3 free base frequencies (fourth determined simplex constraint), 5 free GTR exchangeability rates (sixth, GT, fixed 1 identifiability), 1 gamma shape parameter. Base frequencies parameterized softmax (additive log-ratio) transformation: sampler operates three unconstrained real-valued parameters \(\alpha_A, \alpha_C, \alpha_G\) (\(\alpha_T = 0\) reference), frequencies recovered \(\pi_k = \exp(\alpha_k) / \sum_j \exp(\alpha_j)\). avoids cascading interval() constraints otherwise break componentwise samplers AMWG one frequency proposed near boundary.

previous_headings: Example 1: GTR+\(\Gamma\) substitution model estimation
title: Phylodynamic inference with lucifer
code: # ---- Data list ---- n_sites <- ncol(woodmouse)  Data <- list(     # Required lucifer fields     mon.names  = c("LP", "LL"),     parm.names = c("alpha_A", "alpha_C", "alpha_G",                    "q_AC", "q_AG", "q_AT", "q_CG", "q_CT",                    "shape"),     # Phylogenetic data (passed through to Model)     tree = tree_rooted,     pdat = pdat,     N    = n_sites,     phylo_loglik = phylo_loglik )  # ---- Model function ---- Model <- function(parm, Data) {      # --- Base frequencies via softmax (unconstrained parameterization) ---     # parm[1:3] are log-ratio parameters (alpha_A, alpha_C, alpha_G);     # alpha_T = 0 is the reference category. This avoids cascading     # interval() constraints that break componentwise samplers like AMWG.     alpha <- c(parm[1:3], 0)     alpha <- alpha - max(alpha)  # numerical stability     bf    <- exp(alpha) / sum(exp(alpha))      # GTR rates: all positive, GT fixed at 1     q_AC <- interval(parm[4], 1e-4, 100)     q_AG <- interval(parm[5], 1e-4, 100)     q_AT <- interval(parm[6], 1e-4, 100)     q_CG <- interval(parm[7], 1e-4, 100)     q_CT <- interval(parm[8], 1e-4, 100)     parm[4:8] <- c(q_AC, q_AG, q_AT, q_CG, q_CT)      Q <- c(q_AC, q_AG, q_AT, q_CG, q_CT, 1)  # GT = 1 (reference)      # Gamma shape     shape <- interval(parm[9], 0.01, 100)     parm[9] <- shape      # --- Log-likelihood ---     res <- Data$phylo_loglik(bf, Q, shape, Data$tree, Data$pdat)     LL  <- res$logLik      # --- Priors ---     # Dirichlet(1,1,1,1) is uniform on the simplex; in the unconstrained     # alpha space the prior contributes only the log-Jacobian of the     # softmax transformation: log|J| = sum(log(pi_k))     pi_prior <- sum(log(bf))     # Exponential(1) on each GTR rate     q_prior <- sum(dexp(c(q_AC, q_AG, q_AT, q_CG, q_CT),                         rate = 1, log = TRUE))     # Exponential(1) on gamma shape     shape_prior <- dexp(shape, rate = 1, log = TRUE)      LP <- LL + pi_prior + q_prior + shape_prior      # --- Posterior predictive (monitor log-likelihood) ---     yhat <- rep(LL / Data$N, Data$N)      list(LP = LP, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = c(LP, LL),          yhat = yhat, parm = parm) }  # ---- Initial values ---- # Start near uniform/default values # First 3 are softmax log-ratios: (0,0,0) maps to uniform (0.25 each) Initial.Values <- c(     0, 0, 0,                 # softmax alphas (uniform start)     1, 1, 1, 1, 1,          # GTR rates (all equal = JC-like start)     1                        # gamma shape )

text: phylogenetic likelihood computed phangorn::pml(), opaque compiled function analytical gradients available. Gradient-based samplers NUTS resort finite-difference approximations, requiring \(2p\) additional likelihood evaluations per gradient (18 9-parameter model) many gradients per leapfrog trajectory, making prohibitively slow. Prescribe confirms diagnosis: detects gradients unavailable recommends componentwise Metropolis algorithms. use AMWG (Adaptive Metropolis-within-Gibbs [20]), updates parameter individually automatically tuned proposal scales requires one likelihood evaluation per component update.
code: # Run Prescribe to verify algorithm recommendation rx <- Prescribe(Model, Data, Initial.Values) print(rx)  # Fit with AMWG (componentwise; no gradients needed) fit_gtr <- lucifer(     Model, Data, Initial.Values,     Iterations = 20000, Status = 5000, Thinning = 10,     Algorithm = "AMWG",     Specs = list(B = NULL, n = 0, Periodicity = 50) )  # Diagnostics print(fit_gtr) Consort(fit_gtr)

code: Data_jc <- list(     mon.names  = c("LP", "LL"),     parm.names = c("shape"),     tree = tree_rooted,     pdat = pdat,     N    = n_sites,     phylo_loglik = phylo_loglik )  Model_jc <- function(parm, Data) {     shape <- interval(parm[1], 0.01, 100)     parm[1] <- shape      bf <- rep(0.25, 4)     Q  <- rep(1, 6)     res <- Data$phylo_loglik(bf, Q, shape, Data$tree, Data$pdat)     LL  <- res$logLik      shape_prior <- dexp(shape, rate = 1, log = TRUE)     LP <- LL + shape_prior      yhat <- rep(LL / Data$N, Data$N)     list(LP = LP, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = c(LP, LL),          yhat = yhat, parm = parm) }  IV_jc <- c(1)  # Fit JC model fit_jc <- lucifer(     Model_jc, Data_jc, IV_jc,     Iterations = 10000, Status = 5000, Thinning = 5,     Algorithm = "AMWG",     Specs = list(B = NULL, n = 0, Periodicity = 50) )

code: Data_hky <- list(     mon.names  = c("LP", "LL"),     parm.names = c("alpha_A", "alpha_C", "alpha_G", "kappa", "shape"),     tree = tree_rooted,     pdat = pdat,     N    = n_sites,     phylo_loglik = phylo_loglik )  Model_hky <- function(parm, Data) {     # Base frequencies via softmax     alpha <- c(parm[1:3], 0)     alpha <- alpha - max(alpha)     bf    <- exp(alpha) / sum(exp(alpha))      # Transition/transversion ratio     kappa <- interval(parm[4], 0.01, 200)     parm[4] <- kappa      # Gamma shape     shape <- interval(parm[5], 0.01, 100)     parm[5] <- shape      # HKY: transitions (AG, CT) have rate kappa; transversions rate 1     Q <- c(1, kappa, 1, 1, kappa, 1)      res <- Data$phylo_loglik(bf, Q, shape, Data$tree, Data$pdat)     LL  <- res$logLik      # Priors     pi_prior    <- sum(log(bf))  # Dirichlet(1,1,1,1) + Jacobian     kappa_prior <- dexp(kappa, rate = 0.1, log = TRUE)     shape_prior <- dexp(shape, rate = 1, log = TRUE)     LP <- LL + pi_prior + kappa_prior + shape_prior      yhat <- rep(LL / Data$N, Data$N)     list(LP = LP, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = c(LP, LL),          yhat = yhat, parm = parm) }  IV_hky <- c(0, 0, 0, 2, 1)  # Fit HKY model fit_hky <- lucifer(     Model_hky, Data_hky, IV_hky,     Iterations = 15000, Status = 5000, Thinning = 5,     Algorithm = "AMWG",     Specs = list(B = NULL, n = 0, Periodicity = 50) )

code: # Helper: softmax transform for posterior alpha samples softmax_bf <- function(alpha_vec) {     alpha <- c(alpha_vec, 0)     alpha <- alpha - max(alpha)     exp(alpha) / sum(exp(alpha)) }  # Build per-site log-likelihood matrices for each model build_jc_site_ll <- function(fit) {     post <- as.matrix(fit$Posterior2)     if (ncol(post) == 1) colnames(post) <- "shape"     S <- nrow(post)     ll_matrix <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = n_sites, ncol = S)     for (s in seq_len(S)) {         res <- phylo_loglik(rep(0.25, 4), rep(1, 6), post[s, 1],                             tree_rooted, pdat)         ll_matrix[, s] <- res$site_ll     }     ll_matrix }  build_hky_site_ll <- function(fit) {     post <- fit$Posterior2; S <- nrow(post)     ll_matrix <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = n_sites, ncol = S)     for (s in seq_len(S)) {         bf    <- softmax_bf(post[s, 1:3])         kappa <- post[s, 4]; shape <- post[s, 5]         Q     <- c(1, kappa, 1, 1, kappa, 1)         res   <- phylo_loglik(bf, Q, shape, tree_rooted, pdat)         ll_matrix[, s] <- res$site_ll     }     ll_matrix }  build_gtr_site_ll <- function(fit) {     post <- fit$Posterior2; S <- nrow(post)     ll_matrix <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = n_sites, ncol = S)     for (s in seq_len(S)) {         bf    <- softmax_bf(post[s, 1:3])         Q     <- c(post[s, 4:8], 1)         shape <- post[s, 9]         res   <- phylo_loglik(bf, Q, shape, tree_rooted, pdat)         ll_matrix[, s] <- res$site_ll     }     ll_matrix }  # Compute LOO-PSIS for each model ll_mat_jc  <- build_jc_site_ll(fit_jc) ll_mat_hky <- build_hky_site_ll(fit_hky) ll_mat_gtr <- build_gtr_site_ll(fit_gtr)  loo_jc  <- LOO(ll_mat_jc) loo_hky <- LOO(ll_mat_hky) loo_gtr <- LOO(ll_mat_gtr)  # Compare all three loo_comp <- loo_compare(list(JC = loo_jc, HKY = loo_hky, GTR = loo_gtr)) print(loo_comp)  # LOO diagnostics for best model summary(loo_gtr) plot(loo_gtr)

title: Phylodynamic inference with lucifer

title: Phylodynamic inference with lucifer
text: strict clock, branches share single evolutionary rate \(r\). substitution branch length branch \(\) \(b_i = r \cdot t_i\).
code: Data_strict <- list(     mon.names  = c("LP", "LL"),     parm.names = c("rate", "kappa", "alpha_A", "alpha_C", "alpha_G", "shape"),     tree = tree_ultra,     pdat = pdat,     time_lengths = time_lengths,     N = n_sites,     phylo_loglik = phylo_loglik )  Model_strict <- function(parm, Data) {     # Global clock rate     rate <- interval(parm[1], 1e-6, 100)     parm[1] <- rate      # HKY parameters     kappa <- interval(parm[2], 0.01, 200)     parm[2] <- kappa      # Base frequencies via softmax     alpha <- c(parm[3:5], 0)     alpha <- alpha - max(alpha)     bf    <- exp(alpha) / sum(exp(alpha))      shape <- interval(parm[6], 0.01, 100)     parm[6] <- shape      Q <- c(1, kappa, 1, 1, kappa, 1)      # Scale time-tree by global rate     scaled_tree <- Data$tree     scaled_tree$edge.length <- Data$time_lengths * rate      res <- Data$phylo_loglik(bf, Q, shape, scaled_tree, Data$pdat)     LL  <- res$logLik      # Priors     rate_prior  <- dlnorm(rate, meanlog = 0, sdlog = 2, log = TRUE)     kappa_prior <- dexp(kappa, rate = 0.1, log = TRUE)     pi_prior    <- sum(log(bf))  # Dirichlet(1,1,1,1) + Jacobian     shape_prior <- dexp(shape, rate = 1, log = TRUE)      LP <- LL + rate_prior + kappa_prior + pi_prior + shape_prior      yhat <- rep(LL / Data$N, Data$N)     list(LP = LP, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = c(LP, LL),          yhat = yhat, parm = parm) }  IV_strict <- c(1, 5, 0, 0, 0, 0.5)  # Fit with AMWG (phangorn likelihood, no analytical gradients) fit_strict <- lucifer(     Model_strict, Data_strict, IV_strict,     Iterations = 20000, Status = 5000, Thinning = 10,     Algorithm = "AMWG",     Specs = list(B = NULL, n = 0, Periodicity = 50) )  print(fit_strict)

title: Phylodynamic inference with lucifer
text: relaxed clock, branch rate drawn lognormal distribution estimated hyperparameters. hierarchical model \(n_{\text{branches}} + 2\) clock parameters (hyperparameters \(\mu_r, \sigma_r\) plus branch-specific rates) addition substitution model parameters. use non-centered parameterization branch rates: instead sampling \(r_i\) directly, sample standardized scores \(z_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\) recover rates \(r_i = \exp(\mu_r + \sigma_r z_i)\). reparameterization puts branch parameters common unit scale, improves AMWG’s componentwise adaptation since step size \(z_i\) operates natural scale regardless overall rate magnitude. lognormal prior density Jacobian exponential transformation cancel exactly, prior \(z_i\) reduces standard normal.
code: parm_names_relaxed <- c(     "mu_r", "sigma_r",     paste0("z_", seq_len(n_branches)),     "kappa", "alpha_A", "alpha_C", "alpha_G", "shape" )  Data_relaxed <- list(     mon.names  = c("LP", "LL", "mean_rate"),     parm.names = parm_names_relaxed,     tree = tree_ultra,     pdat = pdat,     time_lengths = time_lengths,     n_branches = n_branches,     N = n_sites,     phylo_loglik = phylo_loglik )  Model_relaxed <- function(parm, Data) {     nb <- Data$n_branches      # Hyperparameters for branch rate distribution     mu_r    <- parm[1]  # log-scale mean (unconstrained)     sigma_r <- interval(parm[2], 0.01, 5)     parm[2] <- sigma_r      # Non-centered parameterization: z ~ N(0,1), rate = exp(mu_r + sigma_r * z)     # The lognormal density and exponential Jacobian cancel, so the     # prior on z is simply standard normal.     z     <- parm[3:(nb + 2)]     rates <- exp(mu_r + sigma_r * z)      # HKY substitution parameters     idx <- nb + 2     kappa <- interval(parm[idx + 1], 0.01, 200)     parm[idx + 1] <- kappa      # Base frequencies via softmax     alpha <- c(parm[(idx + 2):(idx + 4)], 0)     alpha <- alpha - max(alpha)     bf    <- exp(alpha) / sum(exp(alpha))      shape <- interval(parm[idx + 5], 0.01, 100)     parm[idx + 5] <- shape      Q <- c(1, kappa, 1, 1, kappa, 1)      # Scale time-tree by branch-specific rates     scaled_tree <- Data$tree     scaled_tree$edge.length <- Data$time_lengths * rates      res <- Data$phylo_loglik(bf, Q, shape, scaled_tree, Data$pdat)     LL  <- res$logLik      # --- Priors ---     z_prior     <- sum(dnorm(z, 0, 1, log = TRUE))     mu_prior    <- dnorm(mu_r, mean = 0, sd = 2, log = TRUE)     sigma_prior <- dhalfcauchy(sigma_r, scale = 1, log = TRUE)     kappa_prior <- dexp(kappa, rate = 0.1, log = TRUE)     pi_prior    <- sum(log(bf))  # Dirichlet(1,1,1,1) + Jacobian     shape_prior <- dexp(shape, rate = 1, log = TRUE)      LP <- LL + z_prior + mu_prior + sigma_prior +           kappa_prior + pi_prior + shape_prior      yhat <- rep(LL / Data$N, Data$N)     mean_rate <- mean(rates)      list(LP = LP, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = c(LP, LL, mean_rate),          yhat = yhat, parm = parm) }  # Initial values: mu_r from strict clock posterior, z = 0 (at the mean), # substitution parameters from reasonable starting points. strict_rate_mean <- mean(fit_strict$Posterior2[, 1]) IV_relaxed <- c(     log(strict_rate_mean), 0.5,   # mu_r, sigma_r     rep(0, n_branches),           # z-scores (all branches at mean rate)     5, 0, 0, 0, 0.5              # kappa, alpha_A, alpha_C, alpha_G, shape )  # AMWG evaluates the Model once per parameter per iteration (35 x 8K = # 280K pml calls). The phylo_loglik wrapper calls gc() every 100 pml() # evaluations, which prevents the C-level heap corruption that phangorn # accumulates during intensive repeated evaluation. The non-centered # parameterization avoids scale mismatch on the branch rates. fit_relaxed <- lucifer(     Model_relaxed, Data_relaxed, IV_relaxed,     Iterations = 8000, Status = 4000, Thinning = 5,     Algorithm = "AMWG",     Specs = list(B = NULL, n = 0, Periodicity = 50),     Chains = 1 )  print(fit_relaxed)

previous_headings: Example 4: coalescent demographic inference
title: Phylodynamic inference with lucifer
text: define coalescent log-likelihood demographic parameterization. genealogy \(n\) tips, \(n - 1\) coalescent intervals durations \(\Delta t_j\) lineage counts \(k_j\), log-likelihood piecewise-constant demographic function \[\log L = \sum_{j=1}^{n-1} \left[ \log \binom{k_j}{2} - \log N_j - \frac{\binom{k_j}{2} \Delta t_j}{N_j} \right]\] \(N_j\) effective population size interval \(j\).
code: #' Coalescent log-likelihood for piecewise-constant Ne #' @param Ne Numeric vector of population sizes (one per interval or grouped) #' @param intervals Numeric vector of interval durations (n-1 values) #' @param lineages Integer vector of lineage counts (n-1 values) #' @param groups Integer vector mapping intervals to Ne groups (optional) #' @return Scalar log-likelihood coal_loglik <- function(Ne, intervals, lineages, groups = NULL) {     n_int <- length(intervals)     if (is.null(groups)) groups <- seq_len(n_int)      choose_k <- lineages * (lineages - 1) / 2     ll <- 0     for (j in seq_len(n_int)) {         Ne_j <- Ne[groups[j]]         ll <- ll + log(choose_k[j]) - log(Ne_j) -               choose_k[j] * intervals[j] / Ne_j     }     ll }

text: simplest demographic model assumes constant effective population size \(N_e\) throughout history sample. model one free parameter.
code: Data_const <- list(     mon.names  = c("LP"),     parm.names = c("Ne"),     intervals  = intervals,     lineages   = lineages,     n_int      = n_int,     N          = n_int,  # "observations" = coalescent intervals     coal_loglik = coal_loglik  # pass for callr visibility )  Model_const <- function(parm, Data) {     Ne <- interval(parm[1], 1e-6, 1e6)     parm[1] <- Ne      LL <- Data$coal_loglik(Ne, Data$intervals, Data$lineages,                            groups = rep(1, Data$n_int))      # Prior: log-uniform (Jeffreys prior on scale parameter)     Ne_prior <- -log(Ne)      LP <- LL + Ne_prior     yhat <- rep(LL / Data$N, Data$N)      list(LP = LP, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = LP,          yhat = yhat, parm = parm) }  # Analytical MLE (used for initial values and comparison) choose_k <- lineages * (lineages - 1) / 2 Ne_mle <- sum(choose_k * intervals) / (n_tips - 1)  IV_const <- c(Ne_mle)  fit_const <- lucifer(     Model_const, Data_const, IV_const,     Iterations = 20000, Status = 5000, Thinning = 5,     Algorithm = "NUTS",     Specs = list(A = 5000, delta = 0.8, epsilon = NULL, Lmax = 10) )  cat("MLE Ne:", Ne_mle, "\n") cat("Posterior mean Ne:", mean(fit_const$Posterior2), "\n")
