title: Bayesian inference for stochastic differential equations
text: \[dX = \kappa(\mu - X)\,dt + \sigma\sqrt{X}\,dW\] transition density involves non-central chi-squared distribution. Defining \(c = 2\kappa/[\sigma^2(1-e^{-\kappa\Delta t})]\), \(q = 2cX(s)e^{-\kappa\Delta t}\) (non-centrality), \(\nu = 4\kappa\mu/\sigma^2\) (degrees freedom), transition \(2cX(t) \sim \chi^2_\nu(q)\). Feller condition \(2\kappa\mu \geq \sigma^2\) ensures \(X(t) > 0\) .s. stationary distribution Gamma: \(X_\infty \sim \text{Gamma}(2\kappa\mu/\sigma^2, 2\kappa/\sigma^2)\). Cox-Ingersoll-Ross process canonical model interest rates positive-valued mean-reverting quantities [10]. transition density involves non-central chi-squared distribution, lucifer evaluates via R’s dnchisq function. Feller condition \(2\kappa\mu \geq \sigma^2\) determines whether CIR process stays strictly positive. violated, process can reach zero positive probability. lucifer’s CIR family constructor issues warning initial parameter values violate condition, helping user diagnose potential boundary issues fitting.
code: set.seed(123) true_k <- 1.5; true_m <- 2; true_s <- 0.4; true_osd <- 0.05 times_cir <- seq(0, 15, by = 0.15) n_cir <- length(times_cir)  x_cir <- numeric(n_cir); x_cir[1] <- true_m for (k in 2:n_cir) {     dt <- times_cir[k] - times_cir[k - 1]     ekt <- exp(-true_k * dt)     c_val <- 2 * true_k / (true_s^2 * (1 - ekt))     q <- 2 * c_val * x_cir[k - 1] * ekt     nu <- 4 * true_k * true_m / true_s^2     x_cir[k] <- rchisq(1, df = nu, ncp = q) / (2 * c_val)     x_cir[k] <- max(x_cir[k], 1e-6) } y_cir <- x_cir + rnorm(n_cir, 0, true_osd) y_cir <- pmax(y_cir, 0.01) sde_cir <- SDE(data = y_cir, times = times_cir, family = "cir") fit_cir <- SDE.fit(sde_cir, Algorithm = "HARM",                     Iterations = 20000, Status = 1000, Thinning = 5) summary(fit_cir) plot(fit_cir, type = "trajectory") plot(sde_cir, type = "prior_predictive", n.paths = 100) plot(fit_cir, type = "predictive", n.paths = 100)

text: double-well potential \(dX = \alpha(X - X^3)dt + \sigma\,dW\) two stable equilibria \(X = \pm 1\) separated unstable equilibrium \(X = 0\). Noise-induced transitions wells produce bistable dynamics characteristic many physical biological systems [17]. EKF handles mildly nonlinear system efficiently. EKF deterministic, MCMC iteration produces log-likelihood parameter values. eliminates noisy likelihood estimates degrade mixing pseudo-marginal methods. cost per iteration comparable Euler-Maruyama stochastic engine without acceptance rate penalties caused likelihood noise.
code: set.seed(99) true_alpha <- 1; true_sig <- 0.6; true_osd2 <- 0.1 times_dw <- seq(0, 20, by = 0.05) n_dw <- length(times_dw)  x_dw <- numeric(n_dw); x_dw[1] <- 0.5 for (k in 2:n_dw) {     dt <- times_dw[k] - times_dw[k - 1]     x_dw[k] <- x_dw[k - 1] +         true_alpha * (x_dw[k - 1] - x_dw[k - 1]^3) * dt +         true_sig * sqrt(dt) * rnorm(1) } y_dw <- x_dw + rnorm(n_dw, 0, true_osd2) sde_dw <- SDE(data = y_dw, times = times_dw, family = "double_well") cat("Method:", sde_dw$method, "\n")  # should be "ekf"  fit_dw <- SDE.fit(sde_dw, Algorithm = "HARM",                    Iterations = 20000, Status = 1000, Thinning = 5) summary(fit_dw) plot(fit_dw, type = "trajectory") plot(sde_dw, type = "prior_predictive", n.paths = 100) plot(fit_dw, type = "predictive", n.paths = 100)

title: Bayesian inference for stochastic differential equations
text: \[dS = \mu S\,dt + \sigma S\,dW\] Ito’s formula, \(d\log S = (\mu - \sigma^2/2)dt + \sigma\,dW\). transition density log-space \[\log S(t) \mid \log S(s) \sim N\left(\log S(s) + (\mu - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2)\Delta t,\; \sigma^2\Delta t\right)\] expected value \(E[S(t)] = S(0)e^{\mu t}\) (exponential growth), variance \(\text{Var}[S(t)] = S(0)^2 e^{2\mu t}(e^{\sigma^2 t} - 1)\). GBM stationary distribution; non-stationary. Geometric Brownian motion standard model asset prices [19]. log-price follows random walk drift: \(d\log S = (\mu - \sigma^2/2)dt + \sigma\,dW\), consequence Ito’s formula applied exponential transformation.
code: set.seed(77) true_mu_gbm <- 0.1; true_sig_gbm <- 0.25 times_gbm <- seq(0, 1, by = 1/252) n_gbm <- length(times_gbm) log_s <- numeric(n_gbm); log_s[1] <- log(100) for (k in 2:n_gbm) {     dt <- times_gbm[k] - times_gbm[k - 1]     log_s[k] <- log_s[k - 1] +         (true_mu_gbm - 0.5 * true_sig_gbm^2) * dt +         true_sig_gbm * sqrt(dt) * rnorm(1) } prices <- exp(log_s) sde_gbm <- SDE(data = prices, times = times_gbm, family = "gbm") fit_gbm <- SDE.fit(sde_gbm, Algorithm = "HARM",                     Iterations = 15000, Thinning = 3) summary(fit_gbm) plot(fit_gbm, type = "trajectory") plot(sde_gbm, type = "prior_predictive", n.paths = 100) plot(fit_gbm, type = "predictive", n.paths = 100)  # Forecast 60 trading days pred_gbm <- predict(fit_gbm, n.ahead = 60, n.paths = 500) plot(pred_gbm)

title: Bayesian inference for stochastic differential equations
text: \[dS = \mu S\,dt + \sigma S\,dW + S(e^J - 1)\,dN(\lambda), \quad J \sim N(\mu_J, \sigma_J^2)\] characteristic function log-returns interval \(\Delta t\) \[\phi(u) = \exp\left[iu(\mu - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 - \lambda(e^{\mu_J + \sigma_J^2/2} - 1))\Delta t - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 u^2 \Delta t + \lambda\Delta t(e^{iu\mu_J - \sigma_J^2 u^2/2} - 1)\right]\] excess kurtosis relative GBM \(\lambda\Delta t(\mu_J^4 + 6\mu_J^2\sigma_J^2 + 3\sigma_J^4)/(\sigma^2\Delta t + \lambda\Delta t(\mu_J^2 + \sigma_J^2))^2\), always positive, producing heavy tails observed financial returns. Merton model [19] extends geometric Brownian motion log-normal jumps arriving Poisson rate \(\lambda\). jump component generates heavy-tailed returns discontinuous price paths. model 5 parameters: drift \(\mu\), diffusion \(\sigma\), jump intensity \(\lambda\), jump mean \(\mu_J\), jump standard deviation \(\sigma_J\).
code: set.seed(123) true_mu_m <- 0.05; true_sig_m <- 0.15; true_lam <- 2 true_jmu <- -0.02; true_jsd <- 0.08 times_m <- seq(0, 2, by = 1/252) n_m <- length(times_m) S <- numeric(n_m); S[1] <- 100 for (k in 2:n_m) {     dt_m <- times_m[k] - times_m[k - 1]     dW <- rnorm(1, 0, sqrt(dt_m))     n_jumps <- rpois(1, true_lam * dt_m)     J_sum <- if (n_jumps > 0)         sum(rnorm(n_jumps, true_jmu, true_jsd)) else 0     S[k] <- S[k - 1] * exp((true_mu_m - 0.5 * true_sig_m^2) * dt_m +         true_sig_m * dW + J_sum) } # Log-returns distribution: heavier tails than normal log_ret <- diff(log(S)) ret_df <- data.frame(returns = log_ret) ggplot2::ggplot(ret_df, ggplot2::aes(x = .data$returns)) +     ggplot2::geom_histogram(ggplot2::aes(y = ggplot2::after_stat(density)),         bins = 80, fill = "#2196F3", alpha = 0.6, color = "white") +     ggplot2::stat_function(fun = dnorm,         args = list(mean = mean(log_ret), sd = sd(log_ret)),         color = "#FF5722", linewidth = 0.8, linetype = "dashed") +     ggplot2::labs(x = "Log-return", y = "Density",         title = "Merton jump-diffusion: heavy-tailed returns",         subtitle = "Dashed line: fitted normal (fails to capture tails)") +     theme_relab() sde_mer <- SDE(data = S, times = times_m, family = "merton") fit_mer <- SDE.fit(sde_mer, Algorithm = "HARM",                     Iterations = 15000, Thinning = 5) summary(fit_mer) plot(fit_mer, type = "trajectory") plot(fit_mer, type = "predictive", n.paths = 25)

title: Bayesian inference for stochastic differential equations
text: Heston model [21] extends Black-Scholes [37] making volatility stochastic, following CIR-type mean-reverting process. 2D system \[d\log S = \left(\mu - \frac{V}{2}\right)dt + \sqrt{V}\,dW_1, \quad dV = \kappa(\theta_v - V)\,dt + \sigma_v\sqrt{V}\,dW_2\] \(\text{Cor}(dW_1, dW_2) = \rho\). parameters : \(\mu\) (drift), \(\kappa\) (volatility mean-reversion speed), \(\theta_v\) (long-run variance), \(\sigma_v\) (volatility volatility), \(\rho\) (leverage effect, typically negative equities). Feller condition \(2\kappa\theta_v \geq \sigma_v^2\) ensures variance stays positive.
code: set.seed(42) true_mu_h <- 0.05; true_kappa_h <- 2; true_theta_v <- 0.04 true_sig_v <- 0.3; true_rho <- -0.7 times_h <- seq(0, 2, by = 1/252) n_h <- length(times_h) logS <- numeric(n_h); V_h <- numeric(n_h) logS[1] <- log(100); V_h[1] <- true_theta_v for (k in 2:n_h) {     dt_h <- times_h[k] - times_h[k - 1]     z1 <- rnorm(1); z2 <- true_rho * z1 + sqrt(1 - true_rho^2) * rnorm(1)     v <- max(V_h[k - 1], 1e-8)     logS[k] <- logS[k - 1] + (true_mu_h - v/2) * dt_h +         sqrt(v * dt_h) * z1     V_h[k] <- max(v + true_kappa_h * (true_theta_v - v) * dt_h +         true_sig_v * sqrt(v * dt_h) * z2, 1e-8) } prices_h <- exp(logS) # Price and volatility paths heston_df <- data.frame(     time = rep(times_h, 2),     value = c(prices_h, sqrt(V_h) * sqrt(252) * 100),     variable = rep(c("Price", "Annualized volatility (%)"),         each = n_h) ) ggplot2::ggplot(heston_df, ggplot2::aes(x = .data$time,     y = .data$value)) +     ggplot2::geom_line(color = "#2196F3", linewidth = 0.4) +     ggplot2::facet_wrap(~variable, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +     ggplot2::labs(x = "Time (years)", y = NULL,         title = "Heston stochastic volatility: simulated paths") +     theme_relab() sde_heston <- SDE(data = as.matrix(prices_h), times = times_h,                    family = "heston") fit_heston <- SDE.fit.pmmh(sde_heston, N.particles = 100,                              Iterations = 3000, Thinning = 2) summary(fit_heston) plot(fit_heston, type = "trajectory") # QQ-plot: model vs. empirical return distribution ret_h <- diff(log(prices_h)) post_h <- colMeans(if (!is.null(fit_heston$Posterior2)) fit_heston$Posterior2 else fit_heston$Posterior1) # Simulate returns from fitted model set.seed(1) n_sim <- 5000 sim_ret <- rnorm(n_sim, post_h[1] * (1/252),     sqrt(post_h[3]) * sqrt(1/252))  qq_df <- data.frame(     empirical = sort(ret_h),     theoretical = quantile(sim_ret,         probs = seq_along(ret_h) / (length(ret_h) + 1)) ) ggplot2::ggplot(qq_df, ggplot2::aes(x = .data$theoretical,     y = .data$empirical)) +     ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 0.8, color = "#2196F3") +     ggplot2::geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0,         linetype = "dashed", color = "#FF5722") +     ggplot2::labs(x = "Fitted model quantiles",         y = "Empirical quantiles",         title = "QQ-plot: Heston vs. empirical returns") +     theme_relab()

title: Bayesian inference for stochastic differential equations
text: \[\frac{dV}{dt} = \frac{V - V^3/3 - W + I_{ext}}{\varepsilon}, \quad \frac{dW}{dt} = \varepsilon(V + - bW)\] noise \(dV \mathrel{+}= (\sigma/\sqrt{\varepsilon})\,dW_1\). nullclines \(W = V - V^3/3 + I_{ext}\) (cubic, fast) \(W = (V + )/b\) (linear, slow). intersection determines fixed point. fixed point lies middle branch cubic nullcline, system exhibits oscillations (limit cycle). parameter \(\varepsilon \ll 1\) enforces time-scale separation: \(V\) fast (spikes) \(W\) slow (recovery). FitzHugh-Nagumo model [22] 2D simplification Hodgkin-Huxley equations describing neural excitability. system exhibits limit cycles, excitable behavior, noise-driven transitions resting spiking states. dynamics \[\frac{dV}{dt} = \frac{1}{\varepsilon}\left(V - \frac{V^3}{3} - W + I_{ext}\right), \quad \frac{dW}{dt} = \varepsilon(V + - bW)\] \(V\) membrane voltage (fast variable), \(W\) recovery variable (slow variable), \(\varepsilon\) controls time-scale separation, \(\) \(b\) shape nullclines, \(I_{ext}\) external current. Noise enters voltage equation amplitude \(\sigma/\sqrt{\varepsilon}\). \(V\) observed Gaussian noise. trajectory plot shows posterior mean filtered voltage 95% credible bands overlaid noisy observations. residuals approximately centered zero; systematic patterns indicate model misspecification (e.g., wrong time-scale separation \(\varepsilon\)).
code: # Simulate FitzHugh-Nagumo with known parameters set.seed(42) true_eps <- 0.08; true_a <- 0.7; true_b <- 0.8 true_I <- 0.5; true_sig <- 0.3; true_osd <- 0.15 times_fhn <- seq(0, 30, by = 0.15) n_fhn <- length(times_fhn) V <- numeric(n_fhn); W <- numeric(n_fhn) V[1] <- 0; W[1] <- 0 dt_fhn <- 0.001  # fine integration step for (k in 2:n_fhn) {     n_steps <- round((times_fhn[k] - times_fhn[k - 1]) / dt_fhn)     v <- V[k - 1]; w <- W[k - 1]     for (s in seq_len(n_steps)) {         dv <- (v - v^3/3 - w + true_I) / true_eps         dw <- true_eps * (v + true_a - true_b * w)         v <- v + dv * dt_fhn +             (true_sig / sqrt(true_eps)) * sqrt(dt_fhn) * rnorm(1)         w <- w + dw * dt_fhn     }     V[k] <- v; W[k] <- w } y_fhn <- V + rnorm(n_fhn, 0, true_osd) # Phase portrait: voltage vs. recovery (colored by time) phase_df <- data.frame(V = V, W = W, time = times_fhn) ggplot2::ggplot(phase_df, ggplot2::aes(x = .data$V, y = .data$W,     color = .data$time)) +     ggplot2::geom_path(linewidth = 0.4, alpha = 0.8) +     ggplot2::scale_color_viridis_c(option = "plasma") +     ggplot2::labs(x = "Voltage V", y = "Recovery W",         color = "Time",         title = "FitzHugh-Nagumo phase portrait") +     theme_relab() sde_fhn <- SDE(data = y_fhn, times = times_fhn,                family = "fitzhugh_nagumo") fit_fhn <- SDE.fit.pmmh(sde_fhn, N.particles = 150,                           Iterations = 5000, Thinning = 3) summary(fit_fhn) # Full diagnostic suite plot(fit_fhn, type = "trajectory") plot(fit_fhn, type = "predictive", n.paths = 15) plot(fit_fhn, type = "residuals") plot(fit_fhn, type = "posterior")

title: Bayesian inference for stochastic differential equations
text: \(N\) species generalized interaction matrix: \[\frac{dX_i}{dt} = X_i\left(r_i - \sum_{j=1}^{N} A_{ij} X_j\right) + \sigma_i X_i\,dW_i\] interaction matrix \(\) encodes: \(A_{ii} > 0\) (self-regulation / carrying capacity), \(A_{ij} > 0\) \(\neq j\) (competition predation), \(A_{ij} < 0\) (mutualism facilitation). deterministic fixed point satisfies \(\mathbf{x}^* = \mathbf{r}\), \(\mathbf{x}^* = ^{-1}\mathbf{r}\) \(\) invertible. Stability requires eigenvalues \(-\text{diag}(\mathbf{x}^*) \) negative real parts (community matrix criterion, May 1974 [30]). stochastic Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model nonlinear dynamics Poisson observations, requiring particle filtering inference. example demonstrates SDE.fit.pmmh() wrapper auxiliary particle filter. filtered state plot shows particle filter’s running estimate latent prey predator populations (top panels) effective sample size time (bottom panel). Low ESS regions indicate time points particle cloud degenerated resampling occurred.
code: set.seed(42) times_lv <- seq(0, 20, by = 0.5) n_lv <- length(times_lv)  # Simulate from the stochastic Lotka-Volterra system alpha <- 0.5; beta <- 0.025; gamma <- 0.3 sigma1 <- 0.1; sigma2 <- 0.1 prey <- numeric(n_lv); pred_pop <- numeric(n_lv) prey[1] <- 50; pred_pop[1] <- 30 dt_sim <- 0.01 for (k in 2:n_lv) {     t_int <- times_lv[k] - times_lv[k - 1]     n_steps <- round(t_int / dt_sim)     x1 <- prey[k - 1]; x2 <- pred_pop[k - 1]     for (s in seq_len(n_steps)) {         x1 <- max(x1 + (alpha * x1 - beta * x1 * x2) * dt_sim +             sigma1 * x1 * sqrt(dt_sim) * rnorm(1), 1e-3)         x2 <- max(x2 + (beta * x1 * x2 - gamma * x2) * dt_sim +             sigma2 * x2 * sqrt(dt_sim) * rnorm(1), 1e-3)     }     prey[k] <- rpois(1, max(x1, 0.1))     pred_pop[k] <- rpois(1, max(x2, 0.1)) } sde_lv <- SDE(data = cbind(prey, pred_pop), times = times_lv,               family = "lotka_volterra", pf.type = "auxiliary") print(sde_lv)  fit_lv <- SDE.fit.pmmh(sde_lv, N.particles = 300,                          Iterations = 5000, pf.type = "auxiliary") summary(fit_lv)  # Trajectory and phase portrait plot(fit_lv, type = "trajectory") plot(fit_lv, type = "phase")  # Filtered state estimates with ESS plot(fit_lv, type = "filtered")

previous_headings: Built-in SDE families > Lotka-Volterra and N-species community
title: Bayesian inference for stochastic differential equations
text: generalized Lotka-Volterra family supports arbitrary numbers interacting species. \(N\) species, dynamics \[\frac{dX_i}{dt} = X_i\left(r_i - \sum_{j=1}^{N} A_{ij} X_j\right) + \sigma_i X_i\,dW_i\] \(r_i\) intrinsic growth rate species \(\), \(A_{ij}\) interaction coefficient (competition, predation, mutualism), \(\sigma_i\) noise amplitude. parameter vector \(N + N^2 + N = N(N+2)\) entries: growth rates, interaction matrix (row-major), noise amplitudes. named species, community family reads column names data matrix: community family uses hierarchical priors: log-normal growth rates, normal interaction coefficients (allowing competition mutualism), half-normal noise amplitudes. large \(N\), \(N^2\) interaction parameters may require regularizing priors structured parameterizations.
code: # Simulate a 3-species system set.seed(42) times_c <- seq(0, 15, by = 0.5) sp1 <- rpois(length(times_c), 50 + 20 * sin(0.5 * times_c)) sp2 <- rpois(length(times_c), 30 + 10 * cos(0.3 * times_c)) sp3 <- rpois(length(times_c), 20 + 15 * sin(0.7 * times_c + 1))  # Using the lotka_volterra family with 3 columns sde_3sp <- SDE(data = cbind(sp1, sp2, sp3), times = times_c,                family = "lotka_volterra") cat("Parameters:", length(sde_3sp$parm.names), "(3+9+3=15)") print(sde_3sp) community_data <- cbind(Fox = sp1, Rabbit = sp2, Grass = sp3) sde_eco <- SDE(data = community_data, times = times_c,                family = "community") cat("Species:", paste(sde_eco$state.names, collapse = ", "))

title: Bayesian inference for stochastic differential equations
text: example demonstrates lucifer’s N-species community model simulated 3-species competitive system. interaction matrix \(\) determines community structure: diagonal elements represent self-regulation (carrying capacity effects), -diagonal elements encode interspecific competition facilitation [30], [31]. interaction matrix heatmap reveals community structure: diagonal elements (self-regulation) largest, -diagonal elements show interspecific effects. Red cells indicate competition (positive \(A_{ij}\), reduces growth), blue cells indicate facilitation (negative \(A_{ij}\)).
code:
# Simulate a 3-species competitive community set.seed(77) N_sp <- 3 true_r <- c(0.5, 0.3, 0.4)      # intrinsic growth rates true_A <- matrix(c(     0.01,  0.005, 0.002,    # species 1: self-reg, competes with 2 and 3     0.003, 0.008, 0.004,    # species 2: weaker self-reg     0.001, 0.003, 0.012     # species 3: strongest self-reg ), N_sp, N_sp, byrow = TRUE) true_sig <- c(0.05, 0.04, 0.06)  # process noise  times_eco <- seq(0, 30, by = 0.5) n_eco <- length(times_eco) X_eco <- matrix(NA, n_eco, N_sp) X_eco[1, ] <- c(50, 40, 30)  # initial populations dt_eco <- 0.01  for (k in 2:n_eco) {     n_sub <- round((times_eco[k] - times_eco[k - 1]) / dt_eco)     x <- X_eco[k - 1, ]     for (s in seq_len(n_sub)) {         x <- pmax(x, 1e-3)         drift <- x * (true_r - as.numeric(true_A %*% x))         diff_v <- true_sig * x         x <- x + drift * dt_eco + diff_v * sqrt(dt_eco) * rnorm(N_sp)     }     X_eco[k, ] <- pmax(x, 0.1) } # Poisson observations Y_eco <- matrix(rpois(n_eco * N_sp, pmax(X_eco, 0.1)), n_eco, N_sp) colnames(Y_eco) <- c("Prey", "Mesopredator", "Apex") # Plot observed counts eco_df <- data.frame(     time = rep(times_eco, N_sp),     count = as.vector(Y_eco),     species = rep(colnames(Y_eco), each = n_eco) ) ggplot2::ggplot(eco_df, ggplot2::aes(x = .data$time, y = .data$count,     color = .data$species)) +     ggplot2::geom_line(alpha = 0.7) +     ggplot2::geom_point(size = 0.8, alpha = 0.5) +     ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = c(         Prey = "#4CAF50", Mesopredator = "#FF9800", Apex = "#F44336")) +     ggplot2::labs(x = "Time", y = "Count",         title = "3-species community: observed Poisson counts",         color = "Species") +     theme_relab() # Fit the community model sde_eco <- SDE(data = Y_eco, times = times_eco, family = "community") cat("Parameters:", sde_eco$dim_theta,     "(3 growth + 9 interaction + 3 noise = 15)
") cat("State names:", paste(sde_eco$state.names, collapse = ", "), "
")  fit_eco <- SDE.fit.pmmh(sde_eco, N.particles = 100,                           Iterations = 3000, Thinning = 2) summary(fit_eco) # Filtered trajectories for all species plot(fit_eco, type = "trajectory") # Reconstruct posterior interaction matrix posterior_eco <- fit_eco$Posterior2 if (is.null(posterior_eco)) posterior_eco <- fit_eco$Posterior1 A_post <- colMeans(posterior_eco[, 4:12])  # columns 4-12 are A entries A_mat <- matrix(A_post, N_sp, N_sp, byrow = TRUE) rownames(A_mat) <- colnames(A_mat) <- colnames(Y_eco)  # Heatmap of posterior mean interaction matrix a_df <- expand.grid(     To = colnames(Y_eco),     From = colnames(Y_eco) ) a_df$value <- as.vector(t(A_mat)) ggplot2::ggplot(a_df, ggplot2::aes(x = .data$From, y = .data$To,     fill = .data$value)) +     ggplot2::geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +     ggplot2::geom_text(ggplot2::aes(         label = sprintf("%.4f", .data$value)),         color = "white", size = 3.5) +     ggplot2::scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2196F3", mid = "grey90",         high = "#F44336", midpoint = 0) +     ggplot2::labs(x = "Effect of", y = "On",         fill = "Interaction
strength",         title = "Posterior mean interaction matrix") +     theme_relab() # Compare posterior estimates with true values true_theta <- c(true_r, as.vector(t(true_A)), true_sig) post_mean <- colMeans(posterior_eco) post_sd <- apply(posterior_eco, 2, sd)  comp_df <- data.frame(     Parameter = sde_eco$parm.names,     True = round(true_theta, 4),     `Posterior mean` = round(post_mean, 4),     `Posterior SD` = round(post_sd, 4),     `Covered` = ifelse(         true_theta >= post_mean - 1.96 * post_sd &         true_theta <= post_mean + 1.96 * post_sd,         "Yes", "No"),     check.names = FALSE ) knitr::kable(comp_df, caption = "3-species community: parameter recovery")

what: Comparison of EKF vs. particle filter
title: Bayesian inference for stochastic differential equations
text: OU process (linear SDE), EKF bootstrap particle filter produce similar results, EKF faster deterministic. section compares :
code: # EKF sde_ekf <- SDE(     drift = function(x, theta, t) theta[1] * (theta[2] - x),     diffusion = function(x, theta, t) theta[3],     data = y_ou, times = times, x0 = y_ou[1],     obs.model = "gaussian",     obs.noise = function(theta) theta[4],     prior = function(theta) {         if (theta[1] <= 0 || theta[3] <= 0 || theta[4] <= 0)             return(-Inf)         sum(dnorm(theta, 0, 10, log = TRUE))     },     parm.names = c("kappa", "mu", "sigma", "obs_sd"),     method = "ekf" )  # Particle filter (same model) sde_pf <- SDE(     drift = function(x, theta, t) theta[1] * (theta[2] - x),     diffusion = function(x, theta, t) theta[3],     data = y_ou, times = times, x0 = y_ou[1],     obs.model = "gaussian",     obs.noise = function(theta) theta[4],     obs.loglik = function(y_k, x, theta) {         dnorm(y_k, x, theta[4], log = TRUE)     },     prior = function(theta) {         if (theta[1] <= 0 || theta[3] <= 0 || theta[4] <= 0)             return(-Inf)         sum(dnorm(theta, 0, 10, log = TRUE))     },     parm.names = c("kappa", "mu", "sigma", "obs_sd"),     method = "particle", N.particles = 200 )  # Compare likelihoods at true parameters theta_true <- c(true_kappa, true_mu, true_sigma, true_obs_sd) ekf_ll <- sde_ekf$Model(theta_true, sde_ekf$Data)$Monitor[1] set.seed(1) pf_ll <- sde_pf$Model(theta_true, sde_pf$Data)$Monitor[1]  # EKF is deterministic (same theta -> same LL) r1 <- sde_ekf$Model(theta_true, sde_ekf$Data)$Monitor[1] r2 <- sde_ekf$Model(theta_true, sde_ekf$Data)$Monitor[1]  knitr::kable(data.frame(     Method = c("EKF (deterministic)", "Particle filter (N=200)"),     `Log-likelihood` = round(c(ekf_ll, pf_ll), 4),     Deterministic = c("Yes", "No"),     check.names = FALSE ), caption = "EKF vs. particle filter likelihood comparison at true parameters")

code: algos <- c("HARM", "twalk", "AMWG") fits_algo <- list() for (algo in algos) {     t0 <- proc.time()[3]     fits_algo[[algo]] <- SDE.fit(sde_ou, Algorithm = algo,         Iterations = 10000, Thinning = 5)     fits_algo[[algo]]$wall_time <- proc.time()[3] - t0 } algo_results <- data.frame(     Algorithm = algos,     `Acceptance rate` = sapply(fits_algo,         function(f) round(f$Acceptance.Rate, 3)),     `Wall time (s)` = sapply(fits_algo,         function(f) round(f$wall_time, 1)),     `ESS (kappa)` = sapply(fits_algo, function(f) {         post <- f$Posterior2         if (is.null(post)) post <- f$Posterior1         round(coda::effectiveSize(coda::as.mcmc(post[, 1])), 0)     }),     check.names = FALSE ) knitr::kable(algo_results,     caption = "Algorithm comparison on OU process") # Trace plot comparison trace_dfs <- lapply(algos, function(algo) {     post <- fits_algo[[algo]]$Posterior2     if (is.null(post)) post <- fits_algo[[algo]]$Posterior1     data.frame(         iteration = seq_len(nrow(post)),         kappa = post[, 1],         mu = post[, 2],         algorithm = algo     ) }) trace_df <- do.call(rbind, trace_dfs)  ggplot2::ggplot(trace_df, ggplot2::aes(x = .data$iteration,     y = .data$kappa, color = .data$algorithm)) +     ggplot2::geom_line(alpha = 0.5, linewidth = 0.3) +     ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = true_kappa, linetype = "dashed") +     ggplot2::facet_wrap(~algorithm, ncol = 1) +     ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = c(         HARM = "#2196F3", twalk = "#FF9800", AMWG = "#4CAF50")) +     ggplot2::labs(x = "Iteration", y = expression(kappa),         title = expression(paste("Trace plots of ", kappa,             " across algorithms"))) +     ggplot2::guides(color = "none") +     theme_relab()

previous_headings: Posterior diagnostics and model checking
title: Bayesian inference for stochastic differential equations
text: SDE models present unique convergence challenges: log-likelihood may noisy (particle filter), parameter space may ridges (e.g., \(\kappa\) \(\sigma\) correlated OU process), observation noise process noise may confounded. section demonstrates diagnostics go beyond standard trace plots. Geweke diagnostic compares mean first 10% chain mean last 50%. z-score exceeding \(\pm 1.96\) indicates chain converged 5% significance level. SDE models, observation noise parameter \(\sigma_{obs}\) typically converges fastest (directly identified residual variance), reversion speed \(\kappa\) converges slowest (requires long series distinguish unit-root behavior).

title: Bayesian inference for stochastic differential equations
text: central question SDE modelling process best describes data. lucifer supports model comparison via DIC (computed automatically fitting) LOO-PSIS (via LOO() function). following example compares three candidate models mean-reverting data: OU process, CIR process, double-well potential. Since data generated OU process, expect OU model lowest DIC. CIR model close competitor reduces OU state far zero, non-central chi-squared likelihood adds unnecessary complexity. double-well model penalizes cubic drift match linear data-generating process.
code: # Use the OU data from above sde_m1 <- SDE(data = y_ou, times = times, family = "ou") sde_m2 <- SDE(data = pmax(y_ou, 0.01), times = times, family = "cir") sde_m3 <- SDE(data = y_ou, times = times, family = "double_well")  fit_m1 <- SDE.fit(sde_m1, Algorithm = "HARM",                    Iterations = 20000, Thinning = 5) fit_m2 <- SDE.fit(sde_m2, Algorithm = "HARM",                    Iterations = 20000, Thinning = 5) fit_m3 <- SDE.fit(sde_m3, Algorithm = "HARM",                    Iterations = 20000, Thinning = 5) # Extract DIC from each fit dic_table <- data.frame(     Model = c("OU (exact)", "CIR (exact)", "Double-well (EKF)"),     DIC = c(         extract_dic(fit_m1)$DIC,         extract_dic(fit_m2)$DIC,         extract_dic(fit_m3)$DIC     ) ) dic_table$Delta_DIC <- dic_table$DIC - min(dic_table$DIC) knitr::kable(dic_table, digits = 1,              caption = "DIC comparison of three SDE models")

yhat_m     res_list[[nm]] <- data.frame(         time = times[seq_along(residuals_m)],         residual = residuals_m,         model = nm     ) } res_all <- do.call(rbind, res_list)  ggplot2::ggplot(res_all, ggplot2::aes(x = .data$time,     y = .data$residual)) +     ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 0.8, color = "#2196F3") +     ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",         color = "grey50") +     ggplot2::geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE,         color = "#F44336", linewidth = 0.6) +     ggplot2::facet_wrap(~model, ncol = 2) +     ggplot2::labs(x = "Time", y = "Residual",         title = "One-step-ahead residuals by model",         subtitle = "Red: LOESS smooth (should be flat at zero)") +     theme_relab()

text: latent dynamics can observed different observation models. example compares fitting OU process observation noise (correct) versus without (misspecified): Omitting observation noise forces \(\sigma\) absorb measurement variability, producing biased parameter estimates worse DIC.
code: sde_correct <- SDE(data = y_ou, times = times, family = "ou") sde_misspec <- SDE(     drift = function(x, theta, t) theta[1] * (theta[2] - x),     diffusion = function(x, theta, t) theta[3],     data = y_ou, times = times, x0 = y_ou[1],     obs.model = "gaussian",     obs.noise = function(theta) 1e-10,     prior = function(theta) {         if (theta[1] <= 0 || theta[3] <= 0) return(-Inf)         sum(dnorm(theta, 0, 10, log = TRUE))     },     parm.names = c("kappa", "mu", "sigma"),     method = "exact", family = "ou")  fit_c <- SDE.fit(sde_correct, Algorithm = "HARM", Iterations = 15000, Thinning = 3) fit_m <- SDE.fit(sde_misspec, Algorithm = "HARM", Iterations = 15000, Thinning = 3)  dic_c <- extract_dic(fit_c)$DIC dic_m <- extract_dic(fit_m)$DIC knitr::kable(data.frame(     Model = c("With observation noise (correct)", "Without observation noise (misspecified)"),     DIC = round(c(dic_c, dic_m), 1),     Delta_DIC = round(c(dic_c, dic_m) - min(dic_c, dic_m), 1) ), caption = "Observation model comparison via DIC")

text: example demonstrates posterior predictive checks systematically reveal specific types model misspecification. fit two wrong models OU data show different PPC statistics diagnose failure mode. diagnostic pattern revealing. GBM fails ACF check mean-revert: simulated ACF decays slowly () compared observed exponential decay \(\rho(\tau) = e^{-\kappa\tau}\). double-well model may pass ACF check short lags (cubic drift produces local mean-reversion around well) generates occasional large jumps wells inflate variance produce excess kurtosis present data.
code: # OU data: the correct model # Misspecification 1: GBM (no mean reversion, exponential growth) # Misspecification 2: Double-well (cubic nonlinearity)  sde_right <- SDE(data = y_ou, times = times, family = "ou") sde_wrong1 <- SDE(data = abs(y_ou) + 0.1, times = times, family = "gbm") sde_wrong2 <- SDE(data = y_ou, times = times, family = "double_well")  fit_right <- SDE.fit(sde_right, Algorithm = "HARM",     Iterations = 15000, Thinning = 5) fit_wrong1 <- SDE.fit(sde_wrong1, Algorithm = "HARM",     Iterations = 15000, Thinning = 5) fit_wrong2 <- SDE.fit(sde_wrong2, Algorithm = "HARM",     Iterations = 15000, Thinning = 5) # Side-by-side trajectory comparison par_list <- list(     list(fit = fit_right, name = "OU (correct)"),     list(fit = fit_wrong1, name = "GBM (no mean-reversion)"),     list(fit = fit_wrong2, name = "Double-well (cubic drift)") )  traj_dfs <- lapply(par_list, function(p) {     post <- p$fit$Posterior2     if (is.null(post)) post <- p$fit$Posterior1     theta_hat <- colMeans(post)     yhat <- p$fit$sde$Model(theta_hat, p$fit$sde$Data)$yhat     data.frame(         time = times[seq_along(yhat)],         observed = y_ou[seq_along(yhat)],         fitted = yhat,         model = p$name     ) }) traj_all <- do.call(rbind, traj_dfs)  ggplot2::ggplot(traj_all) +     ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(x = .data$time,         y = .data$observed), color = "grey40", size = 0.5, alpha = 0.5) +     ggplot2::geom_line(ggplot2::aes(x = .data$time,         y = .data$fitted), color = "#2196F3", linewidth = 0.6) +     ggplot2::facet_wrap(~model, ncol = 1) +     ggplot2::labs(x = "Time", y = "Value",         title = "Filtered trajectories: correct vs. misspecified models",         subtitle = "Grey points: observations; blue line: posterior mean") +     theme_relab() # PPC comparison: autocorrelation structure models_list <- list(     "OU (correct)" = list(sde = sde_right, fit = fit_right),     "GBM (wrong)" = list(sde = sde_wrong1, fit = fit_wrong1),     "Double-well (wrong)" = list(sde = sde_wrong2, fit = fit_wrong2) )  acf_comp_dfs <- list() for (nm in names(models_list)) {     post <- models_list[[nm]]$fit$Posterior2     if (is.null(post)) post <- models_list[[nm]]$fit$Posterior1     n_r <- min(30, nrow(post))     idx_r <- sample.int(nrow(post), n_r)     acf_reps <- matrix(NA, n_r, 21)     for (r in seq_len(n_r)) {         sim <- simulate(models_list[[nm]]$sde,             theta = post[idx_r[r], ], n.paths = 1)         acf_reps[r, ] <- acf(sim$trajectories[, 1, 1],             lag.max = 20, plot = FALSE)$acf[, , 1]     }     acf_q <- apply(acf_reps, 2, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))     acf_obs <- acf(y_ou, lag.max = 20, plot = FALSE)$acf[, , 1]     acf_comp_dfs[[nm]] <- data.frame(         lag = 0:20,         obs = acf_obs,         median = acf_q[2, ],         lo = acf_q[1, ],         hi = acf_q[3, ],         model = nm     ) } acf_comp <- do.call(rbind, acf_comp_dfs)  ggplot2::ggplot(acf_comp) +     ggplot2::geom_ribbon(ggplot2::aes(x = .data$lag, ymin = .data$lo,         ymax = .data$hi), fill = "#2196F3", alpha = 0.3) +     ggplot2::geom_line(ggplot2::aes(x = .data$lag, y = .data$median),         color = "#1565C0") +     ggplot2::geom_line(ggplot2::aes(x = .data$lag, y = .data$obs),         color = "black", linewidth = 0.6) +     ggplot2::facet_wrap(~model, ncol = 1) +     ggplot2::labs(x = "Lag", y = "ACF",         title = "PPC: autocorrelation under correct and misspecified models",         subtitle = "Black: observed; blue: posterior predictive 95% band") +     theme_relab()

title: Bayesian inference for stochastic differential equations
text: Simulation-based calibration (SBC) verifies inference procedure well-calibrated: data simulated prior predictive, posterior rank statistics uniformly distributed. stringent self-consistency check detects bugs likelihood, incorrect constraint handling, poor MCMC mixing [32]. Uniform rank histograms indicate correct calibration. U-shaped histogram indicates credible intervals narrow (overconfident); inverted-U indicates wide (underconfident); skewed histogram indicates systematic bias.
code: # SBC for the OU model with a small number of replications set.seed(42) n_sbc <- 20  # increase to 200+ for production n_obs_sbc <- 50 times_sbc <- seq(0, 5, by = 0.1) ranks <- matrix(NA, n_sbc, 4) colnames(ranks) <- c("kappa", "mu", "sigma", "obs_sd")  for (rep in seq_len(n_sbc)) {     # Draw parameters from prior     kappa_p <- abs(rnorm(1, 0, 3))     mu_p <- rnorm(1, 0, 5)     sigma_p <- abs(rnorm(1, 0, 2))     obs_sd_p <- abs(rnorm(1, 0, 1))     theta_p <- c(max(kappa_p, 0.1), mu_p,                  max(sigma_p, 0.01), max(obs_sd_p, 0.01))      # Simulate data from prior predictive     x_sbc <- numeric(length(times_sbc))     x_sbc[1] <- mu_p     for (k in 2:length(times_sbc)) {         dt_s <- times_sbc[k] - times_sbc[k - 1]         ekt <- exp(-theta_p[1] * dt_s)         x_sbc[k] <- rnorm(1,             theta_p[2] + (x_sbc[k-1] - theta_p[2]) * ekt,             theta_p[3] * sqrt((1 - exp(-2 * theta_p[1] * dt_s)) /                 (2 * theta_p[1])))     }     y_sbc <- x_sbc + rnorm(length(times_sbc), 0, theta_p[4])      # Fit     sde_sbc <- SDE(data = y_sbc, times = times_sbc, family = "ou")     fit_sbc <- SDE.fit(sde_sbc, Algorithm = "RWM",                         Iterations = 2000, Thinning = 2)     post_sbc <- fit_sbc$Posterior1      # Compute ranks     for (j in 1:4)         ranks[rep, j] <- mean(post_sbc[, j] < theta_p[j]) } # SBC rank histogram: should be uniform rank_df <- data.frame(     rank = as.vector(ranks),     parameter = rep(colnames(ranks), each = n_sbc) ) ggplot2::ggplot(rank_df, ggplot2::aes(x = .data$rank)) +     ggplot2::geom_histogram(bins = 10, fill = "#2196F3",         alpha = 0.6, color = "white") +     ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = n_sbc / 10, linetype = "dashed",         color = "#FF5722") +     ggplot2::facet_wrap(~parameter, scales = "free_y") +     ggplot2::labs(x = "Rank (quantile of true value in posterior)",         y = "Count",         title = "Simulation-based calibration",         subtitle = paste0(n_sbc, " replications; dashed: uniform reference")) +     theme_relab()

text: lucifer’s RobustBayes() function performs power-scaling sensitivity analysis [18] assess sensitive posterior inferences prior likelihood. SDE models, useful diagnosing prior-data conflict (e.g., informative prior \(\kappa\) contradicts data) identifying parameters whose posteriors dominated prior rather data. sensitivity plot shows parameter’s posterior shifts prior likelihood power-scaled. Parameters high prior sensitivity low likelihood sensitivity poorly identified data. Parameters high likelihood sensitivity low prior sensitivity well-informed data. RobustBayes() function works sde_fit objects exactly demonoid fit, since sde_fit inherits demonoid. lucifer’s RobustBayes() [18] performs power-scaling sensitivity analysis SDE fits, assessing posterior inferences depend prior likelihood: sensitivity plot reveals parameters prior-dominated (high prior sensitivity, low likelihood sensitivity) versus data-informed (low prior sensitivity, high likelihood sensitivity). well-identified SDE models, observation noise \(\sigma_{obs}\) typically well-informed data, reversion speed \(\kappa\) may sensitive prior time series short relative mean-reversion timescale \(1/\kappa\). Power-scaling sensitivity analysis [18] perturbs prior likelihood raising power \(\alpha\), examines posterior shifts. diagnoses: (1) prior-data conflict (prior likelihood pull different directions), (2) prior sensitivity (posterior changes substantially prior weakened), (3) likelihood sensitivity (posterior changes likelihood weakened, indicating fragile inference). Parameters classified “prior-sensitive” posteriors dominated prior rather data. typically occurs parameters weakly identified likelihood (e.g., observation noise \(\sigma_{obs}\) small relative process noise \(\sigma\)). Parameters classified “well-identified” posteriors driven data regardless prior perturbation.
code: rb_ou <- RobustBayes(fit_m1) summary(rb_ou) plot(rb_ou) rb <- RobustBayes(fit_ou) summary(rb) plot(rb) # Full RobustBayes analysis on OU fit rb <- RobustBayes(fit_ou) summary(rb) # Power-scaling sensitivity plot plot(rb) # Compare prior vs. likelihood sensitivity rb_df <- data.frame(     Parameter = rb$parm.names,     Prior_sensitivity = round(rb$prior_sensitivity, 4),     Likelihood_sensitivity = round(rb$likelihood_sensitivity, 4),     Diagnosis = ifelse(rb$prior_sensitivity > 0.05, "Prior-sensitive",         ifelse(rb$likelihood_sensitivity > 0.05, "Likelihood-sensitive",             "Well-identified")) ) knitr::kable(rb_df,     caption = "RobustBayes parameter sensitivity classification")

text: well-identified models large samples, Bayesian posterior summaries converge frequentist maximum-likelihood estimates (Bernstein-von Mises theorem). lucifer’s frequentist bridge functions allow direct comparison. example fits OU process SDE.fit() (Bayesian) LaplaceApproximation() (frequentist-like), compares via confint_compare(). confint_compare() forest plot shows point estimates 95% intervals method. well-identified model 400 observations, Bayesian credible intervals frequentist confidence intervals nearly overlap, confirming asymptotic equivalence. Discrepancies indicate either prior influence (small sample) multimodality (poor mixing). profile likelihood curves show curvature log-likelihood around parameter’s MLE. Symmetric curves indicate well-behaved quadratic approximation (Laplace approximation accurate); asymmetric curves suggest posterior may skewed MCMC preferable.
code: # Large OU dataset for good asymptotics set.seed(42) true_k <- 3; true_m <- 5; true_s <- 0.8; true_o <- 0.15 times_fb <- seq(0, 20, by = 0.05) n_fb <- length(times_fb) x_fb <- numeric(n_fb); x_fb[1] <- true_m for (k in 2:n_fb) {     dt_fb <- times_fb[k] - times_fb[k - 1]     ekt <- exp(-true_k * dt_fb)     x_fb[k] <- rnorm(1, true_m + (x_fb[k - 1] - true_m) * ekt,         true_s * sqrt((1 - exp(-2 * true_k * dt_fb)) / (2 * true_k))) } y_fb <- x_fb + rnorm(n_fb, 0, true_o) # Bayesian fit via MCMC sde_fb <- SDE(data = y_fb, times = times_fb, family = "ou") fit_bayes <- SDE.fit(sde_fb, Algorithm = "HARM",                       Iterations = 30000, Thinning = 10)  # Frequentist-like fit via Laplace approximation # LaplaceApproximation requires a clean Data list (no internal SDE fields), # so we build a minimal wrapper. la_Model <- sde_fb$Model la_Data <- list(     N = length(y_fb),     parm.names = sde_fb$parm.names,     mon.names = "LP" ) # Wrap Model to return scalar Monitor (LA expects single mon.names = "LP") la_Model_wrap <- function(parm, Data) {     res <- sde_fb$Model(parm, sde_fb$Data)     res$Monitor <- res$LP     res } fit_laplace <- LaplaceApproximation(     la_Model_wrap, sde_fb$Initial.Values, la_Data,     Method = "NM", Iterations = 5000) # Compare confidence/credible intervals # confint_compare expects demonoid class; strip sde_fit wrapper fit_bayes_dem <- fit_bayes class(fit_bayes_dem) <- "demonoid" confint_compare(     list("MCMC (Bayesian)" = fit_bayes_dem,          "Laplace (frequentist)" = fit_laplace),     true_values = c(kappa = true_k, mu = true_m,                     sigma = true_s, obs_sd = true_o) ) # Profile likelihood: frequentist CI shape prof <- profile_likelihood(fit_laplace, la_Model_wrap, la_Data,                             parm = c("kappa", "mu"), n_grid = 40) plot(prof) # Frequentist summary with p-values and CIs fs <- freq_summary(fit_laplace) knitr::kable(fs$coefficients, digits = 4,     caption = "Frequentist summary of OU parameter estimates")

title: Bayesian inference for stochastic differential equations
text: SDEs state-dependent (multiplicative) noise, Ito Stratonovich stochastic integrals produce different transition densities. Stratonovich SDE \(dX = f(X)dt + g(X) \circ dW\) equivalent Ito SDE \[dX = \left[f(X) + \frac{1}{2}g(X)\frac{\partial g}{\partial X}(X)\right]dt + g(X)\,dW\] correction \(\frac{1}{2}g\,g'\) noise-induced drift [1]. additive noise (\(g\) constant, \(g' = 0\)), two interpretations identical.

previous_headings: Appendix: Ito vs. Stratonovich interpretation
title: Bayesian inference for stochastic differential equations
text: drift diffusion specified expressions (character strings quote()), lucifer’s symbolic differentiation engine computes \(g'(x)\) automatically adds correction drift. user specifies interpretation = "stratonovich" rest handled internally. two specifications produce identical log-posteriors lucifer symbolically differentiates \(g(x) = \sigma x\) obtain \(g'(x) = \sigma\), adds \(\frac{1}{2}\sigma x \cdot \sigma = \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2 x\) drift, matches manual correction exactly.
code: # Stratonovich geometric growth: dX = mu*X dt + sigma*X o dW # The Ito equivalent adds a noise-induced drift: (mu + 0.5*sigma^2)*X # This means the Stratonovich drift mu produces HIGHER effective growth # than the Ito drift mu (by 0.5*sigma^2).  # Simulate data from the Ito version (true model) set.seed(42) true_mu <- 0.1; true_sigma <- 0.3; true_obs_sd <- 0.2 times_s <- seq(0, 10, by = 0.1) n_s <- length(times_s) x_s <- numeric(n_s); x_s[1] <- 2 for (k in 2:n_s) {     dt_s <- times_s[k] - times_s[k - 1]     # Ito dynamics (drift = mu*X, no correction)     x_s[k] <- x_s[k - 1] + true_mu * x_s[k - 1] * dt_s +         true_sigma * x_s[k - 1] * sqrt(dt_s) * rnorm(1)     x_s[k] <- max(x_s[k], 0.01) } y_s <- abs(x_s + rnorm(n_s, 0, true_obs_sd)) # Fit as Stratonovich model: lucifer auto-corrects the drift sde_strat <- SDE(     drift = "theta[1] * x[1]",       # Stratonovich drift (no manual correction)     diffusion = "theta[2] * x[1]",   # multiplicative noise     data = y_s, times = times_s, x0 = y_s[1],     obs.model = "gaussian",     obs.noise = function(theta) theta[3],     prior = function(theta) {         if (theta[2] <= 0 || theta[3] <= 0) return(-Inf)         dnorm(theta[1], 0, 1, log = TRUE) +             dnorm(theta[2], 0, 1, log = TRUE) +             dexp(theta[3], 5, log = TRUE)     },     parm.names = c("mu", "sigma", "obs_sd"),     method = "ekf",     interpretation = "stratonovich"   # auto-conversion to Ito )  # Fit as Ito model (manual correction for comparison) sde_ito <- SDE(     drift = "theta[1] * x[1] + 0.5 * theta[2]^2 * x[1]",  # manual Ito correction     diffusion = "theta[2] * x[1]",     data = y_s, times = times_s, x0 = y_s[1],     obs.model = "gaussian",     obs.noise = function(theta) theta[3],     prior = function(theta) {         if (theta[2] <= 0 || theta[3] <= 0) return(-Inf)         dnorm(theta[1], 0, 1, log = TRUE) +             dnorm(theta[2], 0, 1, log = TRUE) +             dexp(theta[3], 5, log = TRUE)     },     parm.names = c("mu", "sigma", "obs_sd"),     method = "ekf",     interpretation = "ito" )  # Both should produce identical log-posteriors theta_test <- c(0.1, 0.3, 0.2) lp_strat <- sde_strat$Model(theta_test, sde_strat$Data)$LP lp_ito <- sde_ito$Model(theta_test, sde_ito$Data)$LP knitr::kable(data.frame(     Specification = c("Stratonovich (auto-corrected)", "Ito (manual correction)"),     `Log-posterior` = round(c(lp_strat, lp_ito), 6),     Identical = c("", ifelse(abs(lp_strat - lp_ito) < 1e-6, "Yes", "No")),     check.names = FALSE ), caption = "Stratonovich vs. manual Ito correction: identical log-posteriors")

previous_headings: Appendix: Ito vs. Stratonovich interpretation
what: Worked example: effect of interpretation on inference
title: Bayesian inference for stochastic differential equations
text: Ito-Stratonovich distinction practical consequences parameter interpretation. Consider population model multiplicative noise: Stratonovich interpretation, drift parameter \(\mu\) represents “physical” growth rate (measure deterministic experiment), Ito, effective growth rate \(\mu - \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2\) (noise-induced drift reduces net growth). Fitting wrong interpretation biases growth rate estimate \(\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2\). two posterior distributions nearly identical, confirming automatic Stratonovich correction produces inference manual approach. practical advantage users working physical ecological models Stratonovich form can specify model naturally without worrying noise-induced drift correction.
code: # Fit both interpretations to the same data fit_strat <- SDE.fit(sde_strat, Algorithm = "HARM",                       Iterations = 10000, Thinning = 3) fit_ito <- SDE.fit(sde_ito, Algorithm = "HARM",                     Iterations = 10000, Thinning = 3)  # Compare posterior means post_strat <- colMeans(fit_strat$Posterior1) post_ito <- colMeans(fit_ito$Posterior1) knitr::kable(data.frame(     Specification = c("Stratonovich (auto)", "Ito (manual)"),     `Posterior mean mu` = round(c(post_strat[1], post_ito[1]), 4),     `Posterior mean sigma` = round(c(post_strat[2], post_ito[2]), 4),     `Posterior mean obs_sd` = round(c(post_strat[3], post_ito[3]), 4),     check.names = FALSE ), caption = "Posterior parameter comparison: Stratonovich vs. manual Ito") # Compare posterior distributions of mu require_package("ggplot2") post_df <- data.frame(     mu = c(fit_strat$Posterior1[, 1], fit_ito$Posterior1[, 1]),     model = rep(c("Stratonovich (auto-corrected)",                   "Ito (manual correction)"),                 each = nrow(fit_strat$Posterior1)) ) ggplot2::ggplot(post_df, ggplot2::aes(x = .data$mu, fill = .data$model)) +     ggplot2::geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +     ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = c(         "Stratonovich (auto-corrected)" = "#2196F3",         "Ito (manual correction)" = "#FF9800")) +     ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = true_mu, linetype = "dashed",         color = "black") +     ggplot2::annotate("text", x = true_mu + 0.02, y = 0,         label = paste0("true mu = ", true_mu),         hjust = 0, vjust = -0.5) +     ggplot2::labs(x = expression(mu), y = "Posterior density",         title = expression(paste(             "Posterior of ", mu,             ": Stratonovich vs. manual It\u00f4 correction")),         fill = "Interpretation") +     theme_relab()

text: additive noise (\(g\) depend \(x\)), Ito Stratonovich interpretations identical. lucifer’s symbolic differentiator detects case (\(g' = 0\)) skips correction:
code: # Additive noise: g(x) = sigma (constant, independent of x) sde_add <- SDE(     drift = "theta[1] * (theta[2] - x[1])",  # OU drift     diffusion = "theta[3]",                    # additive noise     data = y_ou, times = times, x0 = y_ou[1],     obs.model = "gaussian",     obs.noise = function(theta) theta[4],     prior = function(theta) {         if (theta[1] <= 0 || theta[3] <= 0 || theta[4] <= 0) return(-Inf)         sum(dnorm(theta, 0, 10, log = TRUE))     },     parm.names = c("kappa", "mu", "sigma", "obs_sd"),     method = "ekf",     interpretation = "stratonovich"  # no correction needed: g' = 0 )  # Same LP as Ito (no correction applied) theta_ou <- c(2, 3, 0.5, 0.1) sde_add_ito <- SDE(     drift = "theta[1] * (theta[2] - x[1])",     diffusion = "theta[3]",     data = y_ou, times = times, x0 = y_ou[1],     obs.model = "gaussian",     obs.noise = function(theta) theta[4],     prior = function(theta) {         if (theta[1] <= 0 || theta[3] <= 0 || theta[4] <= 0) return(-Inf)         sum(dnorm(theta, 0, 10, log = TRUE))     },     parm.names = c("kappa", "mu", "sigma", "obs_sd"),     method = "ekf", interpretation = "ito" ) lp_add_s <- sde_add$Model(theta_ou, sde_add$Data)$LP lp_add_i <- sde_add_ito$Model(theta_ou, sde_add_ito$Data)$LP knitr::kable(data.frame(     Interpretation = c("Stratonovich", "Ito"),     `Log-posterior` = round(c(lp_add_s, lp_add_i), 6),     `Correction applied` = c("None (g' = 0)", "None"),     check.names = FALSE ), caption = "Additive noise: Stratonovich = Ito (no correction needed)")

previous_headings: Practical examples
title: Sequential Monte Carlo samplers in lucifer
text: SMC() function shares model specification interface lucifer() VariationalBayes(). model function must return list LP (log-posterior), Dev (deviance), Monitor, yhat, parm. following example uses normal-normal conjugate model posterior analytically available validation.
code: library(lucifer)  Model <- function(parm, Data) {   mu <- parm[1]   sigma <- interval(parm[2], 1e-100, Inf)   parm[2] <- sigma   LL <- sum(dnorm(Data$y, mu, sigma, log = TRUE))   LP <- LL + dnorm(mu, 0, 10, log = TRUE) +     dhalfcauchy(sigma, 25, log = TRUE)   yhat <- rnorm(Data$n, mu, sigma)   list(LP = LP, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = mu,        yhat = yhat, parm = parm) }  set.seed(42) y <- rnorm(100, mean = 3, sd = 1.5) MyData <- list(   y = y, n = length(y),   mon.names = "mu",   parm.names = c("mu", "sigma") )

code: # Simulate a local level model: y_t = x_t + v_t, x_t = x_{t-1} + w_t set.seed(42) T_len <- 100 x_true <- cumsum(rnorm(T_len, 0, sqrt(0.5))) y <- x_true + rnorm(T_len, 0, 1.0)  sde <- SDE(family = "ou", data = y, times = 1:T_len)  # Custom SSM builder for local level build_ll <- function(parm) {     list(F = array(1, c(1, 1, 1)),          Q = array(parm[1]^2, c(1, 1, 1)),          H = array(1, c(1, 1, 1)),          R = array(parm[2]^2, c(1, 1, 1)),          m0 = 0, P0 = matrix(10, 1, 1)) }  # Conjugate Gibbs update for noise variances theta_fn <- function(parm, states, Data) {     y_dat <- as.vector(Data$.y)     x_state <- states[, 1]     resid <- y_dat - x_state     sigma_v_sq <- 1 / rgamma(1, length(resid)/2, sum(resid^2)/2)     dx <- diff(x_state)     sigma_w_sq <- 1 / rgamma(1, length(dx)/2, sum(dx^2)/2)     c(sqrt(sigma_w_sq), sqrt(sigma_v_sq)) }  sde$parm.names <- c("sigma_w", "sigma_v") sde$Initial.Values <- c(1, 1)  fit <- SSM(sde, Algorithm = "FFBS", Iterations = 2000,            Specs = list(theta_update_fn = theta_fn,                         build_ssm = build_ll),            verbose = TRUE, Status = 500)  print(fit) summary(fit) plot(fit, type = "states") plot(fit, type = "parameters")

Define extended target \[ \tilde{\pi}(x_{1:T}^{1:N}, a_{1:T-1}^{1:N}) = \frac{1}{N^T} \prod_{t=1}^T \prod_{=1}^N q(x_t^\mid x_{t-1}^{a_{t-1}^}, \theta) \cdot \prod_{t=1}^{T-1} \prod_{=1}^N w_t(x_t^{a_{t}^}), \] \(a_t^\) denotes ancestor index particle \(\) time \(t\) \(q\) proposal distribution (taken transition density bootstrap filter). code: # Simulate OU process set.seed(42) T_len <- 100 kappa_true <- 2; mu_true <- 5; sigma_true <- 1; obs_sd_true <- 0.5 dt_sim <- rep(0.1, T_len) x_true <- numeric(T_len); x_true[1] <- mu_true for (t in 2:T_len)     x_true[t] <- x_true[t-1] + kappa_true * (mu_true - x_true[t-1]) * dt_sim[t] +         sigma_true * sqrt(dt_sim[t]) * rnorm(1) y <- x_true + rnorm(T_len, 0, obs_sd_true)  sde <- SDE(family = "ou", data = y, times = seq(0.1, 10, length.out = T_len))  # Random-walk parameter update (positivity enforced) theta_fn <- function(parm, states, Data) {     proposal <- parm + rnorm(length(parm), 0, 0.02)     if (any(proposal[c(1, 3, 4)] <= 0)) return(parm)     proposal }  fit <- SSM(sde, Algorithm = "PGAS", Iterations = 500,            Specs = list(N.particles = 30,                         theta_update_fn = theta_fn),            verbose = TRUE, Status = 250)  print(fit) plot(fit, type = "states")

text: following example demonstrates PGAS nonlinear ecological model latent population follows Ricker dynamics observed Poisson counting noise. case neither FFBS (nonlinear dynamics) KSC (non-SV observation model) apply, making PGAS natural choice.
code: # Simulate Ricker-Poisson SSM # x_t = log(N_t), latent log-population # x_t = x_{t-1} + r * (1 - exp(x_{t-1}) / K) + w_t  (Ricker on log-scale) # y_t ~ Poisson(exp(x_t)) set.seed(123) T_len <- 150 r_true <- 0.5        # intrinsic growth rate K_true <- 100        # carrying capacity sigma_w <- 0.1       # process noise SD  x_true <- numeric(T_len) x_true[1] <- log(50) for (t in 2:T_len) {     x_true[t] <- x_true[t-1] + r_true * (1 - exp(x_true[t-1]) / K_true) +         rnorm(1, sd = sigma_w) } y_counts <- rpois(T_len, lambda = exp(x_true))  # Build SDE model with Poisson observations sde_ricker <- SDE(     drift = function(x, theta, t) theta[1] * (1 - exp(x[1]) / theta[2]),     diffusion = function(x, theta, t) theta[3],     data = y_counts,     times = 1:T_len,     x0 = log(50),     obs.model = "poisson",     obs.link = function(x, theta) exp(x[1]),     prior = function(theta) {         if (any(theta <= 0)) return(-Inf)         sum(dnorm(log(theta), log(c(0.5, 100, 0.1)), 1, log = TRUE))     },     parm.names = c("r", "K", "sigma_w"),     Initial.Values = c(0.3, 80, 0.2),     method = "particle", N.particles = 100 )  # MH parameter update: log-normal random walk preserves positivity theta_fn <- function(parm, states, Data) {     parm * exp(rnorm(length(parm), 0, 0.05)) }  fit_ricker <- SSM(sde_ricker, Algorithm = "PGAS", Iterations = 2000,                   Specs = list(N.particles = 100,                                theta_update_fn = theta_fn),                   verbose = TRUE, Status = 500)  print(fit_ricker) summary(fit_ricker) plot(fit_ricker, type = "states") plot(fit_ricker, type = "parameters")

text: SMC\(^2\) general algorithm state-space models unknown static parameters, requiring neither full conditional distributions tractable transition densities. introduced Chopin, Jacob, Papaspiliopoulos [5] nests two levels sequential Monte Carlo: outer SMC sampler operates parameter space, inner particle filter estimates likelihood \(p(y_{1:t} \mid \theta)\) parameter particle. outer level incorporates observations sequentially; time new observation arrives, every outer particle’s inner particle filter advanced one step, producing incremental weight. outer ESS drops, parameter particles resampled rejuvenated via MCMC, inner particle filters re-initialized accepted proposals. mathematical framework proceeds follows. stage \(t\), outer particle \(\theta^{()}\) carries inner particle filter \(\{x_{1:t}^{(,j)}, w_t^{(,j)}\}_{j=1}^{N_{\text{inner}}}\) provides unbiased estimate marginal likelihood time \(t\): \[ \hat{p}(y_{1:t} \mid \theta^{()}) = \prod_{k=1}^t \left( \frac{1}{N_{\text{inner}}} \sum_{j=1}^{N_{\text{inner}}} w_k^{(,j)} \right). \] observation \(y_{t+1}\) arrives, inner particle filter advances one step, yielding incremental weight \(\Delta \log w^{()} = \log \hat{p}(y_{t+1} \mid y_{1:t}, \theta^{()})\) updates outer particle’s importance weight. outer ESS computed \(\text{ESS} = (\sum_i W_i^2)^{-1}\), \(W_i\) normalized outer weights. ESS falls threshold (default: \(0.5 \times N_{\text{outer}}\)), outer particles resampled rejuvenated: particle, new \(\theta^*\) proposed via random-walk Metropolis, fresh particle filter run obtain \(\hat{p}(y_{1:t} \mid \theta^*)\), proposal accepted rejected via standard MH ratio. key theoretical guarantee SMC\(^2\) normalizing constant estimate \(\hat{p}(y_{1:T})\) unbiased regardless number inner particles, although inner particles reduce variance. property makes SMC\(^2\) suitable model comparison via Bayes factors: ratio \(\hat{p}(y_{1:T} \mid \mathcal{M}_1) / \hat{p}(y_{1:T} \mid \mathcal{M}_2)\) provides consistent estimator Bayes factor two competing SSM specifications. computational cost SMC\(^2\) \(O(T \cdot N_{\text{outer}} \cdot N_{\text{inner}} \cdot d_x)\) per time step, can substantial. advantage complete generality: conjugacy, gradient, user-specified samplers. marginal likelihood estimate byproduct, enabling model comparison competing SSM specifications. Typical settings moderate-sized problems use \(N_{\text{outer}} = 100\)-\(500\) \(N_{\text{inner}} = 20\)-\(50\). lucifer implementation uses dedicated C++ backend (ssm_smc2_cpp src/ssm_engines.cpp) runs entire triple-nested loop (outer particles, time steps, inner particles) natively. inner particle filters use Euler-Maruyama propagation R callbacks user-defined drift diffusion functions; systematic resampling weight normalization handled entirely C++. outer rejuvenation step runs quick C++ particle filter proposed parameter value accepts rejects via standard MH ratio approximate log marginal likelihood. SMC\(^2\) chosen modeller neither conjugate full conditionals \(\theta\) ability write theta_update_fn, transition density intractable (e.g., jump-diffusion processes agent-based models). models theta_update_fn available, PGAS generally efficient avoids quadratic cost maintaining \(N_{\text{outer}}\) independent particle filters.

text: example shows SMC\(^2\) model drift function complex parameterization obvious conjugate structure, illustrating “plug play” nature algorithm. user needs define SDE model; theta_update_fn required.
code: # Simulate a mean-reverting process with time-varying speed # dx = kappa(t) * (mu - x) dt + sigma dW # kappa(t) = a + b * sin(2*pi*t/P) set.seed(42) T_len <- 200 dt <- 0.1 times <- seq(0, by = dt, length.out = T_len) a_true <- 0.5; b_true <- 0.3; P_true <- 50 mu_true <- 2.0; sigma_true <- 0.4  x <- numeric(T_len); x[1] <- mu_true for (t in 2:T_len) {     kappa_t <- a_true + b_true * sin(2 * pi * times[t] / P_true)     x[t] <- x[t-1] + kappa_t * (mu_true - x[t-1]) * dt +         sigma_true * rnorm(1, sd = sqrt(dt)) } y_obs <- x + rnorm(T_len, sd = 0.3)  # SDE model: no theta_update_fn needed for SMC2 sde_tv <- SDE(     data = y_obs,     times = times,     x0 = y_obs[1],     drift = function(x, theta, t) {         kappa <- theta[1] + theta[2] * sin(2 * pi * t / theta[3])         kappa * (theta[4] - x[1])     },     diffusion = function(x, theta, t) theta[5],     obs.model = "gaussian",     obs.noise = function(theta) 0.3,     prior = function(theta) {         if (any(theta[c(1, 5)] <= 0)) return(-Inf)         sum(dnorm(theta, c(0.5, 0.2, 50, 1, 0.5), 2, log = TRUE))     },     parm.names = c("a", "b", "period", "mu", "sigma"),     Initial.Values = c(0.3, 0.2, 40, 1.5, 0.3),     method = "particle", N.particles = 50 )  # SMC2: fully automatic, no user-specified updates fit_smc2 <- SSM(sde_tv, Algorithm = "SMC2",                 Specs = list(N.outer = 200, N.inner = 50,                              rejuvenation_steps = 5))  print(fit_smc2) summary(fit_smc2) plot(fit_smc2, type = "states") plot(fit_smc2, type = "parameters")

text: Kim-Shephard-Chib algorithm [6] specialized Gibbs sampler standard log-stochastic-volatility model: \[ y_t = \exp(h_t / 2) \cdot \varepsilon_t, \qquad h_{t+1} = \mu + \phi(h_t - \mu) + \sigma_\eta \cdot \eta_t, \] \(\varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\) \(\eta_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\). Taking log-squared transformation \(y_t^* = \log(y_t^2 + c)\) (small offset \(c\) handle zeros) yields \(y_t^* = h_t + \log(\varepsilon_t^2)\). distribution \(\log(\chi^2_1)\) non-Gaussian, Kim, Shephard, Chib showed can approximated accurately 7-component Gaussian mixture known weights, means, variances. Conditional mixture indicators \(s_t \\{1, \ldots, 7\}\) select component generated \(\log(\varepsilon_t^2)\), model becomes linear-Gaussian SSM time-varying observation noise, full state trajectory \(h_{1:T}\) can drawn one block via FFBS. 7-component mixture approximation key insight makes KSC computationally efficient. following table reproduces mixture parameters Table 4 Kim et al. [6]: 7-component Gaussian mixture approximation log(chi-squared_1). approximation accurate within 4 decimal places exact \(\log(\chi^2_1)\) density, demonstrated Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests original paper [6]. use mixture approximation introduces small bias relative exact \(\log(\chi^2_1)\) density, Kim et al. showed bias negligible practice affect posterior inference parameters \((\mu, \phi, \sigma_\eta)\). Gibbs cycle alternates five steps: (1) sample mixture indicators \(s_t\) categorical conditional given \((y_t^*, h_t)\); (2) sample \(h_{1:T}\) via FFBS using Kalman filter \(R_t = \sigma^2_{s_t}\); (3) sample \(\mu\) conjugate Gaussian posterior; (4) sample \(\phi\) truncated normal (constraining \(|\phi| < 1\) stationarity); (5) sample \(\sigma_\eta^2\) conjugate inverse-gamma posterior. posterior \(\mu\) \(\mathcal{N}(\hat{\mu}, V_\mu)\) \(V_\mu = (1/V_0 + (1 - \phi)^2 (T-1) / \sigma_\eta^2)^{-1}\) \(\hat{\mu} = V_\mu (m_0/V_0 + (1-\phi)/\sigma_\eta^2 \sum_{t=2}^T (h_t - \phi h_{t-1}))\). posterior \(\sigma_\eta^2\) \(\text{InvGamma}(\alpha_0 + (T-1)/2, \beta_0 + \sum_{t=2}^T (h_t - \mu - \phi(h_{t-1} - \mu))^2 / 2)\). stationarity constraint \(\phi\) enforced rejection sampling truncated normal proposal. KSC activated automatically SSM() detects "sv" SDE family, requires user-supplied theta_update_fn full conditionals built . entire Gibbs loop runs dedicated C++ backend (ssm_ksc_cpp src/ssm_engines.cpp): mixture indicator sampling, Kalman filter/backward simulation, conjugate parameter updates execute natively without crossing R/C++ boundary inner loop. 7-component mixture constants compiled constexpr arrays C++. primary diagnostic KSC convergence autocorrelation \(\phi\) parameter, often exhibits slow mixing persistence parameter tightly coupled volatility trajectory. Running chains 5000 iterations thinning 5 10 typical practice. summary() method reports ESS parameter, plot(fit, type = "parameters") method displays trace plots reveal non-stationarity.

text: Initialize \((\mu, \phi, \sigma_\eta)\), \(h_{1:T}\); compute \(y_t^* = \log(y_t^2 + 10^{-4})\) Sample indicators \(s_t \sim \text{Categorical}\bigl(p_k \cdot \mathcal{N}(y_t^*; h_t + m_k, v_k)\bigr)\) \(k = 1, \ldots, 7\) Sample states \(h_{1:T}\) via FFBS \(F = \phi\), \(Q = \sigma_\eta^2\), \(H = 1\), \(R_t = v_{s_t}\), offset \(= m_{s_t}\) Sample \(\mu \sim \mathcal{N}(m_\mu, V_\mu)\) conjugate posterior Sample \(\phi\) via MH truncated normal proposal (\(|\phi| < 1\)) Sample \(\sigma_\eta^2 \sim \text{InvGamma}(\alpha_n, \beta_n)\) conjugate posterior Return \(\{(\mu, \phi, \sigma_\eta, h_{1:T})^{(t)}\}\)

code: # Simulate SV with leverage effect set.seed(55) T_len <- 600 mu <- -0.3; phi <- 0.98; sigma_eta <- 0.12; rho <- -0.5  h <- numeric(T_len); h[1] <- mu eps <- rnorm(T_len) for (t in 2:T_len) {     eta <- rho * eps[t-1] + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * rnorm(1)     h[t] <- mu + phi * (h[t-1] - mu) + sigma_eta * eta } y_lev <- exp(h / 2) * eps  # Fit standard KSC (ignoring leverage for comparison) sde_sv <- SDE(family = "sv", data = y_lev, times = 1:T_len) fit_sv <- SSM(sde_sv, Algorithm = "KSC", Iterations = 5000,               verbose = TRUE, Status = 1000)  summary(fit_sv) plot(fit_sv, type = "states") plot(fit_sv, type = "parameters")

text: Unscented Kalman Filter, introduced Julier Uhlmann [9] refined Wan van der Merwe [10], propagates deterministic set \(2n + 1\) sigma points exact nonlinear dynamics, avoiding finite-difference Jacobian approximation Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) requires. Given state dimension \(n\) mean \(\hat{x}\) covariance \(P\), UKF generates sigma points \(\chi_0 = \hat{x}\) \(\chi_i = \hat{x} \pm (\sqrt{(n + \lambda)P})_i\) \(= 1, \ldots, n\), \(\lambda = \alpha^2(n + \kappa) - n\) controls spread sigma points around mean. points propagated nonlinear transition function \(f(\cdot)\), predicted mean covariance reconstructed weighted sums propagated points: \[ \hat{x}_{t|t-1} = \sum_{=0}^{2n} w_i^{(m)} f(\chi_i), \qquad P_{t|t-1} = \sum_{=0}^{2n} w_i^{(c)} \bigl(f(\chi_i) - \hat{x}_{t|t-1}\bigr)\bigl(f(\chi_i) - \hat{x}_{t|t-1}\bigr)^\top + Q_t, \] weights \[ w_0^{(m)} = \frac{\lambda}{n + \lambda}, \qquad w_0^{(c)} = \frac{\lambda}{n + \lambda} + (1 - \alpha^2 + \beta), \qquad w_i^{(m)} = w_i^{(c)} = \frac{1}{2(n + \lambda)} \text{ } = 1, \ldots, 2n. \] parameter \(\beta = 2\) optimal Gaussian distributions, \(\alpha \(10^{-4}, 1]\) controls tightly sigma points cluster around mean. observation update, sigma-point transform applied observation function \(h(\cdot)\). cross-covariance predicted state predicted observation \[ P_{xy} = \sum_{=0}^{2n} w_i^{(c)} \bigl(f(\chi_i) - \hat{x}_{t|t-1}\bigr)\bigl(h(f(\chi_i)) - \hat{y}_{t|t-1}\bigr)^\top, \] Kalman gain \(K_t = P_{xy} S_t^{-1}\), \(S_t = \sum_i w_i^{(c)} (h(f(\chi_i)) - \hat{y}_{t|t-1})(h(f(\chi_i)) - \hat{y}_{t|t-1})^\top + R_t\) innovation covariance. update equations \(\hat{x}_t = \hat{x}_{t|t-1} + K_t (y_t - \hat{y}_{t|t-1})\) \(P_t = P_{t|t-1} - K_t S_t K_t^\top\). UKF captures mean covariance exactly third-order Taylor expansion Gaussian inputs second order non-Gaussian inputs, compared EKF’s first-order accuracy. makes substantially accurate models moderate nonlinearity, Van der Pol oscillator double-well potential systems, without requiring Jacobian computation. lucifer implementation uses C++ UKF filter (ukf.cpp) propagates sigma points user-supplied drift diffusion functions Euler-Maruyama substeps. Within Gibbs loop, UKF replaces Kalman filter forward pass, producing filtered state estimates passed theta_update_fn parameter updates. UKF tuning parameters \(\alpha\), \(\beta\), \(\kappa\) controlled via Specs$alpha, Specs$beta, Specs$kappa respectively. primary advantage UKF PGAS nonlinear models computational cost: UKF processes time step fixed number deterministic sigma points rather stochastic ensemble particles, making \(O(T n^3)\) rather \(O(T N n)\). tradeoff accuracy. unscented transform captures mean covariance exactly second-order Taylor expansion nonlinearity, assumes Gaussian state distributions step. models multimodal heavily skewed state posteriors, PGAS remains appropriate choice. code: # Simulate a double-well potential: x_t = x_{t-1} + (x - x^3) * dt + sigma * dW_t set.seed(42) T_len <- 200 dt_sim <- 0.1 x_dw <- numeric(T_len); x_dw[1] <- 0.5 for (t in 2:T_len)     x_dw[t] <- x_dw[t-1] + (x_dw[t-1] - x_dw[t-1]^3) * dt_sim +         0.3 * rnorm(1, sd = sqrt(dt_sim)) y_dw <- x_dw + rnorm(T_len, 0, 0.5)  # Build SDE model with nonlinear drift sde_dw <- SDE(     data = y_dw,     times = seq(0.1, by = dt_sim, length.out = T_len),     x0 = 0.5,     drift = function(x, theta, t) theta[1] * (x[1] - x[1]^3),     diffusion = function(x, theta, t) theta[2],     obs.model = "gaussian",     obs.noise = function(theta) theta[3],     prior = function(theta) {         if (any(theta[2:3] <= 0)) return(-Inf)         sum(dnorm(theta, c(1, 0.3, 0.5), 1, log = TRUE))     },     parm.names = c("drift_scale", "sigma_state", "sigma_obs"),     Initial.Values = c(1.0, 0.3, 0.5),     method = "ekf" )  # Gibbs parameter update theta_fn <- function(parm, states, Data) {     parm + rnorm(length(parm), 0, 0.02) }  # Compare EKF-based PGAS vs. UKF fit_ukf <- SSM(sde_dw, Algorithm = "UKF", Iterations = 2000,                Specs = list(theta_update_fn = theta_fn,                             alpha = 1e-3, beta = 2.0, kappa = 0),                verbose = TRUE, Status = 500)  print(fit_ukf) plot(fit_ukf, type = "states") plot(fit_ukf, type = "parameters")

text: Van der Pol oscillator provides challenging test case UKF dynamics two-dimensional exhibit limit-cycle behaviour. system \[ \dot{x}_1 = x_2, \qquad \dot{x}_2 = \mu (1 - x_1^2) x_2 - x_1 + \sigma_w \xi(t), \] \(\mu\) controls nonlinearity \(\xi(t)\) white noise. Euler-Maruyama discretization, becomes two-dimensional nonlinear SSM observed \(y_t = x_{1,t} + v_t\).
code: # Simulate Van der Pol oscillator set.seed(77) T_len <- 300 dt_sim <- 0.05 mu_vdp <- 1.5 sigma_w <- 0.2 sigma_obs <- 0.5  x1 <- numeric(T_len); x2 <- numeric(T_len) x1[1] <- 1.0; x2[1] <- 0.0 for (t in 2:T_len) {     x1[t] <- x1[t-1] + x2[t-1] * dt_sim     x2[t] <- x2[t-1] + (mu_vdp * (1 - x1[t-1]^2) * x2[t-1] - x1[t-1]) * dt_sim +         sigma_w * rnorm(1, sd = sqrt(dt_sim)) } y_vdp <- x1 + rnorm(T_len, sd = sigma_obs)  # Build model (2D state, 1D observation) sde_vdp <- SDE(     data = y_vdp,     times = seq(0.05, by = dt_sim, length.out = T_len),     x0 = c(1.0, 0.0),     drift = function(x, theta, t) {         c(x[2], theta[1] * (1 - x[1]^2) * x[2] - x[1])     },     diffusion = function(x, theta, t) {         matrix(c(0, theta[2]), 2, 1)     },     obs.model = "gaussian",     obs.noise = function(theta) theta[3],     prior = function(theta) {         if (any(theta[2:3] <= 0)) return(-Inf)         sum(dnorm(theta, c(1, 0.2, 0.5), 1, log = TRUE))     },     parm.names = c("mu", "sigma_w", "sigma_obs"),     state.names = c("x1", "x2"),     Initial.Values = c(1.0, 0.3, 0.4),     method = "particle", N.particles = 50 )  theta_fn <- function(parm, states, Data) {     proposal <- parm + rnorm(length(parm), 0, 0.02)     if (any(proposal[2:3] <= 0)) return(parm)     proposal }  fit_vdp <- SSM(sde_vdp, Algorithm = "UKF", Iterations = 3000,                Specs = list(theta_update_fn = theta_fn,                             alpha = 0.01, beta = 2.0, kappa = 0),                verbose = TRUE, Status = 500)  summary(fit_vdp) plot(fit_vdp, type = "states") plot(fit_vdp, type = "parameters")

text: high-dimensional state spaces maintaining propagating full \(n \times n\) covariance matrix intractable, Ensemble Kalman Filter, introduced Evensen [11], represents filtering distribution empirically via \(N_e\) ensemble members. time step, ensemble member propagated nonlinear transition function independently, ensemble covariance serves forecast covariance Kalman update. stochastic variant perturbs observations adding Gaussian noise \(\varepsilon_t^{(j)} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, R)\) ensemble member’s update, yielding analysis step: \[ x_t^{(j),} = x_t^{(j),f} + P_t^f H^\top (H P_t^f H^\top + R)^{-1} \bigl(y_t + \varepsilon_t^{(j)} - H x_t^{(j),f}\bigr), \] \(P_t^f = \frac{1}{N_e - 1}\sum_{j=1}^{N_e} (x_t^{(j),f} - \bar{x}_t^f)(x_t^{(j),f} - \bar{x}_t^f)^\top\) sample covariance forecast ensemble. ensemble approach avoids ever forming full \(n \times n\) covariance matrix explicitly. Instead, computations can expressed terms \(n \times N_e\) anomaly matrix \(A_t = [x_t^{(1),f} - \bar{x}_t^f, \ldots, x_t^{(N_e),f} - \bar{x}_t^f]\), \(P_t^f = A_t A_t^\top / (N_e - 1)\). matrix inversion Kalman gain involves \(d_y \times d_y\) innovation covariance \(S_t = H P_t^f H^\top + R\), typically low-dimensional even state dimension large. gives EnKF computational cost \(O(T N_e n)\) per iteration, linear state dimension rather cubic. Covariance inflation essential practical technique EnKF. finite ensemble sizes, sample covariance \(P_t^f\) systematically underestimates true forecast covariance, leading overconfident filter estimates can diverge true state. Multiplicative inflation replaces \(P_t^f\) \((1 + \delta) P_t^f\) small \(\delta > 0\) (controlled Specs$inflation, default 1.0 meaning inflation). Typical values \(\delta\) range 0.01 0.10, depending ensemble size model dynamics. Localization, zeroes long-range correlations \(P_t^f\), another technique used geophysical applications state dimension extremely large (\(n > 10^4\)); currently implemented lucifer added via user-supplied localization matrices. lucifer implementation uses C++ EnKF filter (enkf.cpp) propagates ensemble members user-supplied drift diffusion functions Euler-Maruyama substeps. Within Gibbs loop, ensemble mean serves filtered state estimate theta_update_fn. ensemble size set via Specs$N_ensemble (default 100) covariance inflation factor via Specs$inflation (default 1.0, inflation). EnKF algorithm choice state dimension exceeds approximately 10, making UKF’s \(O(n^3)\) cost-per-step prohibitive. moderate state dimensions (\(n < 10\)), UKF generally preferred deterministic sigma-point approximation lower variance stochastic ensemble representation. general nonlinear models low state dimension non-Gaussian posteriors, PGAS provides exact inference neither UKF EnKF can match.

code: # Simulate 5-dimensional coupled oscillator system set.seed(88) T_len <- 200 d_x <- 5 dt_sim <- 0.1 sigma_w <- 0.2 sigma_obs <- 0.5  # Coupling matrix: tridiagonal A <- diag(-0.5, d_x) for (i in 1:(d_x-1)) {     A[i, i+1] <- 0.2     A[i+1, i] <- 0.2 }  x_mat <- matrix(0, T_len, d_x) x_mat[1, ] <- rnorm(d_x) for (t in 2:T_len) {     x_mat[t, ] <- x_mat[t-1, ] + A %*% x_mat[t-1, ] * dt_sim +         sigma_w * rnorm(d_x, sd = sqrt(dt_sim)) } # Observe only first 2 states y_multi <- x_mat[, 1:2] + matrix(rnorm(T_len * 2, sd = sigma_obs),                                   T_len, 2)  sde_multi <- SDE(     data = y_multi,     times = seq(0.1, by = dt_sim, length.out = T_len),     x0 = rep(0, d_x),     drift = function(x, theta, t) {         d <- length(x)         A_loc <- diag(theta[1], d)         for (i in 1:(d-1)) {             A_loc[i, i+1] <- theta[2]             A_loc[i+1, i] <- theta[2]         }         as.vector(A_loc %*% x)     },     diffusion = function(x, theta, t) theta[3],     obs.model = "gaussian",     obs.noise = function(theta) theta[4],     prior = function(theta) {         if (any(theta[3:4] <= 0)) return(-Inf)         sum(dnorm(theta, 0, 2, log = TRUE))     },     parm.names = c("self_coupling", "cross_coupling", "sigma_w", "sigma_obs"),     state.names = paste0("x", 1:d_x),     Initial.Values = c(-0.3, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4),     method = "particle", N.particles = 50 )  theta_fn <- function(parm, states, Data) {     parm + rnorm(length(parm), 0, 0.01) }  fit_enkf_multi <- SSM(sde_multi, Algorithm = "EnKF", Iterations = 2000,                       Specs = list(N_ensemble = 200,                                    inflation = 1.05,                                    theta_update_fn = theta_fn),                       verbose = TRUE, Status = 500)  summary(fit_enkf_multi) plot(fit_enkf_multi, type = "states") plot(fit_enkf_multi, type = "parameters")

code: # Jump-linear model: nonlinear jump state s_t in {-1, +1} # selects between two drift regimes for the linear state x_t # s_t = s_{t-1} * sign(rnorm(1))  [simplified jump dynamics] # x_t = (1 + 0.5 * s_t) * x_{t-1} + w_t # y_t = x_t + v_t  set.seed(42) T_len <- 200 x_true <- numeric(T_len); s_true <- numeric(T_len) x_true[1] <- 0; s_true[1] <- 1 sigma_w <- 0.3; sigma_v <- 1.0  for (t in 2:T_len) {     s_true[t] <- s_true[t-1] * sample(c(1, -1), 1, prob = c(0.95, 0.05))     x_true[t] <- (1 + 0.1 * s_true[t]) * x_true[t-1] + rnorm(1, sd = sigma_w) } y_jl <- x_true + rnorm(T_len, sd = sigma_v)  # Nonlinear transition for jump state nl_trans <- function(s, theta, t) {     sample(c(1, -1), 1, prob = c(theta[1], 1 - theta[1])) * sign(s) }  # Linear SSM builder conditional on jump state build_lin <- function(parm, s_nl) {     F_mat <- array(1 + 0.1 * s_nl, c(1, 1, 1))     list(F = F_mat, Q = array(parm[2]^2, c(1, 1, 1)),          H = array(1, c(1, 1, 1)), R = array(parm[3]^2, c(1, 1, 1)),          m0 = 0, P0 = matrix(10, 1, 1)) }  # Build SDE model for the RBPF (particle filter handles nonlinear part) sde_jl <- SDE(     drift = function(x, theta, t) 0 * x[1],     diffusion = function(x, theta, t) theta[2],     data = y_jl, times = 1:T_len, x0 = 0,     obs.model = "gaussian",     obs.noise = function(theta) theta[3],     prior = function(theta) {         if (any(theta[2:3] <= 0) || theta[1] < 0 || theta[1] > 1) return(-Inf)         sum(dnorm(theta, c(0.9, 0.3, 1), c(0.2, 0.5, 0.5), log = TRUE))     },     parm.names = c("p_stay", "sigma_w", "sigma_v"),     Initial.Values = c(0.9, 0.3, 1.0),     method = "particle", N.particles = 30)  theta_fn <- function(parm, states, Data) {     proposal <- parm + rnorm(length(parm), 0, 0.01)     if (any(proposal[2:3] <= 0) || proposal[1] < 0 || proposal[1] > 1) return(parm)     proposal }  fit_rbpf <- SSM(sde_jl, Algorithm = "RBPF", Iterations = 2000,                 Specs = list(N.particles = 200,                              dim_nl = 1, dim_lin = 1,                              nl_transition_fn = nl_trans,                              build_lin_ssm_fn = build_lin,                              theta_update_fn = theta_fn),                 verbose = TRUE, Status = 500)  print(fit_rbpf) summary(fit_rbpf) plot(fit_rbpf, type = "states") plot(fit_rbpf, type = "parameters")

MS-FFBS Gibbs sampler cycles four steps: (1) run Kim filter forward compute filtered state means, covariances, regime probabilities; (2) sample regime sequence \(S_{1:T}\) backward smoothed regime probabilities, conditioning \(S_{t+1}\) step via \(\Pr(S_t = \mid S_{t+1} = j, y_{1:T}) \propto P_{ij} \cdot \Pr(S_t = \mid y_{1:t})\); (3) conditional sampled regime sequence, construct time-varying system matrices draw full state trajectory \(x_{0:T}\) via standard FFBS; (4) update parameters via theta_update_fn(parm, states, regimes, Data), regimes integer vector sampled regime labels; (5) sample row transition matrix Dirichlet posterior given observed transition counts. user specifies model via Specs$build_ssm_list, list \(K\) functions returning system matrices \((F, Q, H, R, m_0, P_0)\) regime, Specs$n_regimes. theta_update_fn receives sampled regime vector third argument (parm states), enabling regime-conditional parameter updates.
