code: # Simulate a 2-regime local level model set.seed(42) T_len <- 300 K <- 2 P_true <- matrix(c(0.98, 0.02, 0.05, 0.95), 2, 2, byrow = TRUE) sigma_w <- c(0.1, 0.8)   # low vs. high state noise sigma_v <- 1.0  # Generate regime sequence S_true <- integer(T_len); S_true[1] <- 1 for (t in 2:T_len)     S_true[t] <- sample(1:K, 1, prob = P_true[S_true[t-1], ])  # Generate states and observations x_true <- numeric(T_len); x_true[1] <- 0 for (t in 2:T_len)     x_true[t] <- x_true[t-1] + rnorm(1, 0, sigma_w[S_true[t]]) y_ms <- x_true + rnorm(T_len, 0, sigma_v)  # Build model via SSM_model (no SDE needed for discrete-time SSM) sde_ms <- SSM_model(     type = "local_level", data = y_ms, times = 1:T_len,     parm.names = c("sigma_w1", "sigma_w2", "sigma_v"),     Initial.Values = c(0.2, 0.5, 1.0))  # Regime-conditional builders build_ssm_list <- list(     function(parm) {         list(F = array(1, c(1,1,1)), Q = array(parm[1]^2, c(1,1,1)),              H = array(1, c(1,1,1)), R = array(parm[3]^2, c(1,1,1)),              m0 = 0, P0 = matrix(10, 1, 1))     },     function(parm) {         list(F = array(1, c(1,1,1)), Q = array(parm[2]^2, c(1,1,1)),              H = array(1, c(1,1,1)), R = array(parm[3]^2, c(1,1,1)),              m0 = 0, P0 = matrix(10, 1, 1))     } )  # Parameter update (regime-aware: receives regimes as 3rd arg) theta_fn <- function(parm, states, regimes, Data) {     x <- states[, 1]     dx <- diff(x)     # Regime-conditional state noise     for (j in 1:2) {         idx <- which(regimes[-1] == j)         if (length(idx) > 2) {             ss <- sum(dx[idx]^2)             parm[j] <- sqrt(1 / rgamma(1, length(idx)/2, ss/2))         }     }     # Observation noise     resid <- as.vector(Data$.y) - x     ss_v <- sum(resid^2)     parm[3] <- sqrt(1 / rgamma(1, length(resid)/2, ss_v/2))     parm }  fit_ms <- SSM(sde_ms, Algorithm = "MS-FFBS", Iterations = 3000,               Specs = list(n_regimes = 2,                            build_ssm_list = build_ssm_list,                            theta_update_fn = theta_fn),               verbose = TRUE, Status = 500)  print(fit_ms) summary(fit_ms) plot(fit_ms, type = "states") plot(fit_ms, type = "parameters")

code: # Simulate 3-regime local linear trend set.seed(55) T_len <- 400 K <- 3 P_true <- matrix(c(     0.95, 0.04, 0.01,     0.03, 0.94, 0.03,     0.02, 0.05, 0.93 ), 3, 3, byrow = TRUE)  # Regime-specific parameters drift_regime <- c(-0.5, 0.2, 0.8)  # recession, normal, boom sigma_regime <- c(1.5, 0.5, 0.8)   # high, low, medium vol  S <- integer(T_len); S[1] <- 2 for (t in 2:T_len) S[t] <- sample(1:K, 1, prob = P_true[S[t-1], ])  x <- numeric(T_len); x[1] <- 0 for (t in 2:T_len)     x[t] <- x[t-1] + drift_regime[S[t]] + rnorm(1, sd = sigma_regime[S[t]]) y_bc <- x + rnorm(T_len, sd = 0.8)  # Build model via SSM_model sde_bc <- SSM_model(     type = "local_level", data = y_bc, times = 1:T_len,     parm.names = c("sigma_w1", "sigma_w2", "sigma_w3", "sigma_v"),     Initial.Values = c(1.0, 0.5, 0.8, 0.8))  # Three regime builders with different volatilities build_ssm_3 <- list(     function(parm) list(F = array(1, c(1,1,1)), Q = array(parm[1]^2, c(1,1,1)),                         H = array(1, c(1,1,1)), R = array(parm[4]^2, c(1,1,1)),                         m0 = 0, P0 = matrix(10, 1, 1)),     function(parm) list(F = array(1, c(1,1,1)), Q = array(parm[2]^2, c(1,1,1)),                         H = array(1, c(1,1,1)), R = array(parm[4]^2, c(1,1,1)),                         m0 = 0, P0 = matrix(10, 1, 1)),     function(parm) list(F = array(1, c(1,1,1)), Q = array(parm[3]^2, c(1,1,1)),                         H = array(1, c(1,1,1)), R = array(parm[4]^2, c(1,1,1)),                         m0 = 0, P0 = matrix(10, 1, 1)) )  theta_fn_3 <- function(parm, states, regimes, Data) {     x <- states[, 1]     dx <- diff(x)     for (j in 1:3) {         idx <- which(regimes[-1] == j)         if (length(idx) > 2) {             ss <- sum(dx[idx]^2)             parm[j] <- sqrt(1 / rgamma(1, length(idx)/2, ss/2))         }     }     resid <- as.vector(Data$.y) - x     parm[4] <- sqrt(1 / rgamma(1, length(resid)/2, sum(resid^2)/2))     parm }  fit_bc <- SSM(sde_bc, Algorithm = "MS-FFBS", Iterations = 5000,               Specs = list(n_regimes = 3,                            build_ssm_list = build_ssm_3,                            theta_update_fn = theta_fn_3,                            prior_transition = rep(1, 3)),               verbose = TRUE, Status = 1000)  summary(fit_bc) plot(fit_bc, type = "states") plot(fit_bc, type = "parameters")

code: # Multi-step-ahead forecasting from a fitted local level model # After fitting fit_ll from the FFBS section  # Extract posterior parameter draws sigma_w_draws <- fit_ll$Posterior[, "sigma_w"] sigma_v_draws <- fit_ll$Posterior[, "sigma_v"] states_final  <- fit_ll$States[, nrow(fit_ll$States[1,,]), 1]  # Generate forecasts for each posterior draw H <- 20  # forecast horizon n_draws <- nrow(fit_ll$Posterior) forecasts <- matrix(NA, n_draws, H)  for (i in 1:n_draws) {     x_curr <- states_final[i]     for (h in 1:H) {         x_curr <- x_curr + rnorm(1, sd = sigma_w_draws[i])         forecasts[i, h] <- x_curr + rnorm(1, sd = sigma_v_draws[i])     } }  # Predictive mean and 95% interval forecast_mean <- colMeans(forecasts) forecast_lower <- apply(forecasts, 2, quantile, 0.025) forecast_upper <- apply(forecasts, 2, quantile, 0.975)  # Plot forecast fan chart plot(1:H, forecast_mean, type = "l", lwd = 2,      xlab = "Forecast horizon", ylab = "y",      ylim = range(c(forecast_lower, forecast_upper)),      main = "Multi-step-ahead forecast with 95% predictive interval") polygon(c(1:H, H:1), c(forecast_lower, rev(forecast_upper)),         col = rgb(0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 0.3), border = NA) lines(1:H, forecast_mean, lwd = 2, col = "darkblue")

text: section demonstrates complete analysis workflow simulated ecological time series, model specification inference, diagnostics, model comparison, forecasting. data represent annual abundance observations hypothetical population undergoing density-dependent stochastic growth. workflow illustrates several key features SSM module: missing data years 30-35 automatically interpolated Kalman smoother, appropriate uncertainty propagation; model comparison via LOO-PSIS reveals whether density dependence (Gompertz model) supported data relative simple random walk; prior sensitivity analysis identifies parameters well-identified data versus driven prior. Gompertz model’s stationary mean \(/(1-b) \approx 2.67\) autocorrelation coefficient \(b\) typically well-identified time series moderate length (\(T \geq 50\)), process observation noise variances can difficult separate signal--noise ratio close one.
code: # Simulate Gompertz state-space model # x_t = a + b * x_{t-1} + w_t,  w_t ~ N(0, sigma_w^2) # y_t = x_t + v_t,              v_t ~ N(0, sigma_v^2) # where x_t = log(N_t) is log-abundance  set.seed(42) T_len <- 80   # 80 years of data a_true <- 0.8 b_true <- 0.7 sigma_w_true <- 0.15 sigma_v_true <- 0.30  x_true <- numeric(T_len) x_true[1] <- a_true / (1 - b_true)  # stationary mean for (t in 2:T_len) {     x_true[t] <- a_true + b_true * x_true[t-1] + rnorm(1, sd = sigma_w_true) } y_eco <- x_true + rnorm(T_len, sd = sigma_v_true)  # Introduce some missing data (years 30-35 unobserved) y_eco[30:35] <- NA # Step 1: Specify the model via SSM_model with custom build_ssm  build_gompertz <- function(parm) {     a <- parm[1]; b <- parm[2]     sigma_w <- parm[3]; sigma_v <- parm[4]     list(         F = array(b, c(1, 1, 1)),         Q = array(sigma_w^2, c(1, 1, 1)),         H = array(1, c(1, 1, 1)),         R = array(sigma_v^2, c(1, 1, 1)),         m0 = a / (1 - b),         P0 = matrix(sigma_w^2 / (1 - b^2), 1, 1)     ) }  # Conjugate + MH theta update theta_gompertz <- function(parm, states, Data) {     x <- states[, 1]     y_obs <- as.vector(Data$.y)     T_obs <- length(x)      # Observation noise: conjugate inv-gamma     valid <- !is.na(y_obs)     resid <- y_obs[valid] - x[valid]     n_obs <- sum(valid)     sigma_v_sq <- 1 / rgamma(1, 0.001 + n_obs / 2,                               0.001 + sum(resid^2) / 2)      # Process noise: conjugate inv-gamma (conditional on a, b)     dx <- x[2:T_obs] - parm[1] - parm[2] * x[1:(T_obs-1)]     n_dx <- length(dx)     sigma_w_sq <- 1 / rgamma(1, 0.001 + n_dx / 2,                               0.001 + sum(dx^2) / 2)      # a, b: conjugate normal (conditional on sigma_w)     X_mat <- cbind(1, x[1:(T_obs-1)])     y_state <- x[2:T_obs]     V_beta <- solve(crossprod(X_mat) / sigma_w_sq + diag(0.01, 2))     m_beta <- V_beta %*% (crossprod(X_mat, y_state) / sigma_w_sq)     ab_new <- as.vector(m_beta + chol(V_beta) %*% rnorm(2))      # Enforce stationarity: |b| < 1     if (abs(ab_new[2]) >= 1) ab_new <- parm[1:2]      c(ab_new, sqrt(sigma_w_sq), sqrt(sigma_v_sq)) }  mod_gomp <- SSM_model(     data = y_eco,     build_ssm = build_gompertz,     theta_update_fn = theta_gompertz,     parm.names = c("a", "b", "sigma_w", "sigma_v"),     state.names = "log_abundance",     Initial.Values = c(0.5, 0.5, 0.2, 0.3) ) # Step 2: Fit the model fit_gomp <- SSM(mod_gomp, Algorithm = "FFBS", Iterations = 5000,                 Thinning = 2, verbose = TRUE, Status = 1000)  # Step 3: Inspect results print(fit_gomp) summary(fit_gomp) # Step 4: Visualize plot(fit_gomp, type = "states")       # state trajectory + interpolated missing data plot(fit_gomp, type = "parameters")   # trace plots and densities plot(fit_gomp, type = "pairs")        # posterior correlations # Step 5: Convergence diagnostics demon_gomp <- as.demonoid(fit_gomp) Rhat(demon_gomp) ESS(demon_gomp) # Step 6: Model comparison - Gompertz vs. random walk mod_rw <- SSM_model(type = "local_level", data = y_eco) fit_rw <- SSM(mod_rw, Iterations = 5000, Thinning = 2)  demon_rw <- as.demonoid(fit_rw) loo_gomp <- LOO(demon_gomp) loo_rw   <- LOO(demon_rw) loo_compare(loo_gomp, loo_rw) # Step 7: Prior sensitivity analysis rb_gomp <- RobustBayes(demon_gomp, type = "power") summary(rb_gomp) plot(rb_gomp)

text: Bayesian inference requires computing posterior distribution \(p(\theta \mid y) = p(y \mid \theta) \, p(\theta) / p(y)\), \(\theta\) denotes vector model parameters \(y\) observed data. normalizing constant \(p(y) = \int p(y \mid \theta) \, p(\theta) \, d\theta\) generally intractable simplest conjugate models, Markov chain Monte Carlo methods obtain samples posterior without evaluating integral. Variational Bayes (VB) takes fundamentally different approach: recasts posterior inference optimization problem searching family tractable distributions \(\mathcal{Q} = \{q(\theta; \lambda) : \lambda \\Lambda\}\) member closest true posterior [1].

Pathfinder evaluates ELBO iterate: \[ \mathcal{L}_k = \frac{1}{S} \sum_{s=1}^{S} \log p(\theta_k^{(s)}, y) + \frac{1}{2}\log\det(H_k) + \frac{J}{2}(1 + \log 2\pi) \] \(\theta_k^{(s)} \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta_k, H_k)\) Monte Carlo draws, selects \(k^* = \arg\max_k \mathcal{L}_k\). first term estimates expected log-joint approximation, remaining terms give Gaussian entropy. lucifer, \(S = 10\) draws used ELBO estimation (increased 25 \(J > 50\)).

previous_headings: Pathfinder: quasi-Newton variational inference
title: Variational Bayes methods in lucifer
text: single L-BFGS run may get trapped local mode may adequately explore parameter space. Multi-path Pathfinder addresses running \(M\) independent single-path instances jittered initial values combining results. procedure pools draws \(M\) best approximations mixture: \[ q(\theta) = \frac{1}{M} \sum_{m=1}^{M} \mathcal{N}(\theta \mid \theta_{m}^*, H_{m}^*) \] computes importance weights \(w_i = \log p(\theta_i, y) - \log q(\theta_i)\) pooled draw. Pareto smoothed importance sampling (PSIS) applied smooth extreme weights produce reliable resampled set posterior draws. Pareto \(\hat{k}\) diagnostic PSIS step quantifies quality multi-path approximation: \(\hat{k} < 0.5\): good; importance weights well-behaved \(0.5 \leq \hat{k} < 0.7\): acceptable; weight variability generally reliable \(0.7 \leq \hat{k} < 1.0\): questionable; approximation may inaccurate \(\hat{k} \geq 1.0\): unreliable; approximation poor MCMC used lucifer, default \(M = 4\) paths, controlled Covar argument. Setting Covar = 1 gives single-path Pathfinder without PSIS.

title: Variational Bayes methods in lucifer
text: variational methods lucifer share interface: user specifies model function, initial values, data list, calls VariationalBayes() desired Method. following example uses demonsnacks data set fit Bayesian linear regression log-calories log-sodium, weakly informative priors coefficients half-Cauchy prior residual standard deviation. model function returns list five named elements: LP (log-posterior), Dev (deviance, \(-2 \times\) log-likelihood), Monitor (monitored quantities), yhat (posterior predictive draws), parm (parameter vector, potentially constrained interval()). interface shared lucifer(), LaplaceApproximation(), estimation functions.
code: library(lucifer)  # Load and prepare data data(demonsnacks) y <- log(demonsnacks$Calories) X <- cbind(1, as.matrix(log(demonsnacks[, 10] + 1))) J <- ncol(X) for (j in 2:J) X[, j] <- CenterScale(X[, j])  # Parameter setup mon.names  <- "mu[1]" parm.names <- as.parm.names(list(beta = rep(0, J), sigma = 0)) pos.beta   <- grep("beta", parm.names) pos.sigma  <- grep("sigma", parm.names)  PGF <- function(Data) {   beta  <- rnorm(Data$J)   sigma <- runif(1)   return(c(beta, sigma)) }  MyData <- list(   J = J, PGF = PGF, X = X, mon.names = mon.names,   parm.names = parm.names, pos.beta = pos.beta,   pos.sigma = pos.sigma, y = y )  Model <- function(parm, Data) {   beta  <- parm[Data$pos.beta]   sigma <- interval(parm[Data$pos.sigma], 1e-100, Inf)   parm[Data$pos.sigma] <- sigma   beta.prior  <- sum(dnormv(beta, 0, 1000, log = TRUE))   sigma.prior <- dhalfcauchy(sigma, 25, log = TRUE)   mu <- tcrossprod(Data$X, t(beta))   LL <- sum(dnorm(Data$y, mu, sigma, log = TRUE))   LP <- LL + beta.prior + sigma.prior   list(LP = LP, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = mu[1],        yhat = rnorm(length(mu), mu, sigma), parm = parm) }  IV <- c(rep(0, J), 1)

methods <- c("Salimans1", "Salimans2", "ADVI.mf", "ADVI.fr",              "BBVI", "SVGD", "NGD", "Pathfinder") results <- list()  for (m in methods) {   cat("

title: Variational Bayes methods in lucifer
text: model generates data linear regression two predictors correlated \(\rho = 0.95\) known error variance \(\sigma = 0.5\). Using known \(\sigma\) makes posterior three regression coefficients exactly multivariate normal analytical closed form, providing ground truth every VB method can benchmarked without ambiguity. \(\rho_x = 0.95\) posterior correlation beta1 beta2 approximately \(-0.95\): strongly tilted, elongated ellipse exposes structural limitations diagonal variational families.
code: set.seed(321) n2 <- 200 rho_x <- 0.95 x1 <- rnorm(n2) x2 <- rho_x * x1 + sqrt(1 - rho_x^2) * rnorm(n2) X2 <- cbind(1, x1, x2) true_beta2 <- c(1.0, 2.0, -1.5) sigma_known <- 0.5 y2 <- as.numeric(X2 %*% true_beta2) + rnorm(n2, 0, sigma_known)  # Analytical posterior: beta | y ~ N(beta_hat, sigma^2 * (X'X)^{-1}) XtX <- crossprod(X2) beta_hat  <- as.numeric(solve(XtX, crossprod(X2, y2))) post_cov2 <- sigma_known^2 * solve(XtX)  # Model function (known sigma, flat prior) J2 <- 3L parm.names2 <- c("intercept", "beta1", "beta2") mon.names2  <- "LP"  MyData2 <- list(   parm.names = parm.names2,   mon.names  = mon.names2,   X = X2, y = y2, n = n2,   sigma = sigma_known, J = J2,   PGF = function(Data) rnorm(Data$J) )  Model2 <- function(parm, Data) {   beta <- parm   mu   <- Data$X %*% beta   LL   <- sum(dnorm(Data$y, mu, Data$sigma, log = TRUE))   LP   <- LL  # flat prior   list(LP = LP, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = LP,        yhat = rnorm(Data$n, mu, Data$sigma), parm = parm) }  IV2 <- rep(0, J2)

code: library(ggplot2)  # Analytical 95% HDR ellipse for (beta1, beta2) sub_mean <- beta_hat[2:3] sub_cov  <- post_cov2[2:3, 2:3] eig      <- eigen(sub_cov) angles   <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 200) r95      <- sqrt(qchisq(0.95, df = 2)) ell      <- cbind(cos(angles), sin(angles)) %*%             diag(sqrt(eig$values) * r95) %*% t(eig$vectors) ellipse_df <- data.frame(   beta1 = ell[, 1] + sub_mean[1],   beta2 = ell[, 2] + sub_mean[2] )  # Collect 2D posterior draws from all methods scatter_list <- lapply(ok2, function(m) {   draws <- .vb_draws(results2[[m]])   data.frame(     beta1  = draws[, "beta1"],     beta2  = draws[, "beta2"],     Method = m,     stringsAsFactors = FALSE   ) }) scatter_df <- do.call(rbind, scatter_list)  method_cols2 <- setNames(contrasting[seq_along(ok2)], ok2)  ggplot(scatter_df, aes(x = beta1, y = beta2, color = Method)) +   geom_point(alpha = 0.15, size = 0.6) +   geom_path(data = ellipse_df, aes(x = beta1, y = beta2),             color = "red", linewidth = 0.8, linetype = "dashed",             inherit.aes = FALSE) +   geom_point(data = data.frame(beta1 = sub_mean[1], beta2 = sub_mean[2]),              aes(x = beta1, y = beta2),              color = "red", shape = 3, size = 3, stroke = 1.2,              inherit.aes = FALSE) +   facet_wrap(~ Method, ncol = 4) +   scale_color_manual(values = method_cols2) +   labs(x = expression(beta[1]), y = expression(beta[2]),        title = "Joint posterior draws vs. analytical 95% ellipse (red dashed)") +   theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +   theme(legend.position = "none",         strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))

title: Variational Bayes methods in lucifer
text: choice variational algorithm depends number parameters, smoothness posterior, importance posterior correlations, computational budget. table summarizes key properties method. Comparison variational inference methods lucifer. following guidelines summarize practical recommendations. Pathfinder recommended starting point problems: fast, captures correlations via L-BFGS inverse Hessian, scales well dimension, provides built-Pareto \(\hat{k}\) reliability diagnostic. small problems fewer 20 parameters smooth posterior, Salimans2 NGD tried first; capture correlations converge rapidly. moderate-dimensional problems (20-100 parameters), ADVI.mf Salimans1 avoid quadratic cost Hessian computation still providing good mean estimates, though ADVI.mf sacrifices correlation information. posterior correlations important \(J \leq 50\), ADVI.fr best reparameterization-based option. BBVI serves generic fallback methods struggle, cost higher gradient variance slower convergence. SVGD uniquely suited multimodal posteriors computationally demanding reserved problems multimodality genuinely expected. Regardless method chosen, output VariationalBayes() treated approximation. final inference, consider using variational posterior informed initialization MCMC via lucifer(), passing estimated covariance matrix (scaled \(2.38^2/J\)) Covar argument. two-stage strategy combines speed variational methods asymptotic exactness MCMC.

text: 82 MCMC samplers spanning every major family: gradient-based (NUTS, HMC, MALA, SGLD, Barker, autoMALA, GIST-NUTS), adaptive Metropolis (, RAM, DRAM), slice sampling (ESS, AFSS, QSS, LSS, GPSS), ensemble methods (AIES, DEMC, Zeus, DREAM, QMC), geometric Riemannian (RMHMC, Lagrangian MC, Magnetic HMC), piecewise-deterministic (BPS, Boomerang, Zig-Zag, Randomized HMC), multimodal (simulated tempering, NRST, Wang-Landau, NRPT), flow-enhanced (NeuTra, flowMC), constraint-handling (projected Langevin, ProxMCMC). 8 variational Bayes methods including ADVI, BBVI, SVGD, Pathfinder multi-path initialization. 18 Laplace approximation optimizers (BFGS, L-BFGS, Newton-Raphson, trust region, conjugate gradient, others). 3 iterative quadrature rules (AGH, AGHSG, CAGH). PMC SMC adaptive tempering ESS-based resampling. 4 ABC variants (rejection, MCMC, SMC, simulated annealing). 6 simulation-based inference methods (NPE, NLE, NRE, SNPE, SNLE, SNRE) via mixture density networks neural ratio estimation. 5 state-space model engines (FFBS, PGAS, SMC2, KSC, MS-FFBS) Kalman, unscented Kalman, ensemble Kalman, particle filters.

title: lucifer - An exhaustive environment for Bayesian inference with C++ backend and OpenMP parallelization
text: lucifer’s model_spec() DSL translates mathematical notation almost verbatim model object. resulting object contains compiled Model function, data_template() building data list, initial_values() generating starting points. manual log-posterior coding needed.
code: library(lucifer)  spec <- model_spec("   y ~ StudentT(mu, sigma, nu)   mu = alpha[group] + beta * x   alpha[j] ~ Normal(mu_alpha, sigma_alpha), j = 1,...,J   mu_alpha ~ Normal(0, 10)   sigma_alpha ~ HalfCauchy(2.5)   beta ~ Normal(0, 10)   sigma ~ HalfCauchy(2.5)   nu_raw ~ Exponential(0.1)   nu = nu_raw + 2 ")

previous_headings: Quick start
title: lucifer - An exhaustive environment for Bayesian inference with C++ backend and OpenMP parallelization
text: simulate data true model known parameter values can verify posterior recovery. \(J = 10\) groups \(N = 1000\) observations (100 per group), hierarchical hyperparameters \(\mu_\alpha\) \(\sigma_\alpha\) well identified, Student-\(t\) degrees freedom enough tail information reliable estimation. data_template() method constructs list lucifer expects (including parm.names mon.names), initial_values() provides reasonable starting point.
code: set.seed(666)  N <- 1000; J <- 10 group <- rep(1:J, each = N / J) x <- rnorm(N)  # True parameter values alpha_true <- rnorm(J, mean = 3, sd = 1.5) beta_true <- 2.0 sigma_true <- 1.0 nu_true <- 5  y <- alpha_true[group] + beta_true * x + sigma_true * rt(N, df = nu_true)  # Prepare data and initial values Data <- spec$data_template(y = y, x = x, group = group, J = J) Initial.Values <- spec$initial_values(Data)

title: Approximate Bayesian Computation — ABC
text: Performs likelihood-free Bayesian inference via Approximate   Bayesian Computation (ABC). Unlike estimation functions   lucifer, model function acts forward simulator   generates synthetic data rather evaluating log-posterior.   Acceptance determined whether Euclidean distance   summary statistics simulated observed data falls   tolerance \(\varepsilon\), yielding samples approximate   posterior \(p_\varepsilon(\theta \mid S(y_\text{obs})) \propto   p(\theta)\,\Pr(\rho(S(y^*), S(y_\text{obs})) \le \varepsilon)\).   Four algorithms available: rejection sampling, MCMC-ABC, SMC-ABC,   Simulated Annealing ABC (SA-ABC).

code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ # --- Normal mean-variance inference via ABC ---  # Forward simulator (returns synthetic data, not a log-posterior) Simulator <- function(parm, Data) {   mu <- parm[1]; sigma <- parm[2]   if (sigma <= 0) return(rep(1e10, Data$n))   rnorm(Data$n, mu, sigma) }  # Joint prior: mu ~ N(0, 10), sigma ~ Half-Cauchy(0, 5) Prior <- function() c(rnorm(1, 0, 10), abs(rcauchy(1, 0, 5)))  # Sufficient statistics for the normal model Summary.Stats <- function(data) c(mean(data), sd(data))  # Observed data set.seed(42) obs_data <- rnorm(100, mean = 3, sd = 1.5) Observed.Stats <- Summary.Stats(obs_data) Data <- list(n = 100, parm.names = c("mu", "sigma"))  # Rejection ABC fit_rej <- ABC(Simulator, Data, Prior, Summary.Stats, Observed.Stats,                Method = "rejection", N = 2000, Status = 10000) print(fit_rej) summary(fit_rej) plot(fit_rej) plot(fit_rej, type = "distances")  # MCMC-ABC with user-specified proposal covariance fit_mcmc <- ABC(Simulator, Data, Prior, Summary.Stats, Observed.Stats,                 Method = "MCMC", MCMC.iterations = 10000,                 Covar = diag(c(0.3, 0.2)), Status = 5000) print(fit_mcmc) summary(fit_mcmc) plot(fit_mcmc)  # SMC-ABC with adaptive tolerance schedule fit_smc <- ABC(Simulator, Data, Prior, Summary.Stats, Observed.Stats,                Method = "SMC", N = 1000, Status = 100) print(fit_smc) summary(fit_smc) plot(fit_smc)  # SA-ABC with geometric cooling (auto-calibrated) fit_sa <- ABC(Simulator, Data, Prior, Summary.Stats, Observed.Stats,               Method = "SA", SA.iterations = 5000, Status = 2500) print(fit_sa) summary(fit_sa) plot(fit_sa) plot(fit_sa, type = "temperature") } # }

code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ # The following example fits a model as Fit1, then adds a predictor, and # fits another model, Fit2. The two models are compared with Bayes # factors.  library(lucifer)  ##############################  Demon Data  ############################### data(demonsnacks) J <- 2 y <- log(demonsnacks$Calories) X <- cbind(1, as.matrix(log(demonsnacks[,10]+1))) X[,2] <- CenterScale(X[,2])  #########################  Data List Preparation  ######################### mon.names <- "LP" parm.names <- as.parm.names(list(beta=rep(0,J), sigma=0)) pos.beta <- grep("beta", parm.names) pos.sigma <- grep("sigma", parm.names) PGF <- function(Data) {      beta <- rnorm(Data$J)      sigma <- runif(1)      return(c(beta, sigma))      } MyData <- list(J=J, PGF=PGF, X=X, mon.names=mon.names,      parm.names=parm.names, pos.beta=pos.beta, pos.sigma=pos.sigma, y=y)  ##########################  Model Specification  ########################## Model <- function(parm, Data)      {      ### Parameters      beta <- parm[Data$pos.beta]      sigma <- interval(parm[Data$pos.sigma], 1e-100, Inf)      parm[Data$pos.sigma] <- sigma      ### Log-Prior      beta.prior <- sum(dnormv(beta, 0, 1000, log=TRUE))      sigma.prior <- dhalfcauchy(sigma, 25, log=TRUE)      ### Log-Likelihood      mu <- tcrossprod(Data$X, t(beta))      LL <- sum(dnorm(Data$y, mu, sigma, log=TRUE))      ### Log-Posterior      LP <- LL + beta.prior + sigma.prior      Modelout <- list(LP=LP, Dev=-2*LL, Monitor=LP,           yhat=rnorm(length(mu), mu, sigma), parm=parm)      return(Modelout)      }  ############################  Initial Values  ############################# Initial.Values <- GIV(Model, MyData, PGF=TRUE)  ########################  Laplace Approximation  ########################## Fit1 <- LaplaceApproximation(Model, Initial.Values, Data=MyData,      Iterations=10000) Fit1  ##############################  Demon Data  ############################### data(demonsnacks) J <- 3 y <- log(demonsnacks$Calories) X <- cbind(1, as.matrix(demonsnacks[,c(7,8)])) X[,2] <- as.parm.names(list(beta=rep(0,J), sigma=0)) pos.beta <- grep("beta", parm.names) pos.sigma <- grep("sigma", parm.names) PGF <- function(Data) return(c(rnormv(Data$J,0,10), rhalfcauchy(1,5))) MyData <- list(J=J, PGF=PGF, X=X, mon.names=mon.names,      parm.names=parm.names, pos.beta=pos.beta, pos.sigma=pos.sigma, y=y)  ############################  Initial Values  ############################# Initial.Values <- GIV(Model, MyData, PGF=TRUE)  ########################  Laplace Approximation  ########################## Fit2 <- LaplaceApproximation(Model, Initial.Values, Data=MyData,      Iterations=10000) Fit2  #############################  Bayes Factor  ############################## Model.list <- list(M1=Fit1, M2=Fit2) BayesFactor(Model.list) } # }

text: Bayesian quadrature, introduced O'Hagan (1991), treats numerical integration statistical inference problem. integrand modeled realization Gaussian process, integral becomes linear functional GP, inheriting Gaussian posterior distribution. contrasts classical quadrature (IterativeQuadrature) produces point estimate. squared exponential kernel $$k(\theta, \theta') = \sigma_f^2 \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} \sum_{d=1}^D   \frac{(\theta_d - \theta'_d)^2}{\ell_d^2}\right)$$ used automatic relevance determination (ARD) lengthscales. kernel mean embedding Gaussian reference measure \(\pi(\theta) = \mathcal{N}(\mu_0, \Sigma_0)\) yields closed-form posterior integral value. Four algorithms available: BQ (vanilla Bayesian quadrature): baseline method Rasmussen Ghahramani (2003). Models \(f(\theta) = \exp(\text{LP}(\theta))\) GP selects nodes maximizing integral variance reduction. WSABI-L (warped sequential active Bayesian integration, linearized): Gunter et al. (2014). Applies square-root warping \(g = \sqrt{2(f - \alpha)}\) enforce non-negativity likelihood integrand, linearizes inverse warping moment propagation. Recommended marginal likelihood estimation. FWBQ (Frank-Wolfe Bayesian quadrature): Briol et al. (2015). Uses Frank-Wolfe optimization node selection weight computation. Less sensitive GP hyperparameters provable convergence guarantees (exponential rate regularity conditions). BatchBQ: greedy batch selection \(B\) nodes parallel model evaluation. batch selected jointly maximize integral variance reduction, enabling efficient use CPUs argument. Bayesian quadrature practical problems \(d \le 20\) parameters model evaluation moderately expensive. higher-dimensional problems, use IterativeQuadrature algorithm "CAGH", MCMC via lucifer.

title: Big data — BigData
code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ ### Below is an example of a linear regression model specification ### function in which BigData reads in a batch of 1,000 records of ### Data$N records from a data set that is too large to fully open ### in memory.  library(lucifer) N <- 10000 J <- 10 #Number of predictors, including the intercept X <- matrix(1,N,J) for (j in 2:J) {X[,j] <- rnorm(N,runif(1,-3,3),runif(1,0.1,1))} beta.orig <- runif(J,-3,3) e <- rnorm(N,0,0.1) y <- as.vector(tcrossprod(beta.orig, X) + e) mon.names <- c("LP","sigma") parm.names <- as.parm.names(list(beta=rep(0,J), log.sigma=0)) PGF <- function(Data) return(c(rnormv(Data$J,0,0.01),      log(rhalfcauchy(1,1)))) MyData <- list(J=J, PGF=PGF, N=N, mon.names=mon.names,      parm.names=parm.names) filename <- tempfile("X.csv") write.table(cbind(y,X), filename, sep=",", row.names=FALSE,   col.names=FALSE)  Model <- function(parm, Data)      {      ### Parameters      beta <- parm[1:Data$J]      sigma <- exp(parm[Data$J+1])      ### Log(Prior Densities)      beta.prior <- sum(dnormv(beta, 0, 1000, log=TRUE))      sigma.prior <- dhalfcauchy(sigma, 25, log=TRUE)      ### Log-Likelihood      LL <- BigData(file=filename, nrow=Data$N, ncol=Data$J+1, size=1000,           Method="add", CPUs=1, Type="PSOCK",           FUN=function(x, beta, sigma) sum(dnorm(x[,1], tcrossprod(x[,-1],                t(beta)), sigma, log=TRUE)), beta, sigma)      ### Log-Posterior      LP <- LL + beta.prior + sigma.prior      Modelout <- list(LP=LP, Dev=-2*LL, Monitor=c(LP,sigma),           yhat=0, parm=parm)      return(Modelout)      }  ### From here, the user may update the model as usual. } # }

text: Theoretical foundation.   Given observed data \(y\) parametric model likelihood   \(L(\theta \mid y)\), define K-cloned posterior   $$\pi_K(\theta \mid y) \propto [L(\theta \mid y)]^K \, \pi(\theta)$$   \(\pi(\theta)\) prior. Walker (1969) established   asymptotic behaviour posterior distributions repeated   observations; data cloning exploits mechanism   artificially amplifying information content fixed dataset.   \(K \\infty\), three key properties emerge: ()   posterior mean converges MLE,   \(\bar{\theta}_K \\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}\); (ii)   scaled posterior covariance converges inverse Fisher   information, \(K \, \mathrm{Var}_K(\theta) \(\hat{\theta})^{-1}\);   (iii) posterior becomes asymptotically normal,   \(\theta \mid y^{(K)} \xrightarrow{d} N(\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}},\;   K^{-1} (\hat{\theta})^{-1})\). connection Robert's (1993) prior   feedback framework means data cloning can understood   deterministic annealing scheme likelihood temperature   systematically increased. Implementation via LP/Dev decomposition.   lucifer Model interface guarantees log-posterior   decomposes \(\mathrm{LP} = \ell(\theta) + \log \pi(\theta)\)   deviance satisfies \(\mathrm{Dev} = -2\,\ell(\theta)\),   \(\ell(\theta)\) log-likelihood. cloned model therefore   computes \(\mathrm{LP}_K = K\,\ell + \log \pi\)   \(\mathrm{Dev}_K = K \cdot \mathrm{Dev}\) without actual data   duplication. thin wrapper around user's Model function implements   transformation; 55+ MCMC algorithms, multi-chain parallel   infrastructure, modern diagnostics (split R-hat, bulk/tail ESS,   MCSE) work transparently wrapper. Convergence diagnostics.   Three complementary diagnostics computed automatically.   eigenvalue diagnostic (Lele et al. 2010) computes standardized   largest eigenvalue ratio \(\lambda_S(K) = \lambda_{\max}(\Sigma_K) /   \lambda_{\max}(\Sigma_1)\), decrease rate \(1/K\)   identifiable models. scaled variance check monitors   \(K \cdot \mathrm{Var}_K(\theta_j)\) parameter; stabilization   (constant value across K) indicates asymptotic variance   reached. MSE/R-squared diagnostic (Lele et al. 2010) computes   mean Mahalanobis distance posterior draws posterior mean;   convergence approximate \(\chi^2(p)\)   \(p\) number parameters. Estimability identifiability.   n_priors > 1, Campbell Lele (2014) two-stage   ANOVA test applied assess parameter estimability. parameter   estimable posterior mean changes K (concentrates   MLE) depend choice prior. Non-estimable   parameters indicate structural non-identifiability model.   test proceeds fitting data cloning sequence multiple   distinct priors (supplied via prior_generator generated   automatically); two-way ANOVA tests effects clone   size prior posterior mean. prior_generator   supplied, function runs K=1 original model first,   creates informative alternative priors centered   \(\bar{\theta}_1 \pm 3 \, \mathrm{SD}_1\) standard deviation   equal K=1 posterior SD. location-shift approach ensures   alternative priors genuinely pull posterior away   MLE low K, creating detectable prior effect disappears   high K estimable parameters. ANOVA classification   cross-validated eigenvalue scaled-variance diagnostics   guard false negatives original prior already   sufficiently diffuse. Warm starting.   Setting update_prior = TRUE passes posterior mean   covariance clone K initial values proposal covariance   clone K+1. substantially improves sampling efficiency   high K, posterior becomes narrow sampler starting   prior region waste iterations adaptation. Numerical considerations.   large K cloned log-likelihood \(K \cdot \ell(\theta)\) can   overflow -Inf; function validates cloned LP   finite initial values skips K warning .   Fisher information matrix estimated   \((\hat{\theta}) = [K \cdot \Sigma_K]^{-1}\); condition   number asymptotic covariance exceeds   \(1/\sqrt{\epsilon_{\mathrm{mach}}}\), pseudoinverse via SVD   used instead. code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ data(demonsnacks) y <- log(demonsnacks$Calories) X <- cbind(1, as.matrix(log(demonsnacks[,c(1,4,10)]+1))) J <- ncol(X) for (j in 2:J) X[,j] <- CenterScale(X[,j])  mon.names <- c("LP","sigma") parm.names <- as.parm.names(list(beta=rep(0,J), sigma=0)) pos.beta <- grep("beta", parm.names) pos.sigma <- grep("sigma", parm.names) PGF <- function(Data) {      beta <- rnorm(Data$J)      sigma <- runif(1)      return(c(beta, sigma))      } MyData <- list(J=J, PGF=PGF, X=X, mon.names=mon.names,      parm.names=parm.names, pos.beta=pos.beta, pos.sigma=pos.sigma, y=y)  Model <- function(parm, Data)      {      beta <- parm[Data$pos.beta]      sigma <- interval(parm[Data$pos.sigma], 1e-100, Inf)      parm[Data$pos.sigma] <- sigma      beta.prior <- sum(dnormv(beta, 0, 1000, log=TRUE))      sigma.prior <- dhalfcauchy(sigma, 25, log=TRUE)      mu <- tcrossprod(Data$X, t(beta))      LL <- sum(dnorm(Data$y, mu, sigma, log=TRUE))      LP <- LL + beta.prior + sigma.prior      Modelout <- list(LP=LP, Dev=-2*LL, Monitor=LP,           yhat=rnorm(length(mu), mu, sigma), parm=parm)      return(Modelout)      }  Initial.Values <- GIV(Model, MyData, PGF=TRUE) } # }

code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ library(lucifer) data(demonsnacks) y <- log(demonsnacks$Calories) X <- cbind(1, as.matrix(log(demonsnacks[,10] + 1))) J <- ncol(X) for (j in 2:J) X[,j] <- CenterScale(X[,j])  mon.names <- "mu[1]" parm.names <- as.parm.names(list(beta = rep(0, J), sigma = 0)) pos.beta <- grep("beta", parm.names) pos.sigma <- grep("sigma", parm.names) PGF <- function(Data) c(rnorm(Data$J), runif(1)) MyData <- list(J = J, PGF = PGF, X = X, mon.names = mon.names,      parm.names = parm.names, pos.beta = pos.beta,      pos.sigma = pos.sigma, y = y)  Model <- function(parm, Data) {      beta <- parm[Data$pos.beta]      sigma <- interval(parm[Data$pos.sigma], 1e-100, Inf)      parm[Data$pos.sigma] <- sigma      beta.prior <- sum(dnormv(beta, 0, 1000, log = TRUE))      sigma.prior <- dhalfcauchy(sigma, 25, log = TRUE)      mu <- tcrossprod(Data$X, t(beta))      LL <- sum(dnorm(Data$y, mu, sigma, log = TRUE))      LP <- LL + beta.prior + sigma.prior      list(LP = LP, Dev = -2*LL, Monitor = mu[1],           yhat = rnorm(length(mu), mu, sigma), parm = parm) }  Initial.Values <- rep(0, J + 1)  # Adaptive Gauss-Hermite Fit <- IterativeQuadrature(Model, Initial.Values, MyData, Covar = NULL,      Iterations = 100, Algorithm = "AGH",      Specs = list(N = 5, Nmax = 7, Packages = NULL, Dyn.libs = NULL),      CPUs = 1)  # Adaptive Gauss-Hermite Sparse Grid Fit <- IterativeQuadrature(Model, Initial.Values, MyData, Covar = NULL,      Iterations = 100, Algorithm = "AGHSG",      Specs = list(K = 5, Kmax = 7, Packages = NULL, Dyn.libs = NULL),      CPUs = 1)  # Componentwise Adaptive Gauss-Hermite Fit <- IterativeQuadrature(Model, Initial.Values, MyData, Covar = NULL,      Iterations = 100, Algorithm = "CAGH",      Specs = list(N = 3, Nmax = 10, Packages = NULL, Dyn.libs = NULL),      CPUs = 1)  print(Fit) summary(Fit) plot(Fit, MyData, PDF = FALSE)  Pred <- predict(Fit, Model, MyData, CPUs = 1) summary(Pred, Discrep = "Chi-Square") plot(Pred, Style = "Fitted") } # }

code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ library(lucifer) data(demonsnacks) y <- log(demonsnacks$Calories) X <- cbind(1, as.matrix(log(demonsnacks[,10] + 1))) J <- ncol(X) for (j in 2:J) X[,j] <- CenterScale(X[,j])  mon.names <- "mu[1]" parm.names <- as.parm.names(list(beta = rep(0, J), sigma = 0)) pos.beta <- grep("beta", parm.names) pos.sigma <- grep("sigma", parm.names) PGF <- function(Data) c(rnorm(Data$J), runif(1)) MyData <- list(J = J, PGF = PGF, X = X, mon.names = mon.names,      parm.names = parm.names, pos.beta = pos.beta,      pos.sigma = pos.sigma, y = y)  Model <- function(parm, Data) {      beta <- parm[Data$pos.beta]      sigma <- interval(parm[Data$pos.sigma], 1e-100, Inf)      parm[Data$pos.sigma] <- sigma      beta.prior <- sum(dnormv(beta, 0, 1000, log = TRUE))      sigma.prior <- dhalfcauchy(sigma, 25, log = TRUE)      mu <- tcrossprod(Data$X, t(beta))      LL <- sum(dnorm(Data$y, mu, sigma, log = TRUE))      LP <- LL + beta.prior + sigma.prior      list(LP = LP, Dev = -2*LL, Monitor = mu[1],           yhat = rnorm(length(mu), mu, sigma), parm = parm) }  Initial.Values <- rep(0, J + 1) Fit <- LaplaceApproximation(Model, Initial.Values, Data = MyData,      Iterations = 100, Method = "SPG", CPUs = 1) print(Fit) summary(Fit) plot(Fit, MyData, PDF = FALSE)  # Fit$Covar is scaled (2.38^2/d) and submitted to lucifer as Covar. # Fit$Summary[,1] is submitted to lucifer as Initial.Values.  Pred <- predict(Fit, Model, MyData, CPUs = 1) summary(Pred, Discrep = "Chi-Square") plot(Pred, Style = "Fitted") } # }

code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ library(lucifer) data(demonsnacks) y <- log(demonsnacks$Calories) X <- cbind(1, as.matrix(log(demonsnacks[,c(1,4,10)]+1))) J <- ncol(X) for (j in 2:J) {X[,j] <- CenterScale(X[,j])}  mon.names <- "LP" parm.names <- as.parm.names(list(beta=rep(0,J), sigma=0)) pos.beta <- grep("beta", parm.names) pos.sigma <- grep("sigma", parm.names) PGF <- function(Data) return(c(rnormv(Data$J,0,10), rhalfcauchy(1,5))) MyData <- list(J=J, PGF=PGF, X=X, mon.names=mon.names,      parm.names=parm.names, pos.beta=pos.beta, pos.sigma=pos.sigma, y=y)  Model <- function(parm, Data)      {      beta <- parm[Data$pos.beta]      sigma <- interval(parm[Data$pos.sigma], 1e-100, Inf)      parm[Data$pos.sigma] <- sigma      beta.prior <- sum(dnormv(beta, 0, 1000, log=TRUE))      sigma.prior <- dhalfcauchy(sigma, 25, log=TRUE)      mu <- tcrossprod(Data$X, t(beta))      LL <- sum(dnorm(Data$y, mu, sigma, log=TRUE))      LP <- LL + beta.prior + sigma.prior      Modelout <- list(LP=LP, Dev=-2*LL, Monitor=LP,           yhat=rnorm(length(mu), mu, sigma), parm=parm)      return(Modelout)      }  set.seed(666) Initial.Values <- GIV(Model, MyData, PGF=TRUE) Model.Spec.Time(Model, Initial.Values, MyData) } # }

title: Neural ODE inference via Bayesian gradient matching — NODE
text: Fits neural ordinary differential equations (NODEs)   multivariate time series using two-stage Bayesian Neural Gradient   Matching (BNGM) approach Bonnaffe (2023). Stage 1 interpolates   variable sinusoidal neural network extracts analytical temporal   derivatives via chain rule. Stage 2 fits dual-pathway single-layer   perceptron (linear + exponential activations) explain per-capita growth   rates functions state variables, recovering interaction   structure (Jacobian) causal attribution (Geber contributions)   dynamical system without specifying functional form.

title: Neural ODE inference via Bayesian gradient matching — NODE
text: BNGM method decouples inverse problem dynamical systems two independent regression tasks, avoiding costly numerical ODE integration required standard NODE methods (Chen et al. 2018). makes 100-600 times faster standard NODE fitting achieving higher accuracy interaction recovery (Bonnaffe 2023, Table 1). Stage 1 (observation model): variable interpolated sinusoidal neural network \(\hat{y}_i(t) = \sum_{j=1}^{H} w_j \sin(\pi(t \cdot a_j + \phi_j))\), \(H\) number neurons parameters \((w_j, a_j, \phi_j)\) weights, learnable frequencies, phases. Unlike truncated Fourier series, frequencies optimized concentrate representational capacity frequencies actually present signal. temporal derivative \(d\hat{y}_i/dt = \sum_j w_j \pi a_j \cos(\pi(t a_j + \phi_j))\) available analytically, avoiding finite-difference noise amplification. Regularization uses Foresee Hagan (1997) marginal posterior approximation. Stage 2 (process model): per-capita growth rate \(r_i = (1/Y_i)(dY_i/dt)\) variable modeled function state variables using dual-pathway single-layer perceptron: \(f_{p,}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{lin}}^\top (\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{lin}} + \mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{lin}} \mathbf{x}) + \mathbf{v}_{\exp}^\top \exp(\mathbf{b}_{\exp} + \mathbf{W}_{\exp} \mathbf{x})\). linear pathway captures density-independent dynamics; exponential pathway captures nonlinear density-dependent interactions (predation saturation, competitive exclusion, Allee effects). Uncertainty quantification: stages use anchored Bayesian ensembles (Pearce et al. 2018): \(K\) random parameter initializations optimized independently via BFGS (parallelized OpenMP), best \(\rho K\) fraction retained. Ensemble spread provides approximate posterior uncertainty without MCMC sampling. Interaction inference: Jacobian matrix \(e_{ij} = \partial f_{p,} / \partial x_j\) gives effect variable \(j\) growth rate variable \(\) (positive = facilitation, negative = suppression). Geber method (Hairston et al. 2005) weights effects temporal variation explain, yielding normalized contributions \(\bar{c}_{ij}\) sum 1 per target variable. Limitations: method assumes dynamically important variables observed. Systems converge monotonically equilibrium without oscillations provide insufficient temporal variation reliable interaction recovery. Numerical differentiation amplifies observation noise, noisy data degrades process model observation model.

code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ library(lucifer) data(demonsnacks) y <- log(demonsnacks$Calories) X <- cbind(1, as.matrix(log(demonsnacks[,c(1,4,10)]+1))) J <- ncol(X) for (j in 2:J) X[,j] <- CenterScale(X[,j])  mon.names <- "LP" parm.names <- as.parm.names(list(beta=rep(0,J), sigma=0)) pos.beta <- grep("beta", parm.names) pos.sigma <- grep("sigma", parm.names) PGF <- function(Data) {      beta <- rnorm(Data$J)      sigma <- runif(1)      return(c(beta, sigma))      } MyData <- list(J=J, PGF=PGF, X=X, mon.names=mon.names,      parm.names=parm.names, pos.beta=pos.beta, pos.sigma=pos.sigma, y=y)  Model <- function(parm, Data)      {      beta <- parm[Data$pos.beta]      sigma <- interval(parm[Data$pos.sigma], 1e-100, Inf)      parm[Data$pos.sigma] <- sigma      beta.prior <- sum(dnormv(beta, 0, 1000, log=TRUE))      sigma.prior <- dhalfcauchy(sigma, 25, log=TRUE)      mu <- tcrossprod(Data$X, t(beta))      LL <- sum(dnorm(Data$y, mu, sigma, log=TRUE))      LP <- LL + beta.prior + sigma.prior      Modelout <- list(LP=LP, Dev=-2*LL, Monitor=LP,           yhat=rnorm(length(mu), mu, sigma), parm=parm)      return(Modelout)      }  set.seed(666) Initial.Values <- GIV(Model, MyData, PGF=TRUE) Fit <- PMC(Model, MyData, Initial.Values, Covar=NULL, Iterations=5,      Thinning=1, alpha=NULL, M=1, N=100, CPUs=1) Fit print(Fit) PosteriorChecks(Fit) caterpillar.plot(Fit, Parms="beta") plot(Fit, BurnIn=0, MyData, PDF=FALSE) Pred <- predict(Fit, Model, MyData, CPUs=1) summary(Pred, Discrep="Chi-Square") plot(Pred, Style="Fitted") } # }

code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ library(lucifer)  # Compare two models for normal data: # M1: known mean (mu = 0), estimate sigma # M2: estimate both mu and sigma # Data generated under M1 (true mean = 0), so M1 should be preferred # by the parsimony principle (Occam's razor via Bayes factors).  set.seed(42) y <- rnorm(30, mean = 0, sd = 2)  Model1 <- function(parm, Data) {     sigma <- interval(parm[1], 1e-100, Inf)     parm[1] <- sigma     LL <- sum(dnorm(Data$y, 0, sigma, log = TRUE))     LP <- LL + dhalfcauchy(sigma, 5, log = TRUE)     list(LP = LP, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = LP,          yhat = rnorm(Data$n, 0, sigma), parm = parm) }  Model2 <- function(parm, Data) {     mu <- parm[1]     sigma <- interval(parm[2], 1e-100, Inf)     parm[2] <- sigma     LL <- sum(dnorm(Data$y, mu, sigma, log = TRUE))     LP <- LL + dnorm(mu, 0, 10, log = TRUE) +           dhalfcauchy(sigma, 5, log = TRUE)     list(LP = LP, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = LP,          yhat = rnorm(Data$n, mu, sigma), parm = parm) }  Data1 <- list(y = y, n = length(y),               parm.names = "sigma", mon.names = "LP") Data2 <- list(y = y, n = length(y),               parm.names = c("mu", "sigma"), mon.names = "LP")  ps <- ProductSpace(     Models = list(M1 = Model1, M2 = Model2),     Data = list(M1 = Data1, M2 = Data2),     Iterations = 20000, Pilot.Iterations = 3000,     Chains = 2, CPUs = 2 )  print(ps) summary(ps) plot(ps) plot(ps, type = "trace") plot(ps, type = "bayes_factors") plot(ps, type = "complexity") } # }

title: Split R-hat convergence diagnostic — Rhat
text: split R-hat addresses two weaknesses classical R-hat. First, splitting chain half doubles number chains used -chain variance estimate, makes diagnostic sensitive non-stationarity within individual chains. Second, rank-normalizing draws computing R-hat ensures statistic well-defined even distributions heavy tails infinite variance. rank-normalization proceeds replacing draw corresponding standard normal quantile: $$z_r = \Phi^{-1}\!\left(\frac{r - 3/8}{S - 1/4}\right)$$ \(r\) rank draw among \(S\) draws across chains, \(\Phi^{-1}\) standard normal quantile function. fractional offset \(3/8\) Blom (1958) adjustment. rank-normalization, standard R-hat formula applied transformed, split chains: $$\hat{R} = \sqrt{\frac{\hat{V}}{W}}$$ \(W\) mean within-chain variance \(\hat{V} = \frac{n-1}{n}W + \frac{B}{n}\) \(B\) -chain variance. split R-hat 1.01 generally considered adequate applications. Values 1.05 strongly indicate non-convergence. x single chain (vector) single-chain demonoid, chain split half R-hat computed two halves. multi-chain input, chain split, yielding \(2M\) half-chains. minimum 100 draws per half-chain recommended.

Per-parameter Evans-Moshonov   calibration compares posterior marginal prior   predictive counterpart. Small p-values signal genuine conflict   prior data, suggesting prior concentrated   region data disfavor. Observation influence uses PSIS-LOO importance reweighting   quantify observation's impact posterior without refitting.   observation \(\), leave-one-importance weights   computed pointwise log-likelihoods, shift   posterior marginal moment estimated. Observations whose Pareto-k   diagnostic exceeds 0.7 flagged high-leverage points may   disproportionately drive posterior; k > 1.0 indicates   importance sampling approximation unreliable refitting   advised. Robust aggregation (Yao et al. 2018) combines multiple   models single predictive distribution using model weights.   Three methods available: Bayesian model averaging (BMA),   weights marginal likelihoods; stacking (Wolpert 1992; Yao et al.   2018), optimizes pointwise predictive performance via   leave-one-cross-validation; pseudo-BMA+ (Yao et al. 2018),   applies Bayesian bootstrap stabilize LOO-based BMA   weights. Stacking default targets predictive   accuracy rather posterior probability model correctness,   therefore robust M-open settings candidate model   true data-generating process.

title: Comprehensive posterior sensitivity analysis — RobustBayes
code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ # Simulate data for a simple linear regression set.seed(42) N <- 30 x <- rnorm(N) y <- 0.5 + 1.2 * x + rnorm(N, 0, 0.8)  # Data list with prior generative function for conflict module Data <- list(   mon.names = "LP",   parm.names = c("beta0", "beta1", "log.sigma"),   y = y, x = x, N = N,   PGF = function(Data) {     c(rnorm(1, 0, 10), rnorm(1, 0, 10), log(abs(rcauchy(1, 0, 5))))   } )  # Model with wide N(0,10) priors Model <- function(parm, Data) {   beta0 <- parm[1]; beta1 <- parm[2]; sigma <- exp(parm[3])   mu <- beta0 + beta1 * Data$x   LL <- sum(dnorm(Data$y, mu, sigma, log = TRUE))   LP <- LL + sum(dnorm(parm[1:2], 0, 10, log = TRUE)) +              dhalfcauchy(sigma, 5, log = TRUE)   yhat <- rnorm(Data$N, mu, sigma)   list(LP = LP, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = LP, yhat = yhat, parm = parm) }  # Fit with MCMC fit <- lucifer(Model, Data, Initial.Values = c(0, 0, 0),                Algorithm = "NUTS", Iterations = 5000, Status = 1000)  # Single-model sensitivity (power-scaling, conflict, influence) rb <- RobustBayes(fit, Model = Model, Data = Data) print(rb) summary(rb) plot(rb) plot(rb, type = "power") plot(rb, type = "influence")  # Multi-model: compare wide vs tight priors Model_tight <- function(parm, Data) {   beta0 <- parm[1]; beta1 <- parm[2]; sigma <- exp(parm[3])   mu <- beta0 + beta1 * Data$x   LL <- sum(dnorm(Data$y, mu, sigma, log = TRUE))   LP <- LL + sum(dnorm(parm[1:2], 0, 1, log = TRUE)) +              dhalfcauchy(sigma, 5, log = TRUE)   yhat <- rnorm(Data$N, mu, sigma)   list(LP = LP, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = LP, yhat = yhat, parm = parm) } fit2 <- lucifer(Model_tight, Data, Initial.Values = c(0, 0, 0),                 Algorithm = "NUTS", Iterations = 5000, Status = 1000)  rb2 <- RobustBayes(list(wide = fit, tight = fit2),                     Model = Model, Data = Data) plot(rb2, type = "divergence") plot(rb2, type = "weights") } # }

text: calibration iteration \(\): Draw \(\theta^* \sim p(\theta)\) prior. Simulate \(x^* \sim p(x \mid \theta^*)\). title: Simulation-based inference — SBI
text: Three method families available, training different quantity simulated pairs \((\theta_i, x_i)\) \(\theta_i \sim p(\theta)\) \(x_i \sim p(x \mid \theta_i)\). NPE (neural posterior estimation) directly approximates \(q_\phi(\theta \mid x) \approx p(\theta \mid x)\) using conditional density network. training, posterior samples observation \(x_o\) obtained single forward pass (amortized inference). recommended default. NLE (neural likelihood estimation) approximates \(q_\phi(x \mid \theta) \approx p(x \mid \theta)\), uses MCMC sample \(p(\theta \mid x_o) \propto q_\phi(x_o \mid \theta) p(\theta)\). trained neural likelihood wrapped Model(parm, Data) closure compatible lucifer, giving access 62 MCMC algorithms. NRE (neural ratio estimation) trains classifier distinguish joint pairs \((\theta, x) \sim p(\theta, x)\) marginal pairs \((\theta, x) \sim p(\theta)p(x)\). classifier logit approximates log likelihood--evidence ratio, used log-likelihood MCMC. Sequential variants (SNPE, SNLE, SNRE) refine proposal distribution multiple rounds, concentrating simulations near observed data improved sample efficiency. default backend uses C++ Mixture Density Network (MDN) SELU activations full Cholesky-parametrized covariances. problems ~20 parameters, optional torch backend provides normalizing flows. architectures trained Adam optimizer, gradient clipping, early stopping.

title: Stochastic differential equation model — SDE
text: Stochastic differential equation model core design bridge pattern: SDE() constructs   S3 object class sde_model encapsulates SDE   specification produces standard Model(parm, Data) closure.   closure internally dispatches C++ likelihood engines depending   model structure. user passes sde$Model,   sde$Data, sde$Initial.Values   lucifer, SMC, ABC   unchanged. Four likelihood engines available. "exact" method uses   closed-form Gaussian (OU, GBM, Vasicek) non-central chi-squared (CIR)   transition densities maximum speed accuracy. "euler"   method approximates transition density via Euler-Maruyama   discretization sub-stepping, treating transition Gaussian   mean \(x + f(x)\Delta t\) variance   \(g(x)^2 \Delta t\). "milstein" method adds   higher-order correction \(0.5 g g' (\Delta W^2 - \Delta t)\)   reduce discretization bias. "particle" method uses   bootstrap particle filter produce unbiased log-marginal-likelihood   estimate, suitable pseudo-marginal MCMC via non-Gaussian highly   nonlinear observation models. Jump-diffusion processes form   \(dX = f(X)\,dt + g(X)\,dW + J\,dN(\lambda)\) supported   specifying jump.rate jump.size. Jumps integrated   Euler-Maruyama, Milstein, particle filter engines. Parameter constraints specified parameter must   remain within specific range (e.g., positive scale parameters).   generated Model function calls interval   constrained parameter evaluating likelihood, returns   constrained values parm sampler tracks feasible   region. Without constraints, scale parameters initialized near zero can   produce degenerate likelihoods trap sampler. Algorithm choice. Euler, Milstein, particle-filter   likelihoods call user-supplied R functions (drift, diffusion) every   sub-step, making evaluation expensive. Gradient-based algorithms   (NUTS, HMCDA, HMC, MALA) multiply cost \(2d+1\) per   gradient evaluation number leapfrog steps per iteration.   SDE models, non-gradient samplers HARM, AMWG, twalk,   RAM produce comparable effective sample sizes fraction   wall-clock time. Reserve NUTS models user-supplied analytical   gradients via Grad argument lucifer,   low-dimensional models per-iteration cost acceptable.

title: Variational Bayes — VariationalBayes
text:
Variational Bayes (VB) family numerical approximation   algorithms deterministic posterior inference. core idea   posit tractable family distributions \(q(	heta; \lambda)\)   parameterized variational parameters \(\lambda\), minimize   Kullback-Leibler divergence \(\mathrm{KL}(q \| p)\)   approximation true posterior. Equivalently, VB maximizes   evidence lower bound (ELBO):   $$\mathcal{L}(\lambda) = \mathbb{E}_q[\log p(	heta, y)] -   \mathbb{E}_q[\log q(	heta; \lambda)]$$   first term expected joint log-density second   entropy approximation. VariationalBayes function provides eight general-purpose   algorithms spanning modern variational inference landscape: Salimans1 implements first algorithm Salimans   Knowles (2013), uses gradient information (Hessian).   precision matrix updated via outer product gradients,   \(P \leftarrow (1-w)P + w \, g g^	op\), making   \(O(J+1)\) Model evaluations per iteration rather   \(O(J^2/2)\) required Salimans2. preferred \(J\)   large posterior twice differentiable.   stochastic averaging convergence scheme Salimans2 used. Salimans2 implements second algorithm Salimans   Knowles (2013), using gradient Hessian stochastic   linear regression framework fixed-form Gaussian VB.   efficient method \(J\) small posterior   smooth. step size \(w = 1/\sqrt{T}\) \(T\)   total number iterations. Convergence checked second half   iterations Polyak averaging stabilizes. ADVI.mf implements mean-field variant Automatic   Differentiation Variational Inference (Kucukelbir et al., 2017).   variational family \(q(	heta) = \prod_j N(	heta_j;   \mu_j, \sigma_j^2)\) \(\sigma_j = \mathrm{softplus}(\omega_j)   = \log(1 + e^{\omega_j})\) unconstrained optimization. Gradients   estimated via reparameterization trick: draw   \(\epsilon \sim N(0,)\), set \(	heta = \mu + \sigma \odot   \epsilon\), differentiate sampling. Optimization   uses Adam (Kingma Ba, 2015) default learning rate 0.01. ADVI.fr implements full-rank variant ADVI, replacing   diagonal covariance \(q(	heta) = N(\mu, LL^	op)\)   \(L\) lower-triangular Cholesky factor. diagonal   \(L\) parameterized softplus positivity.   captures posterior correlations cost \(J(J+1)/2\)   variational parameters. warning issued \(J > 50\) due   quadratic scaling. BBVI implements Black-Box Variational Inference (Ranganath   et al., 2014), uses score function (REINFORCE) estimator   rather reparameterization trick. gradient ELBO   estimated   \(
abla_\lambda \mathcal{L} \approx (1/S) \sum_s f_s   
abla_\lambda \log q(	heta_s; \lambda)\)   \(f_s = \log p(	heta_s, y) - \log q(	heta_s; \lambda)\).   Control variates (per-component baselines) reduce variance.   default uses \(S = 10\) Monte Carlo samples per iteration. SVGD implements Stein Variational Gradient Descent (Liu   Wang, 2016), particle-based method maintains \(K\) particles   updates via functional gradient KL divergence   reproducing kernel Hilbert space. update particle \(k\)   \(	heta_k \leftarrow 	heta_k + \epsilon \, \hat{\phi}^*(	heta_k)\)     \(\hat{\phi}^*(	heta) = (1/K) \sum_j [k(	heta_j, 	heta)   
abla_{	heta_j} \log p(	heta_j, y) + 
abla_{	heta_j}   k(	heta_j, 	heta)]\)   RBF kernel median heuristic bandwidth. default uses   \(K = 20\) particles. method can capture multimodal posteriors   requires \(K 	imes (J+1)\) Model evaluations per iteration. NGD implements Natural Gradient Variational Inference (Amari,   1998; Khan Lin, 2017) mean-field Gaussian family. Natural   gradients account Fisher information geometry   variational family, yielding faster convergence ordinary   gradients. natural parameters \((\eta_1 = \Sigma^{-1}\mu,\;   \eta_2 = -	frac{1}{2}\Sigma^{-1})\) updated Robbins-Monro   schedule \(ho_t = (t + 	au)^{-\alpha}\) \(	au = 10\)   \(\alpha = 0.75\). structurally related Salimans2   information-geometric interpretation different   step-size scheduling. Pathfinder implements quasi-Newton variational inference   method Zhang et al. (2022). Rather iteratively optimizing   variational parameters, Pathfinder runs L-BFGS optimization   log-posterior, stores full trajectory \(\{	heta_k, 
abla_k\}\),   iterate reconstructs L-BFGS inverse Hessian   approximation \(H_k\) define Gaussian approximation   \(q_k(	heta) = N(	heta_k, H_k)\). ELBO estimated   iterate best approximation \(k^* = \arg\max_k   	ext{ELBO}_k\) selected. multi-path mode (default,   \(M = 4\) paths), multiple independent L-BFGS runs launched   jittered initial values, resulting draws pooled   mixture \(q(	heta) = (1/M) \sum_m N(	heta_m, H_m)\), importance   weights \(\log p(	heta) - \log q(	heta)\) computed,   Pareto smoothed importance sampling (PSIS) applied produce   final posterior draws. Pareto \(\hat{k}\) diagnostic quantifies   quality approximation: values 0.5 indicate reliable   estimates, 0.5–0.7 acceptable, 0.7–1.0 questionable,   values 1.0 signal approximation unreliable.   Pathfinder typically requires 1–2 orders magnitude fewer gradient   evaluations ADVI producing comparable sample quality.   number paths controlled Covar (integer, default 4);   set Covar = 1 single-path mode. Method selection guidance. small \(J\) (fewer   ~20 parameters) smooth posteriors, Salimans2   NGD recommended. moderate \(J\) (20–100),   ADVI.mf Salimans1 avoid quadratic cost   Hessian. ADVI.fr appropriate posterior correlations   important \(J \le 50\). BBVI generic   (requiring sampling density evaluation \(q\)),   higher variance. SVGD uniquely suited   multimodal posteriors expensive per iteration.   Pathfinder recommended starting point problems:   fast, captures correlations via L-BFGS inverse Hessian,   Pareto k diagnostic indicates approximation   unreliable.

title: Variational Bayes — VariationalBayes
code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ library(lucifer)  # Setup: regression on demonsnacks data data(demonsnacks) y <- log(demonsnacks$Calories) X <- cbind(1, as.matrix(log(demonsnacks[,10]+1))) J <- ncol(X) for (j in 2:J) X[,j] <- CenterScale(X[,j])  mon.names <- "mu[1]" parm.names <- as.parm.names(list(beta=rep(0,J), sigma=0)) pos.beta <- grep("beta", parm.names) pos.sigma <- grep("sigma", parm.names) PGF <- function(Data) {      beta <- rnorm(Data$J)      sigma <- runif(1)      return(c(beta, sigma))      } MyData <- list(J=J, PGF=PGF, X=X, mon.names=mon.names,      parm.names=parm.names, pos.beta=pos.beta, pos.sigma=pos.sigma, y=y)  Model <- function(parm, Data) {      beta <- parm[Data$pos.beta]      sigma <- interval(parm[Data$pos.sigma], 1e-100, Inf)      parm[Data$pos.sigma] <- sigma      beta.prior <- sum(dnormv(beta, 0, 1000, log=TRUE))      sigma.prior <- dhalfcauchy(sigma, 25, log=TRUE)      mu <- tcrossprod(Data$X, t(beta))      LL <- sum(dnorm(Data$y, mu, sigma, log=TRUE))      LP <- LL + beta.prior + sigma.prior      list(LP=LP, Dev=-2*LL, Monitor=mu[1],           yhat=rnorm(length(mu), mu, sigma), parm=parm)      }  IV <- rep(0, J+1)  # Fixed-form VB (Salimans2, default) Fit1 <- VariationalBayes(Model, IV, Data=MyData, Iterations=1000,      Method="Salimans2", Stop.Tolerance=1e-3) print(Fit1)  # ADVI mean-field Fit2 <- VariationalBayes(Model, IV, Data=MyData, Iterations=1000,      Method="ADVI.mf", Stop.Tolerance=1e-3) print(Fit2)  # SVGD with 20 particles Fit3 <- VariationalBayes(Model, IV, Data=MyData, Iterations=500,      Method="SVGD", Covar=20, Stop.Tolerance=1e-3) print(Fit3)  # Pathfinder with 4 paths (default) Fit4 <- VariationalBayes(Model, IV, Data=MyData, Iterations=1000,      Method="Pathfinder", Covar=4, Stop.Tolerance=1e-5) print(Fit4) summary(Fit4) } # }

what: Coupled MCMC for unbiased estimation — coupled_mcmc
title: Coupled MCMC for unbiased estimation — coupled_mcmc
text: Runs two coupled Markov chains using reflection-maximal   coupling Gaussian random-walk proposals. chains meet   random time \(\tau\), remain coupled forever, enabling unbiased   posterior expectations via debiasing formula Jacob, O'Leary   Atchade (2020) convergence diagnostics meeting-time   distribution.

title: Coupled MCMC for unbiased estimation — coupled_mcmc
code: coupled_mcmc(   Model,   Data,   Initial.Values = NULL,   Covar = NULL,   max_iterations = 10000,   k = 0,   m = 0,   tol = 1e-08,   verbose = FALSE )

title: Coupled MCMC for unbiased estimation — coupled_mcmc
text: Model Model function signature function(parm, Data) returning list least LP (log posterior), Dev (deviance), Monitor, yhat, parm. Data named list data. Must contain parm.names. Initial.Values Numeric vector starting parameter values. NULL, zero vector length length(Data$parm.names) used. Covar Proposal covariance matrix. NULL (default), identity matrix scaled \((2.38)^2 / d\) used, following optimal Gaussian random-walk scaling Roberts, Gelman Gilks (1997). max_iterations Maximum number iterations algorithm gives waiting chains meet. Default 10000. k Lag parameter debiasing estimator. estimator uses samples iteration k onward, larger values discard burn-. Default 0. m Number additional iterations run chains met, providing extra samples variance reduction. Must satisfy \(m \geq k\). Default 0. tol Tolerance detecting two chains met, .e., \(\|X_t - Y_t\|_\infty < \texttt{tol}\). Default 1e-8. verbose Logical. TRUE, progress messages printed console via message(). Default FALSE.

title: Coupled MCMC for unbiased estimation — coupled_mcmc
text: object class "coupled_mcmc" containing: meeting_time Integer. iteration chains first met,     NA meet within max_iterations. met Logical. Whether chains met. samples_X Numeric matrix dimension (T x d) storing     full trajectory chain \(X\). samples_Y Numeric matrix dimension (T-1 x d) storing     trajectory chain \(Y\) (lagged 1 relative \(X\)). log_posterior_X Numeric vector log-posterior values chain     \(X\). log_posterior_Y Numeric vector log-posterior values chain     \(Y\). k lag parameter used. m post-meeting extension used. parm.names Parameter names Data$parm.names. call matched call. minutes Wall-clock time minutes.

title: Coupled MCMC for unbiased estimation — coupled_mcmc
text: algorithm runs two Metropolis-Hastings chains \((X_t)\) \((Y_t)\) shared proposal covariance \(\Sigma\). chain \(Y\) initialized one step behind \(X\) (lag 1). iteration, reflection-maximal coupling proposal kernels ensures proposals chains agree highest possible probability. Specifically, given current states \(x\) \(y\), proposal \(z \sim N(x, \Sigma)\) drawn chain \(X\). probability $$p = \min\left(1, \frac{N(z; y, \Sigma)}{N(z; x, \Sigma)}\right)$$ proposal \(z\) used chain \(Y\); otherwise reflection standardized innovation across separating hyperplane \(x\) \(y\) generates residual proposal \(Y\). chain independently accepts rejects via standard Metropolis-Hastings ratio. chains meet time \(\tau\) (.e., \(X_\tau = Y_{\tau-1}\)), set equal evolve identically thereafter. meeting time \(\tau\) random variable whose distribution characterizes mixing rate underlying kernel. debiasing estimator function \(h\) $$H_k = h(X_k) + \sum_{t=k+1}^{\tau-1} \left[ h(X_t) - h(Y_{t-1}) \right]$$ unbiased estimator \(E_\pi[h(X)]\) regardless choice burn-\(k\), provided \(E[\tau] < \infty\). \(m > k\), time-averaged estimator $$H_{k:m} = \frac{1}{m - k + 1} \sum_{l=k}^{m} H_l$$ lower variance.

title: Coupled MCMC for unbiased estimation — coupled_mcmc
text: Jacob, P. E., O'Leary, J. Atchade, Y. F. (2020). Unbiased Markov chain Monte Carlo methods couplings. Journal Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 82(3), 543–600. doi:10.1111/rssb.12336 Roberts, G. O., Gelman, . Gilks, W. R. (1997). Weak convergence optimal scaling random walk Metropolis algorithms. Annals Applied Probability, 7(1), 110–120. doi:10.1214/aoap/1034625254

text: ExGaussian distribution arises sum independent   normal exponential random variables: \(X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\)   \(Y \sim \mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)\),   \(Z = X + Y\) follows ExGaussian distribution density   $$f(z) = \frac{\lambda}{2} \exp\left(\frac{\lambda}{2}(2\mu +   \lambda\sigma^2 - 2z)\right)   \mathrm{erfc}\left(\frac{\mu + \lambda\sigma^2 - z}{\sigma\sqrt{2}}   \right)$$   \(\mathrm{erfc}\) complementary error function.   mean \(\mu + 1/\lambda\) variance   \(\sigma^2 + 1/\lambda^2\). distribution   widely used reaction time modeling chromatographic peak fitting. Implementation dexgaussian. Refer package vignettes cited references complete algorithmic mathematical description. Implementation pexgaussian. u} \Omega^{-1}(X - M)\Sigma^{-1}(X - M)^T|   ^{-(

title: lucifer — lucifer
code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ library(lucifer) set.seed(666)  ## ----- Synthetic Gaussian linear regression --------------------------- ## The simplest Bayesian model that every MCMC sampler in lucifer can ## fit: an unconstrained intercept, an unconstrained slope, and a ## log-transformed scale so that all three parameters live in R and ## gradient-based samplers (HMC, NUTS, MALA, RMHMC, ...) never collide ## with a positivity boundary. N <- 100 ground_truth <- c(beta0 = 1, beta1 = 2, log.sigma = log(0.5)) X <- cbind(1, rnorm(N)) y <- as.vector(X %*% ground_truth[c("beta0", "beta1")]) +      rnorm(N, 0, exp(ground_truth["log.sigma"]))  ## Data list with PGF for random initial values via GIV() PGF <- function(Data) c(rnorm(2, 0, 1), log(runif(1, 0.1, 1))) Data <- list(N = N, J = 2, X = X, y = y,              mon.names = "LP",              parm.names = c("beta0", "beta1", "log.sigma"),              PGF = PGF)  ## Model specification (Gaussian likelihood, vague Gaussian priors) Model <- function(parm, Data) {      beta  <- parm[1:2]      sigma <- exp(parm[3])      mu    <- as.vector(Data$X %*% beta)      LL    <- sum(dnorm(Data$y, mu, sigma, log = TRUE))      LP    <- LL +               sum(dnorm(beta, 0, 10, log = TRUE)) +               dnorm(parm[3], 0, 1, log = TRUE)      list(LP = LP, Dev = -2 * LL, Monitor = LP,           yhat = rnorm(length(mu), mu, sigma), parm = parm) }  IV <- GIV(Model, Data, PGF = TRUE)  ## ----- Canonical workflow (illustrated with NUTS) --------------------- fit <- lucifer(Model, Data, IV,                Iterations = 2000, Status = 1000, Thinning = 2,                Algorithm = "NUTS", Chains = 3) plot(fit) ppc <- predict(fit, Model = Model, Data = Data) plot(ppc, Style = "Fitted", Data = Data) ppc_dens_overlay(ppc) plot(fit, ground_truth = ground_truth)  ## ----- Sweep over every MCMC algorithm with default specifications ---- ## The vector below enumerates every sampler in lucifer that runs with ## Specs = NULL on a continuous, unconstrained Gaussian target. ## Excluded: ##   * algorithms whose Specs are intrinsically mandatory (AGG, GG, IM, ##     RJ, RSS, SAMWG, SMWG, USAMWG, USMWG, SGLD, SGHMC) and MCMCMC ##     (which needs CPUs > 1 inside Specs); ##   * Polya-Gamma data augmentation (PG), which is restricted to ##     logistic / binomial regression and cannot fit a Gaussian ##     likelihood; ##   * NeuTra and flowMC, which require the torch package. ## All of these are documented in ## vignette("mcmc-algorithms", package = "lucifer"). algos <- c(      ## Random-walk and adaptive Metropolis      "RWM", "AM", "AMM", "RAM", "DRM", "DRAM", "DA", "MTM", "RDMH",      "INCA", "PMCMC",      ## Componentwise and Gibbs samplers      "MWG", "AMWG", "ADMG", "Gibbs", "Zanella",      ## Hamiltonian Monte Carlo      "HMC", "AHMC", "NUTS", "HMCDA", "THMC", "MCHMC", "MEADS",      "autoMALA", "MALT", "AAPS", "GIST",      ## Langevin and stochastic gradient      "MALA", "Barker", "NROLangevin",      ## Slice samplers      "Slice", "AFSS", "ESS", "OHSS", "UESS", "QSS", "LSS", "GPSS",      ## Ensemble and population      "AIES", "DEMC", "DREAM", "Zeus", "twalk",      ## Quadratic Monte Carlo      "QMC", "QMC3", "QMCN", "DQMC", "SQMC", "MAMC", "SAMC", "WMC",      ## Hit-and-run and directional      "HARM", "CHARM", "Refractive",      ## Multimodal and tempering      "NRPT", "SimTemp", "NRST", "WL",      ## Piecewise-deterministic Markov processes      "ZigZag", "BPS", "Boomerang", "RHMC",      ## Riemannian and geometric      "RMHMC", "LMC", "MHMC", "Relativistic",      ## Constraint-handling and infinite-dimensional      "ProjLang", "ProxMCMC", "pCN")  for (alg in algos) {      fit <- lucifer(Model, Data, IV,                     Iterations = 2000, Status = 1000, Thinning = 2,                     Algorithm = alg, Specs = NULL, Chains = 3)      plot(fit)      ppc <- predict(fit, Model = Model, Data = Data)      plot(ppc, Style = "Fitted", Data = Data)      ppc_dens_overlay(ppc)      plot(fit, ground_truth = ground_truth) } } # }

text: function requires rjags package (working   JAGS installation) available. Unlike Stan, JAGS automatically compute pointwise   log-likelihoods. enable LOO() WAIC(), include   pointwise log-density nodes model monitor , pass   resulting matrix via log_lik. Alternatively, compute   pointwise log-likelihoods posterior samples fitting. title: Fit a JAGS model and return a lucifer demonoid object — lucifer_jags
code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ jags_code <- " model {   for (i in 1:N) {     y[i] ~ dnorm(mu, tau)   }   mu ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)   tau ~ dgamma(0.001, 0.001)   sigma <- 1 / sqrt(tau) } "  data_list <- list(N = 100, y = rnorm(100, 3, 2)) fit <- lucifer_jags(     jags_code = jags_code,     data = data_list,     parameters.to.save = c("mu", "sigma"),     n.iter = 10000 )  # Full lucifer post-processing print(fit) summary(fit) plot(fit) } # }

title: Fit a Stan model and return a lucifer demonoid object — lucifer_stan
code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ stan_code <- " data {   int<lower=0> N;   vector[N] y; } parameters {   real mu;   real<lower=0> sigma; } model {   mu ~ normal(0, 10);   sigma ~ cauchy(0, 5);   y ~ normal(mu, sigma); } generated quantities {   vector[N] log_lik;   for (n in 1:N)     log_lik[n] = normal_lpdf(y[n] | mu, sigma); } "  data_list <- list(N = 100, y = rnorm(100, 3, 2)) fit <- lucifer_stan(stan_code = stan_code, data = data_list)  # Full lucifer post-processing print(fit) summary(fit) plot(fit)  # Model comparison LOO(log_lik(fit)) } # }

title: Configure parallelization thread budget — lucifer_threads
text: total Integer total CPUs use. NULL (default), detects automatically via parallel::detectCores(logical = FALSE). omp Integer OpenMP threads per process. Overrides automatic allocation strategy. Set 1 disable OpenMP threading within chains. chains Integer number parallel chain workers. Overrides automatic allocation strategy. strategy Character string controlling allocation strategy: "auto" Distributes threads evenly chains     OpenMP. 8 CPUs 4 chains, chain gets 2 OpenMP threads.     recommended default. "chains_only" CPUs chain parallelism, chain     runs single-threaded (legacy behavior). Safest option systems     threaded BLAS. "omp_only" CPUs OpenMP within single chain     process. Chains run sequentially. Best running single chain     large data. "balanced" "auto".

title: Configure parallelization thread budget — lucifer_threads
text: named list components total_cpus, omp_threads,   chain_workers, strategy (invisibly setting,   visibly querying).

title: Configure parallelization thread budget — lucifer_threads
text: called arguments, returns current settings named list without modifying anything. arguments provided, updates global thread budget applies OpenMP thread count immediately via omp_set_num_threads(). budget respected lucifer, Kfold, SBI, VariationalBayes (Pathfinder), ABC using parallel dispatch. setting respects _R_CHECK_LIMIT_CORES_ environment variable (used CRAN) OMP_THREAD_LIMIT set.

title: Declarative probabilistic model specification — model_spec
text: Two-phase compilation. system first parses notation   structured intermediate representation (IR) classifies   every variable data, parameter, hyperparameter, infers   constraints distribution support, validates consistency.   IR compiled R code following exact patterns used   lucifer Model functions: parameter extraction parm   vector, constraint application via interval, log-prior   computation, deterministic relationships, log-likelihood, posterior   assembly, five-element return list. Parameterization convention. distribution name maps   exactly one parameterization eliminate ambiguity. Normal(mu,   sigma) uses standard deviation; NormalV(mu, var) uses   variance; NormalP(mu, prec) uses precision. full mapping   table documented package vignette. Scope. DSL handles majority common Bayesian   models: GLMs, hierarchical models, multivariate models standard   priors link functions. Models requiring recursive time indexing,   mixture allocation, missing data augmentation, complex control flow   written manually. code() method provides   scaffold can copied extended cases.

Bivariate probability regions may plotted joint.pr.plot function. p.interval function may return different probability intervals: quantile-based probability interval, unimodal Highest Posterior Density (HPD) interval, multimodal HPD intervals. Another type probability interval Lowest Posterior Loss (LPL) interval, calculated LPL.interval function. quantile-based probability interval used commonly, possibly simple, fastest calculate, invariant transformation, closely resembles frequentist confidence interval. lower upper bounds quantile-based probability interval calculated quantile function. 95% quantile-based probability interval reports values posterior probability distribution indicate 2.5% 97.5% quantiles, contain central 95% distribution. quantile-based probability interval centered around median equal-sized tails. Otherwise, HPD interval smallest interval, estimated interval contains highest posterior density. Unlike quantile-based probability interval, HPD interval one-tailed two-tailed, whichever appropriate. text: ten plot types : "convergence" Posterior mean +/- SE vs K (log scale).     primary diagnostic assessing MLE convergence. "eigenvalue" Standardized largest eigenvalue ratio     vs K 1/K reference line. Departure 1/K indicates     non-identifiability. "scaled_variance" log(K * Var_K) vs log(K) per     parameter. Horizontal indicates estimability. "density" Overlaid posterior densities K.     Higher K values opaque. "trace" Trace plots final K run. Delegates     plot.demonoid. "pairs" Bivariate posterior scatter max-K     run MLE overlay. "profile" Profile likelihood curves computed     demand. Requires Model Data .... "estimability" Per-parameter posterior means     different priors K (requires n_priors > 1). "prior_sensitivity" Forest plot MLE +/- SE     prior highest K (requires n_priors > 1). "diagnostics" Multi-panel dashboard. Row 1: convergence     eigenvalue. Row 2: scaled variance density.     n_priors > 1, third row added prior sensitivity     estimability (3x2 grid).
